title: WhatsApp Business or an online store? How to choose—and when to use both
description: Choose between WhatsApp Business and an online store around your products, customers and order workflow—with a practical checklist for using both.
body:
**You do not need to stop selling on WhatsApp to add an online store.** Keep a chat-led process if it suits your products and customers. Consider adding a storefront when buyers should be able to choose an item, provide the required details and place an order without waiting for you to repeat the same steps. Use both when customers need conversation before or after a structured purchase.

The question is not which channel looks more professional. It is **which part of the order still depends on you being available—and whether that dependence is useful or avoidable.**

## First, compare the tools you actually have

WhatsApp Business is not just an ordinary chat thread with a business name. Its app includes a catalogue, collections, quick replies and labels. Customers can put catalogue items into a cart and send their selection as one message. Those tools can make a small shop's existing process easier. [WhatsApp Business features](https://whatsappbusiness.com/products/business-app-features/)

An online store is not automatically a complete business-management system either. Before choosing one, check which product options, payment methods, stock rules, delivery tools and order records it actually provides—and which require another service or manual work.

This guide compares a chat-led selling workflow with a self-service storefront. If you already use additional software or custom integrations, include those capabilities and costs in your own comparison.

## When keeping WhatsApp at the centre makes sense

Conversation can be part of the product, not a problem to eliminate.

A seller making a one-off commission may need to discuss dimensions, materials and a deadline before giving a price. A repeat buyer may know exactly what they want and prefer a short message. Moving either person through an unnecessarily rigid checkout could add work rather than remove it.

Your current process may be sufficient if you can reliably answer these questions:

- What has each customer agreed to buy?
- Which options, personalisation and delivery date did you confirm?
- Has the order been accepted, and has the payment actually arrived?
- Can you find that information without relying on memory?
- Can someone else continue the order if you are unavailable?

There is no universal order count at which every business needs a website. A handful of complex commissions can require more coordination than many identical ready-made items. Start with the failure you want to prevent, not a number someone attached to a growth chart.

## When a storefront becomes useful

A storefront is worth evaluating when the same information has to be collected repeatedly: the product, its available option, quantity, customer details and delivery choice.

Look for recurring friction. Buyers wait for prices already decided. You retype delivery information. A chosen size gets separated from the address message. Someone places an order while another person is updating a stock sheet. None of these automatically proves a platform will fix the problem—but each gives you a specific task to test before committing.

Choose a platform by performing those tasks on a phone. Do not judge it only by its homepage or a long feature list.

| Decision to test | Staying chat-led | Adding a storefront |
|---|---|---|
| Does the buyer need advice before choosing? | Keep the conversation easy to reach. | Make help available without interrupting every straightforward purchase. |
| Can the product be described with a clear price and options? | Use a consistent product reference in the conversation. | Test the actual option-selection and price display. |
| Where is the agreed order recorded? | Choose a dependable record rather than scattered messages. | Check what the order captures and what the merchant can correct. |
| How is payment confirmed? | Define who checks receipt and records it. | Check the difference between gateway status and a manual transfer claim. |
| Who maintains availability? | Make responsibility explicit. | Test stock behaviour; do not assume every platform handles it identically. |
| How will the customer find help? | Keep response expectations clear. | Provide a contact route alongside the buying flow. |

## A handmade-shop example: keep the conversation, standardise the order

Imagine a seller offering ready-made crochet keychains and made-to-order bouquets. This is an illustrative workflow, not a measured customer case.

For a ready-made keychain, the customer may only need the available colour, quantity, delivery information and a way to order. A clear product page could handle that selection while the seller is busy making another item.

A bouquet may need a conversation about colours, an occasion and production time. Keep that discussion. Once the details are agreed, record them in a supported order workflow that both sides can check. Do not force custom requirements into a generic product option if the system cannot preserve them accurately.

The useful division is not “WhatsApp for marketing, website for everything else.” It is **conversation where judgement is needed, and a consistent record where repeating details creates mistakes.**

## An order request is not the same as confirmed payment

A customer choosing products, submitting an order or uploading a transfer screenshot represents a different event from the merchant confirming receipt of money.

Whatever channel you use, make those states clear. Tell the buyer whether their order is awaiting confirmation, payment or fulfilment. Do not promise dispatch merely because a screenshot was submitted.

oBizee's direct-payment workflow separates the customer's payment claim from the merchant's confirmation or dispute. That distinction matters when evaluating a store: adding a website does not remove the merchant's responsibility to check a manual transfer. Availability and configuration must still be checked for your account.

If you use an integrated payment provider, follow the supported payment-status workflow instead. Do not assume that manual transfers and gateway payments have the same confirmation process.

## Prepare the catalogue before changing your buying link

A website cannot clarify information the business has not decided yet. Prepare a small, representative set of products before moving customers to a new checkout.

For each one, gather:

1. A specific name and a photograph showing what the customer receives.
2. The current price and any option that changes it.
3. The available choices, with unavailable combinations handled clearly.
4. What is included—and what is not.
5. Production or dispatch expectations, especially for made-to-order items.
6. Delivery charges or the point at which the customer can see them.
7. Relevant cancellation, return or customisation conditions.

Keep claims and images truthful. If a photo shows several pieces but the listing sells one, explain that beside the buying decision. If an item needs discussion before acceptance, make that visible instead of letting the buyer discover it after paying.

## Move gradually rather than changing every link at once

**Start with one ordinary buying journey.** Open the proposed store on your phone, find a product, choose an option, change the quantity and check the delivery and payment information. Use the platform's safe testing process; do not create an unintended real transaction.

**Check the merchant side as well.** Can you see the selected option and customer details? Is payment status understandable? Can you explain what happens next to the buyer? A successful button click is not enough if the order record is unclear.

**Share the specific page when appropriate.** A buyer asking about a particular product should not have to search an unrelated homepage. Keep a clear route back to you for questions.

**Retain a way to help hesitant customers.** Explain the new ordering process without telling people their preferred way of contacting you is wrong. Use repeated questions to improve the product information.

**Only then change the main buying link.** Before a wider announcement, verify it from another device and check that an unfamiliar person can understand the next step without your explanation.

## Measure whether the change helped your shop

Do not borrow someone else's promise of saving five hours a day. Keep a simple log of a small set of comparable orders before and after the change.

Record the questions asked before purchase, missing details that required another message, corrections after the order, time spent processing it and whether the buyer completed the intended task. Note differences such as a festival rush or a shift from ready-made to customised products.

Treat the result as a practical signal, not a controlled experiment. If the new flow removes repeated questions but customers stop at delivery charges, improve delivery clarity. If the order record is clearer but support messages rise, inspect the wording and contact path.

More visitors or a more attractive page is not the whole result. The change should help suitable customers place an accurate order and help you fulfil it reliably.

## What does each option cost?

WhatsApp describes its Business app as free to download. That does not make every optional service or every hour spent operating a business free. [WhatsApp's app introduction](https://whatsappbusiness.com/resources/resource-library/small-business-use-whatsapp-business-app/)

For any storefront, check platform charges separately from payment-provider fees, shipping, domains, optional services and the time required to maintain your catalogue. Compare the same order value and the same required workflow, not two advertising headlines.

Use [oBizee's current pricing page](https://www.obizee.com/pricing/) for its commercial terms rather than relying on an old screenshot or a copied fee table.

## Choose the next step that fits

**Stay chat-led** if your process is reliable and consultation is central to the sale. Improve the record keeping before adding another tool simply because others have one.

**Add a storefront** if customers should be able to select and order defined products without waiting for routine replies. Test the features your products actually require.

**Use both** if you need conversation and a more structured purchase flow. A website does not have to replace the relationships you built in chat.

If you are considering oBizee, start by preparing one representative product and reviewing the [store-setup guide](https://www.obizee.com/how-to-create-online-store/). Check the resulting customer and merchant journeys before moving the rest of your catalogue.

The aim is not to stop talking to customers. It is to stop losing important order details between conversations.

title: DM2Buy vs oBizee: compare the work behind each order
description: Compare DM2Buy and oBizee around your catalogue, checkout, delivery and costs—and use a practical checklist before moving your store.
body:
**Choose based on the work you need your store to handle, not a table of green ticks.** If your current setup takes accurate orders and is manageable, switching may add work without solving a problem. If you repeatedly correct product selections, reconcile payments or copy order details between tools, test whether another setup improves those specific tasks.

This guide is published by oBizee, one of the products being compared. It is not an independent ranking. Competitor information below comes from public documentation, not a completed merchant-account test. Features, charges and eligibility can change.

## Start with a fair comparison

DM2Buy is not simply an Instagram inbox tool. Its published offering includes an online store, payments and catalogue/order management; some capabilities are plan-dependent. A comparison that dismisses it as having no website is a poor basis for a business decision. [DM2Buy product information](https://dm2buy.com/).

For oBizee, review the [current features](https://www.obizee.com/features/) and ask to see the workflow you need. A feature name on either site is the beginning of your evaluation, not proof that it handles your particular products, delivery area or payment arrangement.

Write down your three most frequent problems before opening a demo. Be specific: “Customers select a sold-out size” is useful. “I need a better platform” is too broad to test.

## 1. Test your difficult products, not just your easiest one

A catalogue can look attractive while still producing incomplete orders. Choose a small representative sample:

- A straightforward product with one price.
- A product with sizes or colours and different available quantities.
- A made-to-order item requiring customer instructions.
- An unavailable item that customers should not be able to order accidentally.

Check the images, selected option, final price, stock behaviour and instructions at each step. Does the order record preserve what the customer chose? Can the merchant distinguish two similar variants without returning to the conversation?

For a clothing seller, a useful test might compare two sizes where only one is available. For a personalised gift, check whether the required spelling or message reaches the merchant clearly. These are illustrative tests, not claims about a particular seller's results.

Do not reject a tool because a demonstration uses different terminology. Equally, do not accept “variants supported” without checking the combinations your catalogue needs.

## 2. Follow the payment and order states

Customer checkout is only part of the journey. Ask what happens when a payment is pending, fails or is claimed by the customer but has not been verified.

These states should not be treated as interchangeable:

| State | What it tells the merchant |
|---|---|
| Order submitted | An order request or record exists |
| Customer says they paid | A claim needs the appropriate verification |
| Payment confirmed | The system or authorised operator has established receipt under that payment method |
| Money settled | Funds have reached the relevant account under the provider's settlement rules |

Ask who confirms each state and where you can see it. Check the handling of cancellation, refund and an interrupted checkout. Do not promise delivery just because a shopper uploaded a screenshot or returned from a payment screen.

For any provider, obtain the applicable payment terms directly. Eligibility, transaction charges, settlement conditions and refund handling are separate questions from whether checkout displays a payment button.

## 3. Evaluate fulfilment as a sequence

“Shipping available” is not enough information to choose a store platform. Run through your actual delivery work:

1. Check whether the destination is serviceable.
2. Confirm the customer-facing delivery charge and estimate.
3. Identify who books the shipment and produces its label.
4. Check pickup arrangements and tracking visibility.
5. Find the procedure and charges for a failed delivery or return.

Ask which parts are included in your plan, which use another provider and which remain manual. A separate shipping tool may be perfectly suitable if it works reliably for your business; an integrated tool is useful only if it covers your real destinations and process.

For local or made-to-order products, also check how preparation time differs from courier transit time. Avoid showing an estimate that sounds like a guaranteed arrival date.

## 4. Compare the whole cost, not the headline

A free-to-start plan and a subscription plan can have very different total costs once you take orders. Use the same assumptions for both products.

Write down subscription, platform fees, payment processing, delivery and returns, optional services and domain costs. Record the billing period and whether tax is included. If an item is unknown, leave it unknown rather than assuming zero.

Then model three periods using your own records: a quiet month, a normal month and a busy month. Include the mix of small and large orders. Percentage fees with a per-order cap behave differently across that mix, so multiplying an average basket by total orders can mislead.

Keep migration effort separate. Even if someone offers catalogue assistance, your team still needs time to review images, options, stock and customer-facing information.

Use [oBizee's pricing page](https://www.obizee.com/pricing/) and the other provider's current terms when filling this worksheet. This guide does not promise that oBizee is cheaper for every seller.

## 5. Check support with a real question

Ask a concrete question before you depend on a platform: “How would I resolve a payment claim that does not match my bank record?” or “What should I do if a product option was imported incorrectly?”

A useful response explains the next action, the relevant screen and any escalation route. A sales reply saying “everything is supported” does not answer an operational question.

Confirm the support channel and availability you can actually rely on. Keep a note of the answer; do not assume that a prompt pre-sales reply establishes a contractual response time.

## 6. Move in a controlled way, if moving is justified

Request an assessment before committing to transfer your whole catalogue. Agree what can be brought across and what needs manual work. Back up the data you are entitled to export, and keep customer information out of public screenshots or casual shared documents.

Review a sample before the full catalogue. Compare product count, options, prices, stock, photos and any personalised-order fields. Check the destination store on a phone, including an out-of-stock state and an interrupted checkout.

Changing a store link does not automatically preserve search visibility, order history, reviews or customer accounts. List those separately. If a domain or indexed URL will change, plan ownership, redirects and recovery with the responsible operator.

Only change public links after the new journey has been reviewed and you know how to reverse the switch. Whether the old service remains available depends on its own terms and account state; no migration guide can guarantee that on its behalf.

## When staying is the sensible choice

Stay with your current setup if it supports your products, the costs are understood and the daily work is manageable. Improving your product information or internal process may solve more than changing software.

Consider a move when a specific recurring problem survives those improvements and the alternative demonstrates a better workflow on your own sample. Record that evidence. Do not switch merely because an article calls its own platform “best”.

## Your next step

Prepare three sample products and the three operational questions you wrote at the beginning. Use them for both evaluations.

If you want to assess oBizee, [request setup or migration guidance](https://www.obizee.com/move-my-store/). Ask for the scope, applicable charges and expected process before proceeding. If you are still deciding whether to add a store at all, start with our [WhatsApp Business versus online-store guide](https://www.obizee.com/blog/online-store-vs-whatsapp-business/).

The goal is not simply to acquire another website. It is to give customers a clear buying journey and give you an order you can act on confidently.

title: An online clothing store starts with clear sizes, stock and order details
description: Prepare your clothing catalogue with clear measurements, size-and-colour stock, useful photos and delivery information before taking online orders.
body:
You already know how to show a customer a garment in person or explain it in a message. Your online store needs to answer the same practical questions when you are not there: What will I receive? Which size should I choose? Is that colour available? When could it arrive?

Start with a small, accurate collection rather than an entire catalogue that customers cannot confidently order. Use the checklist below to prepare it, then test the shopping journey on a phone.

**Considering oBizee? Bring a few representative products and use this guide to assess the catalogue and order workflow before publishing your store.**

## Make size information useful, not just present

A label such as S, M or L is not an explanation of fit. State which measurements belong to the garment and which describe the body it is intended to fit. Explain how a measurement is taken, and keep units clear.

For example, “52 cm across the chest when laid flat” is different from “fits a 104 cm chest”. Do not replace one with the other without checking the actual garment and intended fit. These figures illustrate the distinction; they are not a size recommendation.

Explain relevant details such as length, stretch, lining and whether the cut is relaxed or fitted. Use information supplied or checked by the maker, not an assumed size conversion copied from another brand.

Uncertainty about sizing can prevent shoppers from making a decision; clear measurements are more useful than a reassuring but vague label. [Baymard's apparel usability research](https://baymard.com/research-articles/apparel-5-best-practices) examines this problem. It does not establish a particular sales uplift for your store.

## Treat each sellable option as a real stock decision

Suppose you sell a shirt in blue and cream, with sizes S, M and L. The combinations may have different quantities. “Six shirts available” does not tell a customer whether cream in M is available.

Prepare a simple list before entering products:

| Product | Colour | Size | Available quantity |
|---|---|---|---|
| Example shirt | Blue | S | 2 |
| Example shirt | Blue | M | 0 |
| Example shirt | Cream | M | 1 |

This is an illustrative stock list, not a merchant result. Use your own checked quantities.

After setup, select each option and inspect the price, availability and resulting bag line. A form field collecting a size preference is not necessarily a stock-managed variant. Ask which mechanism your store uses and test what happens when the chosen option is unavailable.

For made-to-order clothing, state that it is made to order. Production capacity and preparation time should not be disguised as ready-to-ship stock.

## Photograph the garment the customer will receive

Prepare a clear main image and additional views that answer real questions: front, back, fabric detail, fastening, embroidery, lining or an included accessory. If the photographed outfit contains a belt, blouse or other item sold separately, say so.

Use your own photographs or assets you have permission to publish. Check that each selected colour matches the photograph shown. Avoid using an attractive image of a different garment as a substitute.

Before uploading, inspect images on a phone. Are dark fabric details visible? Does the crop cut off the garment? Can a customer distinguish two similar colour options? A heavily filtered photo can create an expectation that the delivered item cannot meet.

If you show a person wearing the garment, obtain the necessary image permission and explain any relevant styling or fit context accurately. Do not invent a model's measurements.

## Write a product description that answers buying questions

Start with what the item is and what is included. Then explain the material, fit, available options, care information and fulfilment status where you know them.

Replace “premium quality, perfect for everyone” with concrete details you can support. If you cannot verify a fabric composition, ask the supplier before publishing it. If a piece is handmade and its finish varies, describe the actual variation rather than using a disclaimer to excuse an inaccurate listing.

Keep the most important information easy to scan. A customer should not have to search a long brand story to discover that a photographed set contains only the top.

## Explain preparation, delivery and exchanges before checkout

Separate the time you need to prepare an order from the time a carrier may need to deliver it. A dispatch estimate is not an arrival guarantee.

Check serviceability for the destinations you intend to serve, and make any delivery charge clear before the customer commits. Do not promise that every carrier covers every postcode simply because the platform offers a shipping integration.

Publish the exchange and return information applicable to your business and products. Make the contact route easy to find. This guide does not set a legal return period or replace review of your obligations; avoid copying another store's policy without checking whether it fits your operation.

For custom measurements or alterations, explain how requests are confirmed and what happens when information is incomplete. Do not imply that an automatic approval process exists unless you have tested it.

## Keep Instagram and WhatsApp useful

A store can be the place where customers check product details and make selections while conversations continue where they already happen. You do not have to abandon those conversations.

When replying about one garment, share its specific product link rather than making the buyer search your whole catalogue. After changing stock, price or options, check that your social posts and links are not making an outdated promise.

Decide how offline and message-based sales affect the quantities shown online. If a staff member sells the last piece in person, who updates its online availability? A clear responsibility matters as much as the software setting.

## Test one complete journey before sharing widely

Use a safe test environment or an agreed test procedure; do not create accidental paid orders.

Check that you can:

1. Open a product link on a phone and understand what is included.
2. Find sizing and material information without asking the seller.
3. Choose an available size and colour; recognise an unavailable combination.
4. See the same selection and correct quantity in the bag.
5. Understand the total and delivery conditions before submitting.
6. Identify the selected options in the merchant's order view.
7. Distinguish an order request from confirmed payment.

Record any failure and resolve it before driving more visitors to the page. A polished homepage does not compensate for a wrong size in the order record.

## Prepare your first collection with oBizee

Start with the products that best represent your range: one straightforward item, one size-and-colour product and, if relevant, one made-to-order piece. Bring their photos, prices, quantities and measurement information.

[Request setup guidance](https://www.obizee.com/signup/) to check the current oBizee workflow against those products. Review [current pricing](https://www.obizee.com/pricing/) and the [shipping guide](https://www.obizee.com/how-to-ship-products-online-india/) before committing to operational promises.

The aim is not to finish a website in an arbitrary number of minutes. It is to give a customer enough accurate information to choose—and give you an order you can fulfil.

title: Product catalogue checklist: prepare your products before building a store
description: Prepare product names, photos, prices, variants, stock and delivery facts with this practical checklist for sellers moving a catalogue online.
body:
**Before uploading your catalogue, prepare one complete product record.** It is easier to correct a missing measurement, unclear option or incorrect price once than to repeat the same mistake across every listing.

This checklist works as a preparation document for an existing Instagram seller, handmade business or small shop. It is not a required import format for oBizee or any other platform. Check the destination tool's accepted fields before importing data.

## 1. Give every product a clear identity

Write a name that helps a customer recognise the item. Include distinguishing details where useful, but avoid stuffing the title with unrelated search phrases.

“Floral crochet keychain — yellow” is easier to distinguish from another item than “New beautiful design 3”. An internal code can sit beside the customer-facing name; it does not have to become the title.

Keep a stable identifier for the product and each sellable variant. Do not rely only on row position or a photo filename, which may change when you organise the catalogue.

## 2. State exactly what the buyer receives

Write the quantity, contents, material and dimensions you can substantiate. If the photograph shows styling props or several products, clarify what is included in the price.

For a set, list its components. For a personalised item, identify the information needed from the buyer. If a colour, finish or handmade detail varies, describe that honestly.

Do not add claims such as hypoallergenic, food-safe, waterproof or suitable for children without appropriate evidence. A product description is not a place to guess a material's properties.

## 3. Separate options from instructions

A size or colour can identify a distinct stock item. A gift message is usually an instruction. Treating both as interchangeable text fields can make fulfilment confusing.

For each option, record:

- The option name the customer sees.
- The valid choices or combinations.
- Whether it changes price, stock, image or preparation time.
- Any information the buyer must supply.

Do not list combinations you cannot sell. Test how the destination store handles a missing selection and an unavailable combination. An attractive selector is not proof that the order contains the correct variant.

## 4. Check the selling price and quantities

Record the current price for the item or variant. If you show a comparison price or discount, keep evidence for the comparison and check that the amount selected in the bag matches the offer shown.

Keep stock quantities separate from minimum order quantity, pack size and made-to-order capacity. “One pack of six” should not accidentally become six single items at the pack price.

If you sell through several channels, decide which stock record is authoritative and who updates it. Do not assume two tools synchronise unless the connection has been verified.

## 5. Match images to the actual product

Choose a main image that makes the product identifiable, then add useful detail views. Check that the photos belong to the listed item and selected colour.

Record where each image came from and whether you have permission to publish it. A supplier sending a photograph is not always evidence that they can license every element of it.

Remove visible customer details, shipping labels or unrelated personal information. Write descriptive alternative text for meaningful product images; do not use it as a list of repeated keywords.

Preview the image crop on a phone. Keep an original master copy separately so later optimisation does not force you to work from an already degraded image.

## 6. Prepare fulfilment facts

Write whether the item is ready to ship or made to order. Separate preparation time from delivery estimates. Record the information your shipping workflow actually needs, such as packed weight and dimensions, rather than guessing from the unwrapped product.

Identify restrictions, fragile handling or personalisation checks that affect the order. Explain customer-facing conditions clearly, without claiming a carrier service or guaranteed arrival you have not verified.

Check that the customer can find the applicable delivery and return information before ordering. Product preparation does not replace review of your business policies.

## 7. Organise the catalogue around useful choices

Group products so a shopper can find a relevant selection. For a small catalogue, a few understandable groups are better than many nearly empty categories.

Use the same terminology across product names, categories and social links. If a category image shows one of its products, make sure the image represents the category and you have permission to use it.

Do not assume your store supports every filter you can imagine. Prepare useful attributes, then check which are actually available to shoppers in the chosen storefront.

## Copy this preparation record

Use one record per product, with a separate row for each stock-managed variant where needed.

| Field | Your entry |
|---|---|
| Product identifier and customer-facing name | |
| Category and short description | |
| Contents, material and relevant dimensions | |
| Variant identifier and selected options | |
| Current price and any substantiated comparison price | |
| Available quantity, pack size and minimum quantity | |
| Buyer instructions or personalisation required | |
| Main/detail image references and rights status | |
| Ready-to-ship or made-to-order; preparation estimate | |
| Packed dimensions/weight where required | |
| Applicable delivery, return and contact information | |
| Last checked date and responsible person | |

Keep customer names, phone numbers and order details out of this product worksheet. It is a catalogue record, not a customer database.

## Test one listing before importing everything

Create a sample in a safe preview or agreed test workflow. Inspect the product page, option selection, bag, total and merchant-facing order details. Check an unavailable option as well as a normal purchase path.

When the sample works, add the rest in manageable batches and compare the resulting counts and values. Import completion alone does not prove every photo, variant or price is correct.

Your final check is simple: can someone unfamiliar with your catalogue identify the item, select the right option, understand the cost and conditions, and leave you clear fulfilment instructions?

If you are evaluating oBizee, [bring a sample catalogue for setup guidance](https://www.obizee.com/signup/). If you are transferring an existing store, [ask for a migration assessment](https://www.obizee.com/move-my-store/) before changing its public links. Keep your current store's data and recovery plan until the transfer has been checked.

title: Turn Instagram enquiries into store orders without abandoning your audience
description: Introduce a store alongside Instagram with a manageable catalogue, clear product links and a plan for existing orders, customer questions and stock.
body:
**Keep the conversations that help customers choose. Move the repeatable details into a store when they are ready.** You do not have to replace Instagram, stop answering messages or transfer every product in one launch.

Start with a small collection that a customer can understand and order accurately. Keep your existing order commitments separate, test the new route, then share it deliberately.

## Decide what each channel should do

Instagram might be where someone discovers your work, asks about a customisation or follows a new collection. Your store can provide a consistent place to see the available products, choose options and review order information.

Write down the handoff you want. For example: a customer asks about a particular bag; you answer their question and send the relevant product link; they choose an available colour and review the order there.

That is different from expecting software to automatically read every conversation, understand a custom request and create a correct order. Do not assume a link, catalogue import or connected account provides that automation.

## Choose a first collection you can keep accurate

Use products you understand well and can fulfil reliably. Include a representative option or variation so you test more than the easiest case, but do not begin with every unfinished idea and unavailable piece.

For each product, prepare its name, images, price, available quantities, options, contents and delivery information. Mark made-to-order items honestly. A post showing an old commission may be useful inspiration without being an item you can currently sell.

If you need a preparation structure, make a simple record for each product before uploading. It should be possible to tell which photograph and stock quantity belong to each option without rereading a long caption.

## Treat import as a starting point, not a final check

An import can reduce re-entry, but its output still needs review. Social content may contain announcements, testimonials, videos, old prices or several products in one image. Some details may be missing or ambiguous.

Check the source and account eligibility supported by the importer you choose. In particular, do not assume that a workflow offered for business accounts works for every personal or private profile.

After import, compare the result with your intended catalogue. Check names, prices, quantities, options, categories and photographs. Read any skipped-item or missing-information report instead of treating a completed progress bar as proof that everything transferred.

Use official authorisation screens where required. Do not send passwords, one-time codes or private customer conversations to someone offering to set up the store.

For oBizee, [review the available import workflow](https://www.obizee.com/import/) or [ask for setup guidance](https://www.obizee.com/signup/) before relying on a specific source or account type. Eligibility and the result for your catalogue need to be checked, not assumed from this guide.

## Keep existing orders out of the experiment

Make a private list of orders already accepted: what was promised, payment status, selected options and the next fulfilment action. Continue managing those commitments in the agreed process unless you deliberately transfer them and check the result.

Do not ask a customer to place an accepted order again simply to populate a new dashboard. That can create duplicate requests, duplicate payments or uncertainty about which record to fulfil.

Decide when the new route starts applying. A simple internal note—“New requests from this point use the store; earlier accepted orders stay on the existing list”—can be clearer than quietly changing the process halfway through a conversation.

This is an organisational example, not a requirement imposed by a platform. Choose a process your team can actually follow.

## Try the store as a customer on a phone

Open a product link from the place you intend to share it. Check that the image, options and price load clearly. Select a variant, change quantity and inspect the bag. Check an unavailable option as well as a normal one.

Before submission, the customer should understand the total, delivery conditions and required information. The merchant should receive the selected product and options accurately.

Use a test environment or an agreed test-order procedure. Do not accidentally pay, book a shipment or notify a real customer while checking the flow. Also distinguish an order request from verified payment: a shopper saying they have paid is not the same as confirmed receipt.

Fix any mismatch before sending more visitors through the route. A launch announcement does not compensate for a wrong price or missing option in the order.

## Share the right link for the question

Check the current link controls available in your account and verify the destination after saving. This guide does not assume a particular Instagram interface or native shopping eligibility.

A general profile link can introduce the store, but a reply about one product should make that product easy to find. Check that old shared links still lead somewhere useful when you reorganise the catalogue.

Here is an illustrative reply you can adapt—not a merchant testimonial:

> You can see the available options and current price on this product page. If you need something different, reply here before ordering so we can confirm it.

Only use wording that matches your actual process. Do not promise customisation, availability or a response time you cannot deliver.

## Explain the change without making conversation harder

Tell customers what the store helps them do: see current details, choose an option or review an order. Keep a clear way to ask a question.

Some enquiries still need discussion. A one-off design, unusual delivery request or incomplete measurement may not fit ordinary checkout. Agree those details before asking the buyer to commit.

Avoid sending repeated promotional messages to every past customer just because you have a new link. Use the channels and permissions appropriate to the relationship. Moving a catalogue is not permission to reuse a customer list for unrelated marketing.

## Assign stock and support responsibilities

If you sell the last item through a message or in person, who updates its online quantity? If a shopper reports a problem, who checks whether an order exists before asking them to retry?

Write down those responsibilities. A one-person business needs them too, especially during a busy launch. Keep order status and payment status distinguishable, and retain the reference needed to investigate a problem.

For a technical failure, pause promotion of the affected route and direct enquiries to a clear support channel. Do not encourage repeated submissions or repeated payments without checking the original outcome.

## Review the change using a few honest observations

You do not need a complex dashboard to begin learning. Note which questions still repeat, which products need clarification and where customers report difficulty. Keep those notes free of unnecessary personal details.

If analytics is available, distinguish a product-link click, a setup enquiry and an actual order. They are different outcomes. A traffic increase alone does not show that customers found the process easier.

Review the first collection, correct its weak points and expand when the operating routine is dependable. The aim is a useful path from interest to a clear order—not an arbitrary launch deadline or the largest possible catalogue.

## Ready to assess the next step?

If you are still deciding whether a store adds value, read [WhatsApp Business versus an online store](https://www.obizee.com/blog/online-store-vs-whatsapp-business/). If you already have another store, request a [migration assessment](https://www.obizee.com/move-my-store/) before changing public links or domain settings.

Your audience can stay where it is. The work is to make the next buying step clearer.

title: How to price handmade products without forgetting your time
description: Build a handmade-product price from materials, labour, packaging, overhead and selling costs. Includes a worked example and a margin-versus-markup check.
body:
**Start by calculating what one sellable item costs you—including your time. Then test a price against the market and the actual costs of making a sale.** A materials-only calculation can make a product look profitable while leaving nothing for the work required to produce and deliver it.

This is an educational worksheet, not a recommended price, wage, tax treatment or profit guarantee. All amounts and fee rates in the example are fictional. Replace them with your own records and obtain professional help where your accounting or tax treatment requires it.

## Build a cost record for one product

Choose an item you already make. Measure the material used rather than charging the full purchase price of a supply pack to every item. Allow for normal wastage where you have a reasonable basis for estimating it.

Time the work needed to make the item ready for sale. Decide how you will value that time; do not quietly treat it as free because you enjoy the craft. Account for preparation and finishing, not just the most visible making step.

Allocate shared costs using a method you can explain and revise. An optimistic production forecast can make overhead per unit look artificially small. Be careful not to include the same packaging, labour or delivery expense twice.

This cost-first approach is consistent with [Etsy's seller education on pricing](https://www.etsy.com/seller-handbook/article/1106022743419), which also stresses testing prices against the market. The worksheet below is our own simplified example; it does not use Etsy's fees.

## A fictional ₹300 cost base

Imagine a handmade item with these costs:

| Cost included per item | Illustrative amount |
|---|---:|
| Materials consumed | ₹120 |
| Labour allowance: 30 minutes at an assumed ₹180/hour | ₹90 |
| Packaging | ₹25 |
| Allocated overhead | ₹35 |
| Seller-funded delivery allocation | ₹30 |
| **Total included cost** | **₹300** |

These are not market benchmarks. The delivery amount is not a courier quote, and the labour rate is not a recommendation. If you charge delivery separately, model that income and the actual delivery expense consistently instead of copying this example.

The cost base also does not automatically cover every return, damaged item, advertising expense or tax obligation. Add relevant costs explicitly and state how you estimated them.

## Markup and margin are different calculations

Adding 25% to ₹300 gives a price of ₹375. That is a 25% **markup on cost**.

It is not a 25% margin on the selling price. Before any additional fee, the ₹75 difference is 20% of ₹375.

Now suppose, only for illustration, a selling fee equals 3% of that product price. At ₹375 the fee is ₹11.25, leaving ₹63.75 after the ₹300 included cost. That remainder is **17% of the selling price**.

Label the result carefully. Because this example includes a chosen labour allowance and allocated overhead but may exclude other business costs, call it the **remainder after included costs**, not guaranteed take-home income or an accounting net-profit margin.

## Work backwards from a target remainder

For a simple model where one percentage fee applies to the product price:

`Required price = included cost ÷ (1 − fee rate − target remainder rate)`

Use decimals: 3% is 0.03 and 25% is 0.25.

With ₹300 included cost, a fictional 3% fee and a target remainder of 25% of price:

`₹300 ÷ (1 − 0.03 − 0.25) = ₹416.67 approximately`

If the merchant chooses an illustrative rounded price of ₹420:

| Calculation | Amount |
|---|---:|
| Product revenue in this example | ₹420.00 |
| Hypothetical 3% fee | −₹12.60 |
| Included cost | −₹300.00 |
| **Remainder after included costs** | **₹107.40** |

₹107.40 is about **25.57% of ₹420**. Rounding changed the result slightly; always recalculate after choosing the displayed price.

This formula requires the fee rate plus target remainder rate to be less than 100%. If the denominator is zero or negative, the target cannot be solved with this model. A fee with a minimum, cap, fixed charge or different charging base needs its actual calculation—not a guessed combined percentage.

## Check a discount before announcing it

A 10% discount reduces the example ₹420 price to ₹378. The cost of making the item has not automatically fallen.

At the same fictional 3% fee:

`₹378 − ₹11.34 − ₹300 = ₹66.66`

The remainder falls from ₹107.40 to ₹66.66: a reduction of ₹40.74. It is now about **17.63% of the discounted price**, not the original target.

Before running an offer, include any added packaging, gift, delivery subsidy or advertising cost. A larger order is not necessarily better if the offer consumes the money needed to fulfil it.

## Know the model's cost-recovery floor

With the same assumptions and no target remainder, the arithmetic floor is:

`₹300 ÷ (1 − 0.03) = ₹309.28 approximately`

That is **not a recommended selling price**. It only recovers the included costs under this simplified fee model. Unexpected costs, different fee rounding, returns or incomplete overhead estimates can change the result.

Do not use a mathematical floor as proof that a business is sustainable. You still need a price customers accept, enough capacity to fulfil orders and enough money to cover the costs the worksheet has not captured.

## Copy this worksheet for your own item

| Input or check | Your figure / evidence |
|---|---|
| Material quantity and unit cost | |
| Wastage assumption and its basis | |
| Making/finishing time and labour allowance | |
| Packaging and other direct costs | |
| Allocated overhead and expected production volume | |
| Delivery income and expense, if relevant | |
| Actual platform/payment fee rules and charging bases | |
| Return/damage/other cost assumptions | |
| Candidate selling price | |
| Remainder after all included costs | |
| Remainder as a percentage of the defined revenue | |
| Discounted-price result | |
| Date checked | |

Use one consistent treatment for tax throughout. This worksheet does not determine registration requirements, the applicable tax rate or recoverable tax. Do not count tax collected for remittance as money available to keep.

## Compare with the market without copying blindly

Look at products that are genuinely comparable in materials, workmanship, dimensions and fulfilment. A mass-produced item or a smaller piece may not be a useful price reference for yours.

If buyers will not accept the cost-based price, explore the product or process: material sourcing, batch preparation, packaging, product size or the work involved in personalisation. Do not hide the shortfall by removing your time from the calculation.

Test changes in a controlled way and record what happened. A calculation tells you what a price would leave under its assumptions; it does not prove demand or guarantee sales.

When choosing selling tools, use [current platform pricing](https://www.obizee.com/pricing/) rather than the fictional fee in this example. Once your prices and product details are ready, [request setup guidance](https://www.obizee.com/signup/) to assess the store workflow for your catalogue.

title: Manage stock across Instagram, WhatsApp and your store without promising the same item twice
description: Create one stock record for social and store orders, distinguish held items from available stock, and reconcile changes without assuming automatic sync.
body:
**Choose one stock record, define when an item becomes unavailable, and record every channel's changes against it.** A website does not solve overselling if an item promised in a message still appears available online. Equally, hiding every item someone asks about can make a healthy catalogue look sold out.

The starting point is not a more complicated spreadsheet. It is a clear answer to three questions: What exactly is the item? How many can you sell now? Which event changes that number?

## Start with one sellable item, not a total for the whole design

“Five floral bags” is insufficient if three are blue and two are cream. Give each stock-managed choice a stable reference. Use the same reference in your catalogue, packing notes and private order record.

An item bought as a pack also needs a clear unit. If a customer orders one pack of six, decide whether your record counts packs or individual pieces. Do not subtract one from a quantity measured in pieces and assume the remaining number is correct.

Keep a small lookup sheet if your public product names are longer than your internal references. Your customer should not need to learn your codes to buy; your team should not need to guess which photograph an order refers to.

## Count what is available, not everything you own

Separate items that are sellable now from damaged stock, order commitments and unfinished work. [Shopify's inventory guide](https://www.shopify.com/blog/inventory-management) describes physical counts as a check on recorded quantities. A record is useful only if you compare it with the actual items and investigate differences.

Here is an illustrative manual record, not an oBizee reservation setting:

| One product variant | Quantity |
|---|---:|
| Physically counted | 12 |
| Damaged, not sellable | 2 |
| Held for three agreed orders | 3 |
| Available to offer now | 7 |

With no other changes, selling one available item leaves six available. If all three held items are subsequently released after confirmed cancellations, available quantity becomes nine. Record both events; do not replace the total from memory.

Made-to-order capacity is a separate question. Owning yarn for several pieces does not mean you can finish all of them by the customer's date. Keep promised production work visible alongside finished stock without counting unfinished pieces as ready to dispatch.

## Decide what a hold means before using it

A product enquiry is not necessarily an order. If you offer temporary holds, write a consistent rule covering who creates the hold, when it ends and how the customer is told. Check what your actual selling tool supports; this guide does not claim automatic expiry.

Avoid telling one buyer that an item is reserved while allowing another to purchase it. If your tools do not share reservations, use a controlled manual procedure or allocate separate quantities to the channels. Separate allocations require reconciliation too—they are not extra stock.

Payment and stock states should also remain distinct. A payment screenshot is not, by itself, verified receipt of funds. Follow your payment-confirmation process without silently treating a customer's message as settled money.

## Record events instead of repeatedly rewriting a total

For a manageable catalogue, an event log makes a discrepancy easier to investigate. Keep customer details in the protected order system and use an order reference in the stock sheet.

| Field | What to record |
|---|---|
| Time and responsible person | When the movement was recorded and by whom |
| Product/variant reference | The exact sellable item and counting unit |
| Event | Receipt, sale, hold, release, damage or count correction |
| Quantity change | Which bucket increased or decreased |
| Supporting reference | Order, receipt or count note—not public customer data |
| Remaining available quantity | Result after the recorded event |

Do not make an unexplained adjustment just to force the sheet to match a screen. Keep the reason. Otherwise the next person cannot tell whether the difference was damage, a duplicate order entry or a missed receipt.

## Close the gap between channels

Map how a message-led purchase becomes an order in your system. Decide who records it and which stock record is updated. If more than one person answers messages, avoid two people recording the same conversation as separate orders.

Test any claimed integration with a safe example before relying on it. Does an order reduce the right variant? What happens on cancellation? Does a failed payment reserve anything? Does a manually entered sale update the customer-facing quantity? The answers depend on the tool and configuration.

Without verified synchronisation, assume someone must perform the update. Choose a workable update routine and be honest about availability when you cannot check it immediately. Never use “live stock” to describe an occasionally updated estimate.

## Use a short reconciliation routine

At a frequency that suits your order volume, compare the order record, stock changes and physical items. Start with scarce or frequently sold variants rather than trusting the catalogue-wide total.

- Match each new order reference to one stock movement, not two.
- Review expired or cancelled holds before releasing quantities.
- Inspect returned items before making them sellable again.
- Record newly completed work only when it is genuinely ready.
- Investigate negative balances and repeated manual corrections.

If a discrepancy affects an unfulfilled order, resolve the customer commitment before promoting the item again. Do not let a correction silently create a promise you cannot keep.

## Know when the manual routine has become the problem

Repeated corrections, unclear responsibility and delayed updates are useful warning signs. Record the actual failures you want software to prevent. Evaluate tools against those cases rather than assuming a larger feature list will remove the work.

Bring two variants and a message-led order into a controlled demonstration. Ask to see sale, cancellation and unavailable-stock behaviour. Do not create a real customer order solely to test the system without the necessary authorisation.

Start with the [catalogue-preparation checklist](/blog/product-page-checklist/) if your product references are inconsistent. Use the [Instagram-to-store guide](/blog/instagram-to-online-store/) to introduce a clearer buying route, then [request setup guidance](/signup/) for the workflow you actually need.

title: Check a discount before it turns more orders into less money
description: Compare a discount with your normal order economics using a worked example, bundle check and promotion worksheet before announcing an offer.
body:
**Calculate what the discounted order leaves after its included costs, then compare that with the normal order.** A higher order count is not enough to judge an offer. You may be spending more time and using more stock to leave less money for the business.

This guide uses fictional prices, costs and fee rates. It is a decision worksheet, not a recommended discount, tax calculation or profit guarantee. Replace every assumption with your own records before using the result.

## Give the offer one clear purpose

Write what you want the promotion to achieve: move a particular slow-selling batch, introduce a collection, or encourage a larger relevant order. Avoid “increase sales” as the only objective—it does not tell you which costs or outcomes to compare.

Decide which products and customers qualify, how long the offer runs and what ends it. Check the chosen storefront's actual coupon rules before promising minimum spends, combinations, exclusions or usage limits. A marketing plan is not proof that the checkout supports it.

Shopify's [retail discount guidance](https://www.shopify.com/blog/retail-discounts-with-profits) also frames discounting around objectives and margin. The worked examples below are our own; no conversion result from another retailer is assumed to apply to your store.

## Calculate the normal order first

Suppose a product normally sells for ₹600. Its included cost is ₹380, covering the material, labour allowance, packaging and other costs you chose to include. For illustration only, assume a fee of 3% of the product price and no other charges.

| Normal order | Fictional amount |
|---|---:|
| Product revenue | ₹600.00 |
| Included cost | ₹380.00 |
| Hypothetical 3% fee | ₹18.00 |
| Remainder after included costs | ₹202.00 |

Call this a remainder, not automatically net profit. Advertising, returns, taxes or overhead may be missing from the model. If your actual provider uses capped, fixed or differently based fees, calculate those rules instead of copying the percentage.

## Apply the discount to the revenue—not to the cost

A 15% discount changes the selling price from ₹600 to ₹510. Making the product still costs the assumed ₹380. The hypothetical fee becomes ₹15.30, leaving ₹114.70.

That is ₹87.30 less per fulfilled unit than the normal ₹202 remainder. The discount reduced the price by 15%, but it reduced this model's remainder by about 43.2%.

To produce the same total remainder under these unchanged assumptions, you would need about **1.76 times as many fulfilled units**, or roughly 76.1% more. This is arithmetic, not a forecast that the offer will generate those orders. It also assumes capacity, costs and fulfilment quality do not deteriorate at the higher volume.

If you already have a full production schedule, check whether those extra discounted orders would displace full-price work. An offer can create a capacity problem even when each individual order leaves a positive amount.

## Compare a bundle separately

A bundle is not automatically a better deal for the seller. Price the actual contents and handling.

Two normal units in the example leave ₹404 in total. Suppose you instead offer the pair for ₹1,100. Their combined included cost is ₹760, but assume the shared packaging genuinely saves ₹20, reducing it to ₹740. The hypothetical 3% fee is ₹33. The bundle leaves **₹327**, which is ₹77 less than two normal units.

The bundle may serve a deliberate purpose, but “two items in one order” does not establish its profitability. Verify the packaging saving and delivery cost. Heavier or bulkier parcels may change the result, and customers may choose the bundle instead of two purchases they would otherwise have made.

## Include everything the promotion changes

Run a second pass over the costs. A free gift has a cost even if it was already on your shelf. Free delivery is funded somewhere. Extra packing work still takes time.

- Add campaign advertising and creative costs where applicable.
- Include extra packaging or fulfilment work caused by the offer.
- Check how partial returns, cancellations and refunds affect the calculation.
- Confirm whether discounts can combine, and test the resulting total.
- Keep the same tax treatment in both baseline and offer calculations.

Do not count tax collected for remittance as money you can keep. Obtain appropriate accounting advice for the tax and reporting treatment of your offer; this worksheet does not establish it.

## Write the customer-facing terms clearly

State the products included, the benefit, any minimum spend and the end condition in words a customer can understand. Do not advertise an inflated “before” price to make the saving look larger. Keep evidence for any price comparison you make.

Check the offer on a phone with an eligible bag, an ineligible bag and the boundary value around any threshold. Confirm the displayed total before payment. A banner and a coupon setting can disagree even when each looks plausible in isolation.

If the checkout cannot enforce an important restriction, do not rely on customers overlooking it. Change the offer or explain the limitation before launch.

## Keep a one-page promotion record

| Decision | Your record |
|---|---|
| Purpose and eligible products | |
| Baseline price, included costs and fee rules | |
| Discounted or bundled price | |
| Additional campaign and handling costs | |
| Remainder per normal and promoted order | |
| Capacity and stock available for the offer | |
| Rules actually tested in checkout | |
| Start, end and stop conditions | |
| Outcomes to compare after fulfilment | |

After the campaign, compare completed orders and the costs actually incurred. Keep cancellations and refunds visible. Avoid calling every order during the offer incremental: some customers might have bought anyway, and other campaigns or seasonal demand may have changed at the same time.

If the original cost base is uncertain, start with the [handmade pricing worksheet](/blog/price-handmade-products/). Check [current platform pricing](/pricing/) for actual charges, and [ask for setup guidance](/signup/) before promising a discount workflow you have not tested.

title: Product photography checklist: show what a buyer needs to know
description: Plan a useful product photo set with clear main, detail, scale and variant views, then check crops, colour, rights and filenames before uploading.
body:
**Photograph the questions a customer needs answered, not just the scene you want to create.** A beautiful arrangement can attract attention while leaving the buyer unsure about the item's size, contents or colour. Start with one product and make its photo set useful before repeating the process across the catalogue.

You can begin with the phone and space you already have. The aim of this checklist is a clear, honest listing—not a promise that any camera or a particular number of images will increase sales.

## Write the shot list before setting up

Read your product description as if you have never held the item. List what is difficult to understand from words alone. A crochet piece may need texture and scale; a garment may need its shape and fastening; a gift set needs a clear view of what the price includes.

Etsy's [product photography checklist](https://www.etsy.com/seller-handbook/article/152858121769) includes detail and size/scale shots among useful photograph types. Use that principle to select views for your own product, rather than uploading several nearly identical angles.

| Buyer's question | Useful view to plan |
|---|---|
| Which item is this? | Uncluttered main view with the whole product visible |
| What is the finish or texture? | Close detail without hiding relevant imperfections |
| How large is it? | Clear scale reference alongside written dimensions |
| What comes in the order? | Actual included items together; props distinguished |
| Which option am I selecting? | Photograph of the named colour or variant |
| What cannot be seen from the front? | Relevant reverse, interior, fastening or side view |

Not every product needs every view. Choose the images that remove uncertainty for that item. Do not pad a gallery with duplicate photos simply to reach a count.

## Make a repeatable setup

Choose a background that lets the product stand out and a position you can reproduce. Before photographing the full range, take a test image and inspect it at normal phone size as well as enlarged.

Clean the lens and product surface. Keep the camera steady, focus on the important detail and check whether shadows conceal the item's shape. If the available light changes during the session, compare the first and last products rather than assuming the whole batch matches.

Record a few setup notes: background, camera position, approximate distance and the time or light arrangement that worked. The purpose is to make the next batch consistent, not to force every material into identical lighting. Reflective jewellery and textured fabric may need different adjustments.

## Let the main photo identify the product

The main image often appears smaller in a collection card than on the product page. Make sure the item is still recognisable after that reduction and crop.

Avoid placing essential product details near the edge before testing the template's crop. If several items appear in the scene, a buyer should not have to guess which one is for sale. Explain the included quantity in the product text as well as the photograph.

Styling can support the product, but it should not become a substitute for a clear view. Keep at least one image that shows the actual item without decorative elements obscuring it.

## Keep colour, scale and condition honest

Review edits against the physical product. Do not apply a filter that materially changes the colour or remove a feature the customer will receive. If handmade variation is part of the product, explain it and show a representative example rather than promising identical copies.

A scale photograph supplements dimensions; it does not replace them. A prop's apparent size can be misunderstood. State measurements and identify the relevant part of the product, especially when handles, chains or packaging change its total dimensions.

For seconds, samples or visibly imperfect items, show the relevant condition clearly. Do not hide it only in a distant image or a line the customer is unlikely to find.

## Match every photo to the correct option

Before uploading, group images by product and variant. A blue-item photograph attached to the cream option creates uncertainty even if both products are available.

Use stable references in your filenames, such as `FLR-YELLOW-front` and `FLR-YELLOW-detail`, rather than relying on upload order. These are illustrative naming examples, not a required import format. Check the destination store's accepted formats, limits and image-selection behaviour.

Keep an original master separately from the web copy. Resize and compress the upload version as appropriate for the actual storefront, then inspect it for lost detail. Do not repeatedly edit an already compressed copy and assume its quality will hold.

## Check rights and private information

Use photographs you own or have permission to publish. A picture found on a social account is not automatically available for your catalogue. Check permissions before using recognisable people, customer-submitted photos or someone else's creative work.

Inspect the background for addresses, parcel labels, phone numbers and other private details. Remove the private information from the scene before taking the photo where possible. Do not rely on a small preview to reveal everything that becomes visible when the original image is opened.

Avoid invented “customer photos” or synthetic images that misrepresent the product's appearance. If an illustration is used to explain a concept, label it as an illustration rather than presenting it as fulfilment proof.

## Finish with the storefront, not the camera roll

Upload one complete set to a safe preview. Check the collection card, product page and any image displayed in the bag. Test the mobile view and an option change where supported. A file that looks correct in your photo library may crop differently in the actual template.

Write alternative text that describes the useful visual information. For example, “Yellow crochet flower keychain, front view” is more informative than a string of search phrases. Do not put prices or claims in alt text merely to add keywords.

Keep this final handoff record:

- Product and variant reference.
- Main, detail and scale-image filenames as needed.
- Included-items clarification and relevant dimensions.
- Rights or permission record.
- Original-master location and prepared web copies.
- Mobile crop and option-match check.

If a category has no dedicated image, a representative product photo can be a deliberate choice. Check that it belongs to the category, that you can use it and that the crop still makes sense. Do not use a random attractive image that promises unrelated products.

Combine the photo set with the [catalogue-preparation checklist](/blog/product-page-checklist/). Clothing sellers can also use the [size and stock guide](/for/clothing-stores/). When you are ready to test the complete listing, [request setup guidance](/signup/) with a small, representative collection.

title: A seller’s profile that answers the questions buyers ask first
description: Prepare a trustworthy seller profile with clear product information, response expectations and a tested buying link—without promising features your store does not have.
body:
A customer arriving from a shared post should not have to investigate whether your shop is still operating. Your profile needs to answer a few ordinary questions: what do you sell, where can the customer see the range, how do they order, and where can they get help?

Treat the profile as the entrance to a buying process, not a miniature poster. A beautiful photograph cannot compensate for a broken shop link or contradictory delivery information. This guide is a practical audit, not a claim that changing a profile guarantees sales.

## Start with the question a new visitor would ask

Look at your profile without relying on information you already know. A name such as “The Sunday Edit” might be memorable, but it does not tell a visitor whether you sell clothing, stationery or home accessories. Add a plain-language explanation where it naturally fits.

Write down the five enquiries you answer most often. Separate profile-level questions from product-specific ones. “Do you deliver outside your city?” belongs near the buying information. “Is this necklace adjustable?” belongs on the relevant product page. Trying to answer both in the same tiny space makes neither answer easy to find.

## Make your identity consistent across the journey

Compare your profile name, linked storefront name and the name used in order communications. They need not be identical in every character, but the relationship should be understandable. An unexplained jump to an unrelated brand can make a genuine customer hesitate.

Use a logo or recognisable brand image you have the right to use. Do not add payment-provider marks, certification badges or customer logos merely because they make the account look established. Each trust claim needs a real basis.

If your business name has changed, explain the transition briefly rather than leaving several conflicting identities active. Keep historical order support reachable while you update public information.

## Give each information area one job

A useful profile does not need to list every product. It needs to help visitors choose their next step.

| Customer question | Useful answer | Avoid |
|---|---|---|
| What is this shop? | Product type and meaningful distinction | An unexplained slogan alone |
| Where can I browse? | A direct link to the relevant range | A maze of unrelated destinations |
| How do I order? | The actual store or message-led process | “Instant checkout” when an enquiry is required |
| When will you respond? | Hours you can normally honour | An unsupported 24-hour promise |
| Where is help? | One monitored support route | Several abandoned contact methods |

Keep the detailed returns, shipping and product information at a stable destination. If a policy is not ready, resolve that operational gap; do not replace it with a reassuring phrase that nobody can explain.

## Test the link as a customer, not as the account owner

Open the public link on a phone in a normal browsing session. Check the destination, product availability and the route back to the range. A page that works while you are signed into an editing account may not be publicly usable.

Choose one representative item and follow the path up to, but not through, any real payment or order submission. Confirm that the advertised product, price and options remain understandable. Do not create a real transaction merely to check navigation.

If your profile highlights a temporary collection, set a reminder to replace that link when the collection closes. Sending every customer to a sold-out launch after the campaign ends wastes the interest you have already earned.

## Align response expectations with your working day

A one-person business may answer messages between production and packing. Say so clearly. “Messages answered Monday to Saturday, usually by the next working day” is more useful than “always here” when you cannot be.

Keep an alternative for existing-order problems separate from general browsing if your workflow supports it. Ask customers not to post phone numbers or addresses in public comments. Move necessary order details into your protected support process.

## Review what the profile sends downstream

For one week, keep a simple private tally of repeated questions: ordering, delivery coverage, size, price or trust. Do not collect extra personal information for this exercise. If several visitors ask how to buy, fix the buying route before adding more decorative content.

Use [the Instagram-to-store guide](/blog/instagram-to-online-store/) for the broader transition and [the catalogue checklist](/blog/product-page-checklist/) for product-level gaps. Your profile audit is complete when a new visitor can understand the shop, reach the right item and find a credible way to ask for help.

title: Turn interested followers into product-page visitors
description: Connect a specific Instagram post to the product information a buyer needs, then measure the handoff without confusing followers or clicks with orders.
body:
Followers do not all arrive ready to buy. Some are discovering your work, some are comparing options, and others need one practical answer before placing an order. A useful post-to-store journey respects those differences rather than repeating “shop now” beneath every photograph.

Start with one product and one reason someone might consider it. Build the next step around that reason. This is a method for removing uncertainty; it is not a promise that a particular number of followers will produce a particular number of sales.

## Match the destination to the promise

Suppose a post shows a small pouch holding charging cables. A link to that pouch, with dimensions and an interior photograph, continues the same conversation. A generic homepage featuring unrelated festive gifts makes the customer start again.

A range page can be appropriate when the post genuinely presents a collection. The important question is whether the destination contains what the post led the person to expect. Do not send a post about ready-to-dispatch pieces to a page dominated by made-to-order items without explaining the distinction.

Write the promise and destination next to each other before posting. If you cannot explain their connection in one sentence, choose a clearer link or narrow the post.

## Give useful information before requesting a click

A customer should not need to open a private conversation merely to discover what is being sold. Include the essential context that makes the next step worthwhile: the use, the available choice, or a meaningful constraint.

Avoid hiding every detail as a tactic to collect enquiries. More messages can increase your workload without improving purchase confidence. Equally, do not squeeze the entire product page into a caption. Show enough to make the product understandable, then provide the destination for measurements, options and current availability.

For handmade goods, explain when the photographed piece is an example rather than the exact item that will ship. That distinction matters before a buyer begins imagining a specific colour arrangement or pattern.

## Build a short handoff checklist

Check the transition while the campaign is still editable.

- The destination shows the same product or clearly named collection.
- The photographed option can be identified on the page.
- The customer can understand the unit: one piece, a pair or a set.
- Price and delivery information are not contradicted by the post.
- The primary next action matches the actual ordering process.
- An unavailable item does not silently redirect to a different product.

Use a real phone and the public link. If a campaign requires a special code, confirm where the customer sees its conditions. Do not describe a discount as automatic if the buyer must enter something.

## Write a next step for the current decision

Different questions deserve different actions. A sizing explanation can invite readers to check the measurement guide. A colour comparison can send them to the available variants. A launch announcement can lead to the collection and its dispatch terms.

Illustrative wording for a pouch post might be: “See the measurements and inside view before choosing your colour.” This tells a shopper why to open the link. It does not assume they are ready to pay.

If ordering still happens through messages, say what information to send. Do not imply that a catalogue link is a completed checkout.

## Observe the handoff without inventing attribution

Record which post or campaign you are evaluating and keep the destination stable during the observation period. If your verified analytics setup reports landing visits, use that measure consistently. Do not substitute profile views for product-page visits.

Separate events in your notes: product visit, question, order request, confirmed order and completed sale. They are different outcomes. One customer may see several posts and return later through another route, so a basic tally cannot prove that a single caption caused the sale.
