When traffic is small, read actual enquiry themes alongside the numbers. Three sizing questions may point to a practical information gap, but three visits are not enough to establish a dependable conversion benchmark.

## Fix the weakest step before increasing promotion

If people reach the wrong page, correct the link. If they reach the item but ask what is included, improve the product description. If they understand the item but cannot obtain a delivery estimate, investigate the buying process.

Do not change the caption, photographs, price and destination simultaneously and then claim one change worked. Keep a dated record of the main adjustment and what you observed afterward.

Use [the product-page checklist](/blog/product-page-checklist/) to prepare the destination and [the stock guide](/blog/inventory-for-instagram-sellers/) to keep availability credible. The goal is a connected journey, not merely a busier Instagram account.

title: Build a weekly Instagram plan around buying questions
description: Create a manageable content week from real customer questions, product evidence and operational capacity rather than filling every day with a sales post.
body:
An Instagram calendar is useful when it reduces last-minute work and helps customers understand your products. It is less useful when it becomes a requirement to publish something every day, regardless of whether you have anything helpful to say.

For a small seller, begin with the questions already delaying orders. Plan content that answers those questions, demonstrates the product and gives an appropriate next step. The example below is an editorial routine, not a universal posting frequency or an algorithmic recommendation.

## Collect questions before choosing formats

Read recent enquiries and write down the underlying questions without copying customer names, addresses or private messages into your planning sheet. “Will it fit my laptop?” is more useful than “need another Reel.”

Group the questions into four practical areas: product use, choice, fulfilment and confidence. Product use might need a demonstration. Choice might need a measurement comparison. Fulfilment might need an explanation of production time. Confidence might need a truthful account of materials or your packing process.

Do not turn one customer's private difficulty into public content without permission. Generalise the learning and use your own example or demonstration.

## Select a realistic week

Choose a small number of pieces you can make properly. A calendar with three useful posts that are ready to publish can be more manageable than seven incomplete ideas. That is a workload choice, not a claim about how the platform ranks frequency.

For example, a handmade bag seller might plan:

| Piece | Customer question | Evidence needed | Destination |
|---|---|---|---|
| Interior demonstration | What fits inside? | Actual bag and measured objects | Product page |
| Size comparison | Which size should I choose? | Two labelled products | Measurement information |
| Dispatch explanation | Is it ready for my occasion? | Current production commitments | Shipping or ordering guidance |

Give each piece a specific purpose. Three nearly identical product photographs with different opening sentences are still one idea repeated.

## Prepare the facts with the images

Before drafting a caption, collect the product reference, photographed variant, current availability and any relevant timing information. Save these next to the content task so the person publishing does not guess.

Use a checklist for claims such as washable, waterproof, handmade or suitable for a particular age. If you do not have evidence for a claim, remove or qualify it. Attractive copy should not create a product promise your packaging and support team cannot honour.

Create assets from products you can actually offer. If the item sells out before publication, update the destination and wording rather than posting stale availability from the calendar.

## Batch production without making the posts identical

One photography session can capture several useful views: overall shape, interior, scale and fastening. Those views answer different questions and can support different pieces of content.

Write separate introductions for separate purposes. A scale comparison should not reuse the launch announcement with a few nouns changed. Keep the product facts consistent while changing the explanation to match the customer's decision.

Leave space for an operational update. If dispatch is delayed, a scheduled promotional post may need to move. The calendar should support the business, not force it to advertise beyond its capacity.

## Add ownership and a final check

A useful planning row contains a working title, purpose, asset location, product reference, destination, owner and readiness state. Distinguish “idea” from “facts checked” and “ready.” An asset sitting in a folder is not a completed post.

Before publishing, check the image rights, spelling of the product name, live destination and any dates. Preview the wording on a phone so important conditions do not disappear behind decorative text.

If somebody helps you, name who may approve price or delivery claims. A helper should not infer a promotion because an old caption mentioned one.

## Review the week by question answered

At the end of the week, note what happened: useful enquiries, repeated confusion, product visits where available, and orders that can genuinely be connected to the campaign. Do not label every increase in sales a result of the calendar.

Look for the next unanswered question. If customers still ask about scale after a demonstration, the image may not have communicated scale clearly. If the main response is a delivery question, the product content may be fine while the fulfilment information needs work.

Keep good evergreen explanations in a reusable library, but recheck stock, prices and links before using them again. Start with [the product photography checklist](/blog/product-photography-checklist/) and [catalogue preparation](/blog/product-page-checklist/) when your calendar lacks reliable source material. Consistency comes from a repeatable preparation process, not from manufacturing urgency every morning.

title: Use Stories to explain a product before asking for the sale
description: Plan a short product Story sequence that explains use, choice and the next step, with truthful availability and no reliance on unsupported shopping features.
body:
A product Story can do more than announce that something is available. It can show how an item works, answer a common objection and help a viewer decide whether it suits them. The useful question is not how many frames you can publish; it is what the customer needs to understand by the end.

Plan the sequence before opening a design tool. Keep any platform-specific controls conditional on what your account actually supports. This guide covers the content and buying journey, not a promise that every account has the same linking or shopping features.

## Start with one buying question

Choose a question narrow enough to answer visually. “How much fits in this pouch?” works better than “Why our brand is amazing.” “Which of these two sizes fits a small desk?” gives you a clear comparison to demonstrate.

Use the actual product wherever possible. A decorative scene may establish a mood, but it cannot prove capacity, closure strength or exact dimensions. If you use an illustration to explain a concept, label it so it is not mistaken for a product photograph.

Avoid combining a launch, a competition, a testimonial and a shipping announcement in one short sequence. Each new topic asks the viewer to reconstruct the context.

## Give the sequence a beginning, explanation and next step

An illustrative four-part sequence for a fabric pouch could look like this:

1. Name the question: “Need to organise small charging accessories?”
2. Demonstrate the item with the objects it genuinely holds.
3. Show the dimensions, closure and available choices.
4. Point to the relevant product information or explain how to enquire.

The sequence should still make sense to a viewer who has never seen your earlier posts. Product names and scale cues are not wasted space; they prevent misunderstanding.

Do not promise that the demonstration fits every version of an object. A laptop sleeve shown with one device is not evidence that every laptop with the same advertised screen size will fit.

## Make text support the demonstration

Use short, readable statements that identify what the viewer is seeing. Put important limitations into the visible explanation rather than assuming everyone will ask privately.

If the example is made to order, say that. If accessories are not included, make the distinction clear. If different fabrics can change the appearance, avoid presenting one photograph as a guarantee of identical pattern placement.

Check the content on a small screen. Tiny measurement labels and crowded comparison grids can defeat the purpose of the demonstration. A separate frame for dimensions may be clearer than putting every fact over the opening image.

## Use interaction to learn, not to manufacture demand

A question about preferred colours can help you understand interest. It is not a purchase commitment. Keep the distinction visible in your planning notes so a poll does not become an invented sales forecast.

If you invite questions, decide who will answer them and where. Do not collect addresses or payment details through a public reply. Move necessary private information into your usual protected order process.

When summarising feedback, describe what people actually said. “Several respondents asked for a larger size” is different from “our customers demanded this launch,” particularly when the sample is small.

## Check the destination while the Story is current

Where a link is available, test that it opens the correct item or collection. If you direct viewers to your profile instead, make the named destination easy to recognise. Avoid telling people to hunt through old content for the buying instructions.

Check availability immediately before publishing. If the item becomes unavailable, update the relevant public information promptly where your tools allow. Do not keep an urgency message running simply because the content was scheduled earlier.

The linked page should explain options, price and fulfilment more fully than the Story. Use [the catalogue checklist](/blog/product-page-checklist/) if the destination is missing those details.

## Keep evidence of what you promised

Save your final sequence with its publication date and product reference. This is useful when a customer asks about a claim made during a launch or when you want to reuse a demonstration later.

Before reusing it, check whether the product dimensions, materials or delivery process have changed. Evergreen footage can become inaccurate even when it still looks attractive.

Evaluate the sequence by whether it reduced confusion and led to relevant next steps. Views alone do not show that viewers understood the item or placed orders. Combine the available numbers with actual questions, then improve the part that remained unclear. For better demonstration assets, use [the photography guide](/blog/product-photography-checklist/) rather than adding more promotional text.

title: Diagnose an Instagram campaign that attracts clicks but no orders
description: Investigate message-to-page mismatch, product uncertainty and checkout friction before spending more on an Instagram campaign that is not producing orders.
body:
Clicks with no orders are a symptom, not a diagnosis. A campaign may be attracting the wrong expectation, sending people to the wrong page, or reaching buyers who need information that the store does not provide. It can also be too small or too recent to support a reliable conclusion.

Investigate the buying path in order. Do not immediately reduce every price or increase the budget. Start with the evidence you actually have and label unknowns rather than filling them with a conversion-rate benchmark from another business.

## Check that the visits are what you think they are

Write down the measurement behind the word “click.” A click reported by a promotional tool is not necessarily a loaded product page, and a product visit is not an order attempt. Use the definitions in your own reporting setup.

Keep the time window consistent. Comparing yesterday's clicks with this month's orders produces a misleading picture. Allow for customers who return later, while acknowledging that a basic report may not connect every return visit to its original source.

If you cannot observe the whole journey, say so in your notes. You can still inspect the page and collect enquiry themes without pretending to have complete attribution.

## Compare the advertisement with its destination

Read the advertisement as a new customer. What does it appear to promise: a particular product, a price, immediate dispatch, customisation or a collection?

Now open the destination. If the advertisement shows a ready-made scarf and the page opens a general catalogue of custom products, fix that mismatch first. A shopper should not need to rediscover the item they just chose to view.

Check for outdated offers and sold-out featured variants. Do not use a cheap entry price as the main attraction if the pictured combination costs more and that distinction is hidden.

## Look for unanswered product questions

Ask someone unfamiliar with the range to identify the product's size, contents, material, options and dispatch status using only the page. Their difficulty is useful evidence, even though one person's response is not a market-wide study.

For an illustrative candle listing, a photograph alone may leave the buyer uncertain about container size, quantity and whether the lid is included. Another paragraph calling it “premium” does not answer those questions.

Use [the product-page checklist](/blog/product-page-checklist/) to close factual gaps. Do not add customer ratings, safety statements or material claims unless you can substantiate them.

## Follow the buying process without creating an unwanted order

Check the public journey on a phone: selecting an option, changing quantity, viewing the bag and reaching the information required before confirmation. Stop before a real submission or payment unless you have an authorised test process.

Record the specific point of failure. “Checkout is confusing” is less actionable than “the delivery charge appears only after the customer has entered their address and cannot be reviewed with the item options.”

A failed payment or broken control needs technical investigation. A lack of delivery coverage needs an operational answer. More persuasive copy will not repair either.

## Separate traffic quality from store friction

A simple investigation table keeps these questions apart.

| Observation | Next thing to inspect |
|---|---|
| People cannot find the promoted item | Destination and navigation |
| Repeated questions about size | Measurements and photographs |
| Interest drops when shipping appears | Earlier cost disclosure and actual shipping value |
| People request unavailable colours | Campaign choice and stock accuracy |
| Order attempts fail | Technical and payment workflow |

These are hypotheses to check, not automatic explanations. For example, a shipping question does not prove that the shipping price is excessive; it may mean the information was difficult to find.

## Make one bounded change and observe it

Choose the clearest problem and write down the change, date and intended outcome. Correcting a broken link can be done immediately. For less obvious problems, avoid changing the creative, audience, product price and page layout at the same time.

Set a review point appropriate to your traffic and spending limit. If the sample remains small, keep the conclusion modest. “Fewer buyers asked what the set includes” is a useful operational result even when you cannot yet establish a dependable order-rate change.

Do not keep paying for traffic to an unresolved failure. Pause or reduce the affected promotion while the broken step is repaired, using the controls and permissions available in your account.

Finally, inspect stock and fulfilment capacity before scaling a successful experiment. [The inventory guide](/blog/inventory-for-instagram-sellers/) helps prevent an improved campaign from creating promises the shop cannot keep. A good diagnosis ends with a repaired step and a clearer measurement, not a claim that every visitor should buy.

title: Build an order summary a WhatsApp customer can confirm
description: Use one written order summary to confirm product choices, delivery details and the next action before a WhatsApp enquiry becomes an order.
body:
A long WhatsApp conversation can contain several versions of the same order. The customer changes a colour, asks about a second item, gives a different delivery date and finally says “okay.” Unless you create a clear summary, neither person can be certain which version that agreement refers to.

A summary is not a payment receipt or proof that stock has been reserved. It is a readable statement of the proposed order and what happens next. Build it from checked facts rather than copying the last few messages.

## Identify the actual items

Use the public product name together with the choice that changes what you will supply. Record the colour, size, variant or personalisation exactly enough for somebody else to prepare the order.

For a set, state both the ordered quantity and the contents. “Two” could mean two individual earrings or two pairs. Resolve that before asking the customer to confirm anything.

A product link or photograph can support the description, but it should not replace the written choice. Images can disappear from a conversation, and similar-looking products may have different dimensions or prices.

## Separate confirmed facts from information still needed

Check availability, delivery coverage and any custom-work capacity before presenting the summary as ready to accept. If something remains unknown, label it.

For example, “delivery charge to be confirmed after postcode check” is honest, but the order is not yet a final-total proposal. Do not ask the buyer to agree to a total that can silently change later.

The [WhatsApp Business feature documentation](https://whatsappbusiness.com/products/business-app-features/) describes a catalogue cart as items sent in a message. Treat that incoming message as information to process, not proof that payment, availability and delivery have all been confirmed.

## Use a compact, complete confirmation format

The following is an illustrative structure, not an oBizee notification template:

| Section | Information |
|---|---|
| Reference | Your private enquiry or order reference |
| Items | Product, option, quantity and counting unit |
| Charges | Item amounts, agreed discount and delivery charge |
| Total | The amount and currency the customer is being asked to accept |
| Fulfilment | Ready-made or made-to-order; dispatch estimate |
| Delivery | The necessary address confirmation in the private conversation |
| Next action | What the buyer should confirm and how payment is handled |

Only include information needed for this order. Do not copy identity documents, unrelated conversations or sensitive account information into the summary.

## Ask for confirmation of the important choices

A useful request is specific: “Please confirm the cream colour, one pair and the delivery details above.” It helps the customer notice the parts most likely to cause a packing mistake.

For personalisation, present the exact text separately. Names, initials and dates need explicit checking. Do not rely on autocorrect or assume that an earlier spelling remains current after several revisions.

If you send a revised summary, mark it as the replacement and identify the changed field. Avoid having two apparently valid totals or delivery addresses in use at the same time.

## Record the agreement in the order workflow

Once the customer confirms, transfer the agreed details into your actual order record. Keep a reference connecting the conversation and record so another person does not create the same order again.

Record payment status through your payment-confirmation process. Do not use “confirmed” as a single label for customer approval, stock commitment and money received; those states can happen at different times.

If stock must be held manually, follow the rule you have actually established. [The stock guide](/blog/inventory-for-instagram-sellers/) explains why an enquiry and a reservation should not be treated as the same event.

## Handle changes after confirmation deliberately

When a customer asks to change something, check whether the order has reached production or packing. Do not promise an edit before checking its practical effect.

Create an updated agreement if the change is accepted. Preserve the earlier version in the protected record instead of overwriting the history without explanation. The packer needs the current version; support may need to understand how it changed.

If the change affects the total, obtain the customer's agreement to that difference. Do not quietly substitute an item because it seems similar or costs the same.

## Check your summary with somebody unfamiliar with the chat

Ask whether they could identify the exact item and next action from the summary alone. If they need to read dozens of messages to find the colour or quantity, improve the format.

Keep the summary short enough to read but complete enough to prevent guesswork. For missing product information, start with [catalogue preparation](/blog/product-page-checklist/). The useful outcome is one clear agreement connected to one order record—not a longer conversation with a more official-looking heading.

title: Make quick replies useful without sending the wrong answer
description: Build a small library of accurate saved replies with clear editing fields, review dates and safeguards against sending outdated prices or promises.
body:
Quick replies save time only when the answer remains correct for the person receiving it. A fast message containing the wrong delivery date or another product's care instructions creates more work than a careful manual response.

Think of a saved reply as a checked starting point. Some parts can stay fixed; other parts must be verified each time. The distinction matters more than the number of shortcuts in your library.

## Choose repeated questions with stable answers

Start with questions you genuinely receive: how to find measurements, where to browse the range, what information is needed for an order enquiry, or when support normally responds.

Avoid turning highly variable answers into rigid scripts. Stock availability, personalised pricing and a particular parcel's delivery status need current information. A saved structure can help, but the final answer should come from the relevant record.

[WhatsApp's Business App feature page](https://whatsappbusiness.com/products/business-app-features/) describes quick replies as shortcuts for frequently sent messages. That capability does not verify the facts inside your reply or make your other systems synchronise automatically.

## Separate fixed wording from checked fields

Write the stable explanation first, then identify any field that requires a current value. Make placeholders visually obvious while drafting, but do not send them to customers.

For example, a dispatch reply might have a fixed explanation of working days and a variable estimate based on the customer's item and your workload. “Your order will dispatch tomorrow” should never be the default simply because it is a reassuring sentence.

Keep a private instruction beside the reply: check the product's fulfilment state, verify the estimate, then send. The instruction is for your team, not part of the customer message.

## Give replies understandable names

Use names that describe the question rather than vague labels such as “reply1.” Distinguish pre-purchase delivery guidance from an update about an existing order.

A small library might include “where-to-find-size,” “information-for-custom-order,” “support-hours” and “tracking-check-in-progress.” Choose a naming format your actual tool accepts.

Retire duplicates that differ only slightly. If helpers cannot tell which of three shipping replies is current, the library is creating uncertainty rather than reducing it.

## Keep the tone direct and specific

A saved reply should answer the question before promoting another product. Avoid a long greeting, several emojis and a sales pitch when the customer asked for one measurement.

Illustrative wording for a size enquiry is: “The product page lists the measurements below the description. Compare those with an item that fits you well; if you tell us which measurement is unclear, we can explain it.” Only use this if the page actually contains that information.

Do not promise a fit guarantee that your process does not offer. The reply should help the customer decide, not conceal a limitation.

## Read the conversation before sending

Check whether the customer already supplied the requested information. Asking again for an order reference that is visible in the preceding message makes a shortcut feel like a refusal to listen.

Watch for exceptions. A buyer reporting a damaged parcel needs a resolution process, not the generic delivery-times reply. A customer who has already waited beyond a promised update needs an acknowledgement of that missed commitment.

If a reply no longer fits, write a tailored response and record whether the library needs a new category. Do not force every case into an existing shortcut.

## Review links and promises regularly

Give each reply an owner and a last-checked date. Revisit replies when you change policies, product information, operating hours or order handling.

Test the public links. A saved reply can keep sending customers to a removed page long after the website has changed.

Keep sensitive information out of the library. Never store real customer addresses, payment credentials or private order details as examples. Use clearly fictional placeholders in internal documentation.

## Measure whether the library reduces repeat work

Notice whether customers understand the answer or immediately ask the same question again. A reply that is sent quickly but regularly misunderstood is not successful.

Ask helpers which replies require the most editing. That may reveal that the answer is too variable for a shortcut or that the underlying product information is incomplete.

Use [the catalogue checklist](/blog/product-page-checklist/) to fix recurring factual gaps and [the WhatsApp-versus-store guide](/blog/online-store-vs-whatsapp-business/) to decide which questions belong on a stable page. A useful reply library makes accurate service easier while leaving room for judgement; it should not turn a personal conversation into an inflexible script.

title: Write order-status messages that match what actually happened
description: Write order updates from verified events—request received, accepted, packed and handed over—so customers know what has happened and what remains pending.
body:
“Your order is confirmed” can mean several different things. The customer may understand it as payment received and stock secured, while the seller means only that a message arrived. That ambiguity creates avoidable support work.

Choose status language that matches the actual event. You do not need an automated notification system to do this well. A manual update based on a reliable record is more useful than an automatic message that overstates progress.

## Name the event before writing the message

Separate receipt of an enquiry from acceptance of an order. Separate acceptance from payment verification where payment is required. Separate packing from courier handover.

Write a small internal status dictionary. For each status, define what must be true before somebody uses it and where that fact is recorded.

Do not adopt a status name merely because another store uses it. Your workflow may collect payment or confirm availability at a different stage.

## Give the customer the useful consequence

A status label alone can be unclear. Explain what the event means and whether the customer needs to act.

For example, an enquiry acknowledgement can say that you received the requested items and will check availability. It should not claim that the items are reserved unless your actual process has created that commitment.

A packing update can state that the order is being prepared. A dispatch update should be based on the handover evidence available to you, not just the creation of a shipping label.

## Use a consistent message structure

A useful update contains the reference, verified event, next step and any realistic update time.

| Event | Useful wording direction | Do not imply |
|---|---|---|
| Request received | We have the details and will check the request | Acceptance or payment |
| Order accepted | State the agreed items and next step | An unverified delivery date |
| Packed | Preparation is complete or at the stated stage | Courier possession |
| Handed over | Identify the verified dispatch event | Guaranteed arrival |
| Investigation open | Name what is being checked and next update | Resolution already completed |

These are writing directions, not ready-to-send claims about any particular order. Fill them from the protected order record.

## Keep estimates separate from guarantees

Explain whether a date refers to production completion, dispatch or expected transit. “Three to five days” is incomplete if the customer cannot tell when counting begins.

If a date changes, acknowledge the earlier expectation and provide the best supported update. Avoid silently replacing an old estimate as though it had never been promised.

Do not blame a courier before checking the handover and tracking information. An order still in your packing area requires a different explanation from a parcel delayed after collection.

## Decide who can send each update

A helper may be authorised to acknowledge an enquiry but not approve a refund or a custom delivery commitment. Make those boundaries explicit.

If several people or tools send messages, check that they are not producing contradictory updates. The message history should follow the order history, not become a second competing source of truth.

Do not claim that oBizee or WhatsApp automatically sends a particular notification unless that exact feature and configuration have been verified. This guide describes the communication standard regardless of the tool used.

## Plan for missing or uncertain information

Sometimes the next event cannot be confirmed. Say what you know and what you are checking rather than choosing a more advanced status to reassure the customer.

An illustrative update is: “The label has been prepared, but I’m checking the collection record before confirming dispatch. I’ll update you by the end of the next working day.” Use only a follow-up time you can honour.

Avoid repeatedly sending “please wait” without a next action. A waiting case still needs an owner.

## Keep a record of important promises

Store the relevant update in the order or support history so another person can see what the customer was told. Do not keep critical delivery commitments only in an individual's memory.

When a case closes, confirm the actual outcome rather than merely saying that it has been marked closed. Approval, processing and completion may be separate events.

Use [the inventory guide](/blog/inventory-for-instagram-sellers/) for stock commitments and [the Instagram-to-store guide](/blog/instagram-to-online-store/) for the wider buying path. Accurate order messages reduce uncertainty because their words correspond to real events—not because they sound more polished.

title: Give product variants names customers and packers both understand
description: Separate customer-friendly variant labels from internal references so sizes, colours and product combinations remain clear from browsing through packing.
body:
Variant confusion often begins before checkout. A catalogue uses “natural,” a photograph says “beige,” a message says “cream,” and the packing note contains an internal code nobody recognises. These may all refer to one option—or to three genuinely different products.

Create a small naming system that makes the distinction clear. The purpose is not to make customers learn warehouse codes. It is to preserve the customer's choice as it moves between a product page, a conversation and the order record.

## Define what makes one choice different

Start with the physical or functional difference the customer can select: size, colour, finish, quantity per pack or another meaningful characteristic. Do not combine unrelated choices in a single ambiguous label.

“Blue large” can be readable, but your underlying record should still distinguish colour from size if the tool supports those fields. A free-text field that mixes size, personalisation and delivery instructions becomes difficult to validate and pack.

Avoid offering a choice merely because a supplier spreadsheet contains it. If you cannot explain what changes, clarify the product information before publishing the option.

## Pick one public name for each choice

Use language that buyers understand and that your photographs can support. If two cream shades are genuinely different, explain the difference rather than assigning almost identical names.

Maintain a private lookup where a supplier's label differs from yours. Your customer may see “warm ivory” while the incoming stock uses a supplier reference. Both can coexist if the relationship is recorded consistently.

Do not rename a variant casually after orders exist. If a naming correction is needed, keep a record of the previous label so support can interpret older orders accurately.

## Make labels and photographs agree

Where you show a particular colour or finish, identify it. A gallery of several options without labels forces the customer to guess which selection produces which item.

Check the chosen option after adding the product to a bag or preparing an order request. The label should remain understandable outside the original page. “Option 2” may make sense next to a photograph but becomes useless on a packing slip.

For colour-sensitive products, explain relevant display limitations without using them as a blanket excuse for inaccurate photographs. [The photography guide](/blog/product-photography-checklist/) helps you prepare clearer reference images.

## Keep internal references stable

An internal reference should identify the sellable choice even if the marketing title changes. It need not contain every product detail.

For an illustrative pouch range, a private mapping might be:

| Public product | Customer choice | Internal reference |
|---|---|---|
| Everyday pouch | Small, navy | PCH-101 |
| Everyday pouch | Small, ivory | PCH-102 |
| Everyday pouch | Large, navy | PCH-103 |

These are sample codes, not a required oBizee format. Before importing anything, check which reference fields your actual system supports. Do not assume a title, barcode and stock code are interchangeable.

## Remove impossible combinations

If the large pouch is not made in ivory, do not leave that combination looking orderable. Test the available combinations rather than checking only the default option.

Some tools support specific variant records; others require separate products or a different selection model. Choose the representation your current system can accurately maintain. Do not promise automatic stock validation without testing it.

Where a choice affects price or production time, make the effect visible before the customer agrees. An option should not become an unexpected surcharge discovered during a private follow-up.

## Carry the exact choice into packing

Create a sample order or authorised test record and inspect the downstream description. A packer should be able to identify the variant without reopening the customer's social conversation.

If your process relies on a manual note, define who writes it and when it is checked. Avoid keeping the definitive choice in somebody's memory while the shared order record remains incomplete.

For personalisation, store the exact approved text separately from the standard variant. A size label should not also contain a customer's address or unrelated instructions.

## Audit variants as a set

Check one product across its public page, image labels, order record and stock list. Look for missing choices, duplicate references, inconsistent units and names that changed without history.

Then apply the same audit to the rest of the range. Fixing only the most popular variant can leave rare combinations exposed to packing mistakes.

Use [the catalogue checklist](/blog/product-page-checklist/) before a large upload and [the inventory guide](/blog/inventory-for-instagram-sellers/) when assigning quantities. A good variant system allows the customer to choose naturally while allowing the business to fulfil that choice precisely.

title: Write a product description from evidence, not adjectives
description: Turn verified product details into a readable description that helps customers judge fit, use and fulfilment without exaggerated promises.
body:
A product description has a practical job: help someone decide whether this item is suitable and understand what will arrive. Calling a piece beautiful, premium or perfect does not answer its dimensions, contents or care requirements.

Start with a fact sheet, not a sales paragraph. Once the facts are clear, choose the order that helps the customer make a decision. You can still write warmly; accuracy does not require a catalogue to sound like a machine.

## Gather the information before drafting

Place the product in front of you where possible. Confirm its name, dimensions, material, counting unit, available options and included components. Record how each claim was checked.

For handmade items, distinguish between a measured example and an exact specification you can consistently reproduce. If normal variation is relevant, explain it precisely rather than using a vague disclaimer for every difference.

Do not copy a supplier's claims without checking that they apply to the item you actually sell. A material statement or performance claim may refer to a different version or require evidence you do not have.

## Open with the product and its use

The first sentence should orient the reader. “A small zip pouch for charging cables and everyday essentials” tells someone more than “Meet your new obsession.”

Avoid assuming the reader has seen the social post that brought them to the page. Name the object and its main practical purpose. Then introduce the meaningful distinction: compartments, construction, finish, personalisation or another verified characteristic.

Do not promise suitability for every person or situation. A demonstration can show a possible use without guaranteeing that every customer's belongings will fit.

## Translate features into bounded benefits

A feature describes the item. A benefit explains why that feature may matter. Keep the connection specific and supportable.

| Verified feature | Useful explanation | Claim to avoid without evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Internal pocket | Separates small items from the main compartment | You will never lose anything |
| Removable strap | Offers another carrying option | Suitable for every body size |
| Labelled dimensions | Helps compare with an item you already own | Guaranteed perfect fit |
| Supplied storage pouch | Provides a place to keep the item | Prevents all damage |

These examples illustrate writing choices, not specifications for a particular oBizee product. Use only features present in the item you are describing.

## Explain what the buyer is choosing

Describe variant differences where they matter. A choice called “large” needs a measurement or comparison, not just the reassurance that it is larger than “small.”

State whether one unit means one piece, one pair or a set. List the contents of a bundle when the photograph contains several objects. If styling accessories are excluded, say so near the relevant information.

For personalisation, explain what the customer must provide and when it is approved. Do not hide an important production dependency in a final paragraph below unrelated promotional copy.

## Put fulfilment information in the right place

Separate product characteristics from current availability and order timing. A description can explain that the item is made to order, while the live ordering information should show the current estimate you can support.

Do not leave a dated dispatch promise inside evergreen copy after your workload changes. If delivery information is maintained elsewhere, link to that information and ensure it matches the product's actual process.

Explain care using supported instructions. Avoid inventing washing temperatures, material tolerances or safety guidance because similar products use them.

## Edit for scanning and consistency

Use short paragraphs and a small set of descriptive headings or bullet points. A customer comparing several products should be able to find the same type of information in a predictable place.

Read the description alongside the photographs, variant labels and price presentation. If the copy says “set of four” while the title says “pair,” resolve the contradiction rather than hoping one field will take priority.

Check spelling, units and copied placeholders. A polished opening cannot rescue the wrong measurement or another product's care instructions.

## Test it against real questions

Ask someone unfamiliar with the product to explain what they would receive, which option they would choose and what remains uncertain. Use that feedback to find missing information, not as proof that the description will convert at a particular rate.

Keep a note of repeated customer questions after publication. If several people ask the same factual question, bring the answer into the description or an appropriate guide.

Use [the catalogue checklist](/blog/product-page-checklist/) for the complete listing and [the photography guide](/blog/product-photography-checklist/) for visual evidence. A strong description reduces guesswork while leaving the customer free to decide that a product is not right for them.

title: Build a size guide that explains measurements rather than guarantees
description: Explain what a size measurement means, how it was taken and how buyers can compare it with something they already own.
body:
A size guide is useful only when the customer understands what was measured. “Medium” does not explain a garment's actual dimensions, and a single length does not tell someone whether a bag will hold the object they want to carry.

Create the guide from the product, not from a generic chart found elsewhere. Your aim is to support a sensible comparison without promising that a measurement guarantees fit for every person or use.

## Define the measurement type

For clothing, distinguish a body measurement from a finished-garment measurement. They answer different questions. For a bag or pouch, distinguish outside dimensions from usable internal space where that difference matters.

Explain whether an item is measured flat, around its circumference, stretched or unstretched. Do not assume that a customer will infer the method from the number.

If you cannot establish the method reliably, measure again before publishing. A precise-looking chart with unclear definitions can be worse than no chart because it creates false confidence.

## Measure representative products consistently

Choose the points you will measure and document them with a clear photograph or diagram you have the right to use. Use the same method across sizes.

Record units prominently. Mixing centimetres and inches without labels invites mistakes. If you provide both, check the conversion and rounding rather than independently guessing a second number.

For handmade products, identify any supported tolerance or normal variation from your actual production process. Do not invent a universal allowance or use “handmade” to excuse a substantially inaccurate chart.

## Present only useful comparisons

A compact guide should help the buyer distinguish the options that actually exist. Avoid adding rows for sizes you do not sell simply because a template includes them.

| Information | Why it helps |
|---|---|
| Named measurement | Shows what the number describes |
| Measurement method | Makes comparison repeatable |
| Unit | Prevents conversion assumptions |
| Variant or size | Connects the chart to the selection |
| Relevant limitation | Explains usable space, stretch or other context |

For a laptop sleeve, compare the device's physical dimensions with the supported internal space. Screen diagonal alone does not describe the whole device.

## Show how to compare at home

Suggest comparing the guide with an item the customer already uses comfortably, using the same measurement method where practical. Explain the comparison without making a personal-fit guarantee.

For example, a buyer considering a pouch can measure the objects they intend to carry and inspect the opening as well as the overall size. A narrow opening can matter even when the interior dimensions look sufficient.

For garments, avoid unsupported body-type promises. If a customer needs specialist fitting advice, acknowledge the limitation of a general product guide rather than pretending a chart can resolve every concern.

## Connect the guide to the correct product

Place or link the relevant information where the customer chooses the size. A site-wide chart is inappropriate if different product families use different cuts or measurement methods.

Check that the selected variant's label appears exactly as the chart names it. “Large” in the selector and “L2” in the guide need an explanation if they refer to the same option.

If a supplier or pattern changes, review the guide before selling the new stock under the old measurements. Historical orders may need the earlier specification preserved in your records.

## Check the photographs for contradictory scale

Styling can distort perceived size. A product held by a person, placed beside an object or photographed close up needs enough context to prevent an unintended impression.

Use a scale reference that is understandable to your audience and label it where necessary. Do not use an image of one size beside the dimensions of another without saying so.

[The photography checklist](/blog/product-photography-checklist/) covers the broader role of scale and detail images. The chart and photograph should support each other, not tell different stories.

## Learn from size-related questions and returns

Record the information gap when customers repeatedly ask the same question. Do not automatically conclude that they failed to read the guide; the guide may be difficult to interpret or hard to find.

Where a complaint reveals an inaccurate measurement, correct the information and handle affected orders through your proper support process. Keep the correction traceable.

Use [catalogue preparation](/blog/product-page-checklist/) to check the full listing. A useful size guide ends with a clearer decision, including the possibility that the product is not suitable. That is better than obtaining an order through a promise the item cannot meet.

title: Prepare product data before moving it into a new store
description: Clean and map product records before a catalogue move, preserving identifiers, units, media rights and the distinction between product data and customer data.
body:
Moving a catalogue is easier when you separate data preparation from the actual import. A file that looks tidy in a spreadsheet can still contain duplicate references, inconsistent units and image links that the new store cannot use.

Prepare a controlled copy first. Do not edit the only source of truth while experimenting with a new format, and do not include customer records in a product import simply because they were present in the same export.

## Identify the source you can trust

Choose the current catalogue record, not the newest-looking file in a downloads folder. Check who maintains it and whether it reflects the products you actually offer.

Keep the original export unchanged and record when it was taken. Use a working copy for cleaning and mapping. If the business continues receiving orders during preparation, note which fields may change before the final move.

A catalogue export is not automatically a complete backup of the business. Orders, customer records, media, settings and policies may be stored separately.

## List the fields the destination really accepts

Read the current import specification for the tool you will use. Do not assume it accepts a competitor's column names, variant structure or image format.

Create a mapping from each source field to its destination. Mark fields that have no supported equivalent instead of silently dropping them.

For a basic product move, the mapping might cover names, descriptions, stable references, options, prices, units, availability and media. The exact requirements depend on your actual platform; this guide does not promise a particular oBizee importer.

## Resolve identifiers and units first

Give every sellable choice a consistent reference where your system supports one. Check duplicates before bringing quantities across.

Confirm what each quantity means: individual pieces, pairs, packs or sets. A stock value of ten is meaningless without the unit it counts.

Keep product identifiers separate from row numbers. Sorting a spreadsheet should not change which item an order or photograph refers to.

## Clean content without inventing missing facts

Remove obsolete promotional dates, copied placeholders and descriptions that belong to another product. Correct spelling while preserving the meaning of verified product information.

Where a material, size or care detail is missing, ask the responsible person or measure the product as appropriate. Do not fill the blank with an AI guess or a supplier claim from a similar item.

Preserve deliberate distinctions such as made-to-order versus ready-made. A neat uniform file is not an improvement if it erases information customers need.

## Check media access and ownership

Make sure the images refer to the correct products and that you have permission to use them. A public URL is not proof of usage rights.

Test whether the destination can obtain the media through the supported import process. Temporary links, private account URLs and local file paths may not remain usable after the move.

Keep an association between each image and its product or variant. A folder of correctly named products is not enough if the importer attaches photographs by a different rule.

## Build a representative test set

Before a full import, prepare a small authorised test containing different product shapes: a simple item, a variant product, a set, an unavailable item and a made-to-order item where relevant.

Include inconvenient cases such as punctuation, long descriptions and missing optional images. The easiest product is not a sufficient test of the whole catalogue.

Do not run an experimental import against a live store without the appropriate authority and recovery plan. Know whether the tool creates new records, updates existing ones or can do both.

## Record the handover package

Keep the original export, cleaned working copy, field mapping, exception list and test results together in an appropriately protected location.

A useful exception list identifies the product, missing or conflicting field, responsible person and resolution. Do not label the catalogue ready while unresolved exceptions can change what the customer orders.

Before the actual move, recheck fields that may have changed during preparation, especially availability and prices. Coordinate the cutover rather than assuming an old export is still current.

Use [the catalogue checklist](/blog/product-page-checklist/) for customer-facing completeness and [the stock guide](/blog/inventory-for-instagram-sellers/) for quantity definitions. Preparation succeeds when every important field has a known meaning and destination—not merely when the file uploads without an error.

title: Check an imported catalogue without sampling away the mistakes
description: Verify an imported catalogue with full field checks and representative buying-path tests instead of relying on a successful upload message.
body:
An importer reporting success means its process completed according to its own rules. It does not prove that every product has the right photograph, variant, price or customer-facing description.

Check the result against the prepared source. Use complete checks for fields you can compare mechanically and representative manual checks for presentation and behaviour. Do not use a few attractive examples to stand in for the whole catalogue.

## Preserve the comparison source

Keep the exact file or record set used for the import. If you change that source afterward, you can lose the ability to distinguish an import error from a later edit.

Record the import time, destination and available result report. Identify whether the operation created, updated or skipped records.

Do not include secrets or customer details in a widely shared evidence file. The catalogue check should use the product information needed to establish correctness.

## Reconcile counts with meaning

Compare source and destination counts, but explain what each count represents. One product with six variants may appear as one parent record in one system and several sellable records in another.

Investigate skipped, failed and duplicate entries individually. A matching total can still hide one missing product and one accidental duplicate.

Keep unavailable and draft products in the comparison where they were meant to transfer. Their absence may not be obvious on the public storefront.

## Check critical fields across the whole set

Where export or read access allows, compare stable references, option labels, prices, units and state for every imported item.

A practical checklist includes:

- Each source product maps to the intended destination record.
- Variant combinations remain attached to the correct parent.
- Currency and numeric formats are interpreted correctly.
- Pack quantities have not become individual-piece quantities.
- Unavailable products are not accidentally offered for sale.
- Media references belong to the correct item.

Do not claim a full-field comparison if you only inspected the page visually. Record the boundary of each check.

## Inspect representative presentation cases

Choose products that exercise different layouts and content lengths. Check a long title, several images, multiple variants, a set and any product with special fulfilment information.

Open the public page on a phone. Look for truncated meaning, unreadable tables, missing images and option names that no longer match the description.

A source field can be stored correctly but displayed in the wrong place or not displayed at all. That is why data comparison and presentation inspection are separate tasks.

## Test the selection-to-order handoff safely

Use an authorised preview or test process to check that the chosen variant and quantity remain correct through the bag and order review. Stop before an unwanted real order or payment.

Check more than the default option. A product may display correctly while sending the wrong selection downstream.

Do not assume that a product import also configured payments, shipping, taxes or stock synchronisation. Those are separate capabilities that need their own verified setup.

## Classify differences before correcting them

Sort findings into source-data problems, mapping problems, import failures and display defects. The right repair depends on the cause.

If the source contains an inaccurate material description, rerunning the import will reproduce it. If the importer interprets a decimal incorrectly, manually fixing one product leaves the rest exposed.

Keep a record of corrections and rerun the affected checks. Avoid making simultaneous undocumented changes in both source and destination, which can obscure whether the mapping now works.

## Confirm what happens on a repeat run

If repeat imports are part of your workflow, test their behaviour in an authorised environment. Does the operation update the intended records, create duplicates or ignore changes?

Use a stable identifier and the tool's documented process rather than assuming names alone provide reliable matching. Product names can change or collide.

Keep a recovery route appropriate to the operation. An import that updates live prices is not harmless simply because it does not delete products.

## Close with an explicit exception list

A useful completion note states the source count, destination interpretation, fields checked, representative cases tested and unresolved issues.

Do not write “all good” while known missing photographs or option errors remain. Assign those exceptions without hiding them behind the successful upload result.

Use [catalogue preparation](/blog/product-page-checklist/) to repair content gaps and [the stock guide](/blog/inventory-for-instagram-sellers/) to reconcile available quantities. The catalogue is ready when its information and buying behaviour match the intended source, not when the progress bar reaches the end.

title: Create stock codes that survive a growing product range
description: Design a simple internal stock-code system with unique variant references, clear units and a lookup that remains useful when product names change.
body:
A stock code is an internal identifier. Its value comes from being unique, stable and connected to the correct item—not from containing every detail about the product.

If your shop currently uses “blue bag,” “new blue bag” and “blue bag final,” start by separating public names from internal references. Customers should see understandable product names. Your records need a dependable way to distinguish the exact sellable choices behind those names.

## Decide what receives its own reference

Begin with the unit you manage separately. Different sizes or colours may require different stock references if they have independent quantities. A pack may need its own reference if you receive and sell it as a pack.

Do not assign separate references merely because the same item appears in two marketing collections. A summer collection and a gift collection can point to the same physical stock. Creating two unrelated balances can make one item look like two.

For components and finished bundles, decide how the relationship is recorded. A bundle reference does not create additional pieces of its components.

## Choose a format you can maintain

A short sequential reference can work well. A structured reference can also work if the structure remains understandable. The important choice is consistency.

For an illustrative range, BAG-001, BAG-002 and BAG-003 could identify three sellable variants. A private lookup supplies the full meaning. You do not need to encode the current price, supplier, season and material into every code.

Avoid characters that are easily confused in your workflow. Check any restrictions imposed by the systems, printers or import tools you use before assigning a format across the catalogue.

## Keep a controlled lookup

Create one place where a reference maps to its current description and counting unit.

| Reference | Product and variant | Unit | State |
|---|---|---|---|
| BAG-001 | Everyday pouch, navy, small | One piece | Active |
| BAG-002 | Everyday pouch, ivory, small | One piece | Active |
| SET-001 | Two-piece pouch gift set | One set | Active |

These are examples, not prescribed identifiers or a statement about oBizee's fields. Keep supplier references separately if they serve a different purpose.

Do not put customer information inside stock codes. Codes may appear on labels, exports and shared operational documents.

## Assign codes before importing quantities

Check the list for duplicates and missing variants before entering stock. Two items sharing a reference can create more damaging confusion than two items sharing a similar display name.

If you already have records, build a mapping from old identifiers to new ones. Do not replace references in active orders without understanding how your system links those orders to products.

Keep a copy of the mapping and use an authorised migration process for software changes. Renaming a spreadsheet cell is not necessarily the same as safely changing a system identifier.

## Make the physical location match the record

Label storage positions or containers clearly enough that a helper can find the right item. A code on a sheet is useful only if the physical stock can be identified.

Where several variants look similar, include a human-readable description next to the internal reference. This helps catch a misplaced item before it becomes a wrong dispatch.

Do not assume a handwritten label is a scannable barcode. If you need scanning, verify the tool's actual barcode requirements and test the printed result.

## Preserve history when products change

A marketing title can change without changing the physical item. In that situation, preserve the stable identifier and update the description in a controlled way.

A materially different product may require a new reference, particularly when old and new stock coexist. Record what changed so packing and support do not treat incompatible versions as interchangeable.

Retire discontinued references rather than immediately reusing them for unrelated items. Historical orders and adjustments should remain understandable.

## Check whether the system works in practice

Ask somebody to locate a variant using the record, identify its counting unit and connect it to a sample packing instruction. Watch where they hesitate.

Then inspect a receipt, sale, return and count correction. The same reference should identify the same item across those events. If it does not, fix the mapping before adding more codes.

Use [the stock guide](/blog/inventory-for-instagram-sellers/) for quantity states and [catalogue preparation](/blog/product-page-checklist/) for public product information. The best coding system is one your team can use reliably as the range grows, not the most elaborate code you can invent today.

title: Count physical stock without pausing your entire business
description: Run a controlled physical count with clear locations, units and movement handling, then investigate differences before adjusting stock.
body:
A physical count is a snapshot. If items are being received, packed or moved while you count without a recording rule, the snapshot can become inconsistent before you finish.

You do not always need to close the entire business. You do need to define the area being counted, control movements affecting it and use the same stock definitions throughout the exercise.

## Choose the scope and time

Start with a manageable product group or storage location. Scarce, frequently sold or discrepancy-prone items can be useful priorities, but the choice should reflect your own risks.

Tell everyone helping which items are included and when the count begins. Avoid having one person count a shelf while another quietly picks orders from it.

If you cannot pause movements, record each relevant receipt, pick or transfer with its time so the count can be reconciled to a consistent point. Do not rely on memory at the end.

## Prepare the locations without hiding problems

Make product references and units readable. Separate obviously damaged items, samples and returns awaiting inspection from sellable stock.

Do not move uncertain items into a miscellaneous box simply to make the shelves look organised. That can remove the very evidence the count needs.

Identify stock already packed for orders. Decide how your count records those physical pieces without making them available for another sale.

## Count independently of the expected number

Where practical, let the counter record what is physically present before seeing the expected balance. This helps reduce the temptation to stop counting when the familiar number appears.

Use a second count for meaningful differences or difficult items. The second count should verify the item and unit, not just repeat the first person's arithmetic.

For packs, check whether the outer packaging contains the expected number. A partially used pack should not automatically be counted as a full one.

## Record the state, not just the quantity

A useful count sheet distinguishes the item, location, unit and condition.

| Field | Example purpose |
|---|---|
| Product and variant reference | Identifies exactly what was counted |
| Location | Prevents the same container being counted twice |
| Unit | Distinguishes pieces, pairs and packs |
| Sellable physical quantity | Records inspected stock in that state |
| Other quantity | Separates damage, samples or pending inspection |
| Counter and time | Supports reconciliation with movements |

Keep customer information out of the count sheet. Use order references if packed commitments need to be connected to the order system.

## Reconcile movements during the count

If two pieces were picked after a shelf was counted, account for that event. If a delivery arrived but was not inspected, do not silently include it as sellable stock.

Choose one consistent cut-off point and explain how the count relates to it. Mixing a morning count for one shelf with an afternoon system balance for another can create artificial discrepancies.

Check transfers between counted locations carefully. An item moved from one shelf to another can otherwise be missed or counted twice.

## Investigate differences before updating records

Recount, confirm units and inspect recent movements. A mismatch may reflect a duplicated sale, an unrecorded sample or a returned item placed back too early.

Document the supported reason for any correction. If the cause remains unknown, record that uncertainty rather than inventing an explanation.

Use your authorised stock-adjustment process. A physical count does not give permission to overwrite unrelated product or order data.

## Turn the count into a repeatable routine

Record how long the count took, which locations were difficult and which problems recurred. Improve labelling, storage or movement recording before the next round.

Choose a frequency appropriate to order volume and risk. There is no single schedule that suits a shop with a few handmade pieces and another with hundreds of fast-moving variants.

Keep previous count records so you can distinguish an isolated error from a pattern. Repeated unexplained corrections are a signal to inspect the workflow, not simply count more often.

Use [the multi-channel inventory guide](/blog/inventory-for-instagram-sellers/) for quantity definitions and [catalogue preparation](/blog/product-page-checklist/) if references are unclear. A good count produces an explainable balance and fewer future discrepancies—not just a new total on a screen.

title: Investigate a stock mismatch before changing the total
description: Trace count differences through receipts, commitments, returns and unit mistakes before making a documented stock correction.
body:
A stock record says eight pieces are available, but the shelf contains six. The tempting response is to type six into the system and continue. That may make the screen match the shelf while leaving two customer commitments, a missed supplier receipt or a counting mistake unresolved.

Investigate the difference first. The aim is not to avoid every correction; it is to make corrections explainable and prevent the same problem from recurring.

## Contain the affected promise

Identify the exact product and variant before changing a catalogue-wide quantity. A mismatch for a medium blue shirt does not automatically affect every size or colour.

If the discrepancy could lead to an unfulfillable order, use your authorised process to limit new commitments while you check it. Do not promise availability from a number you already know may be wrong.

Review existing open orders for that variant. Customers with accepted commitments need attention before you restart promotion. Keep their personal details in the order system, using references in the investigation notes.

## Recount the same unit

Count again, preferably without showing the expected result to the person counting. Separate sellable items from damaged pieces, samples, returns awaiting inspection and goods already packed.

Confirm the unit. Three packs of four are not three individual pieces. A supplier receipt, product listing and stock screen can each be internally consistent while using different units.

Check nearby locations and similar variants. Misplaced stock is different from missing stock. Do not record a loss simply because an item was placed on the wrong shelf.

## Establish the last reliable position

Find the most recent physical count or receipt that you can support. Start from that point and list the movements since then.

An illustrative calculation is: ten sellable pieces counted, plus four received, minus five dispatched, minus one damaged. That leaves eight sellable pieces before considering any separate commitments. If your system's “available” number also deducts two held items, six available may be correct even though eight sellable pieces remain physically present.

Do not compare different stock definitions. Write down whether each number means physical, sellable, committed or available quantity.

## Trace one movement at a time

Review the records most likely to explain the difference.

| Possible cause | Evidence to check |
|---|---|
| Receipt not recorded | Supplier delivery and receiving note |
| Sale entered twice | Order reference linked to both movements |
| Cancellation not released | Current order state and hold history |
| Returned item counted too early | Inspection result and restock event |
| Sample removed | Internal issue or photoshoot note |
| Wrong variant picked | Packing record and nearby variant count |

Treat these as investigation paths, not accusations. A duplicate entry can arise from an unclear handover rather than carelessness.

If records are missing, describe the uncertainty. Do not invent a historical movement to make the arithmetic look complete.

## Make the correction with a reason

Once you have established the best supported count, record the adjustment through the tool or procedure you are authorised to use. Include the date, variant, previous quantity, corrected quantity, reason and responsible person.

Separate a confirmed cause from an unexplained variance. “Two units damaged during inspection” is not the same as “two units unaccounted for after recount.” Both may require an adjustment, but they lead to different follow-up work.

Avoid deleting the original movement merely to produce a tidy history. Preserve enough information for the next investigation to understand what happened.

## Repair the workflow that produced the mismatch

A repeated unit error needs a clearer receiving and listing convention. Duplicate entries need one order owner or a reliable duplicate check. Missing cancellation releases need a defined release step.

Test any software change with a controlled example before relying on it. Do not assume that updating one sales channel automatically updates another. The [multi-channel stock guide](/blog/inventory-for-instagram-sellers/) explains how to keep manual and automated boundaries explicit.

Assign the follow-up action to a named person and a date. “Be more careful” is not a process change that can be checked.

## Watch whether the discrepancy returns

Recount the affected variant after the next relevant movement or at a reasonable review point. If the same difference reappears, reopen the cause rather than repeating the same unexplained correction.

Keep a small log of variance types across the range. The pattern can tell you where to spend effort: receiving, packing, returns or channel handoffs.

A trustworthy stock record is not one that has never been corrected. It is one whose quantities, commitments and corrections can be understood. Use [catalogue preparation](/blog/product-page-checklist/) if inconsistent product references are making that understanding difficult.

title: Set a reorder alert from demand and lead time
description: Use observed demand, supplier lead time and a deliberate buffer to create a reorder trigger you can revise as your shop changes.
body:
A reorder alert should give you time to replenish before usable stock runs out. It should not be a copied number that ignores how quickly the item sells or how long replenishment actually takes.

Start with a simple calculation and document its assumptions. For a small or irregular range, judgement and a clear exception list may be more useful than a complicated forecast built on very little data.

## Define the stock you can use

Distinguish available stock from pieces already committed, damaged or waiting for inspection. The reorder decision should not treat those unavailable pieces as free supply.

Also record incoming stock, but do not assume an expected delivery is equivalent to inspected goods on the shelf. A late or short shipment can change the decision.

Use consistent units. A weekly demand figure measured in individual pieces cannot be compared directly with supplier quantities measured in packs.

## Observe demand over a meaningful period

Calculate demand from a period that reflects the item's current role. Note promotions, stockouts and unusual orders that may distort the average.

A stockout can hide demand because customers could not buy. A one-off bulk order can inflate the average if it is unlikely to recur. Keep those limitations visible.

Do not create a confident forecast from two sales simply because a spreadsheet can calculate one. For new items, use a cautious launch allocation and review actual demand before committing heavily.

## Measure replenishment lead time

Count the time from placing a usable replenishment order to having inspected, sellable stock available. Include production, transport and receiving work where relevant.

Use your actual supplier experience when available, not only the shortest quoted delivery. Record variation and known constraints such as minimum quantities or seasonal closures.

For products you make yourself, lead time includes your production queue. Material availability alone does not establish when finished pieces will be ready.

## Build an illustrative trigger

A basic starting point is expected demand during lead time plus a chosen buffer. The buffer is a business judgement, not a guarantee that stockouts cannot happen.

Suppose an item averages three pieces per day, replenishment takes seven days, and you deliberately choose a six-piece buffer. Expected lead-time demand is twenty-one pieces; the illustrative trigger is twenty-seven.

Those numbers are not recommendations for your shop. They show the calculation. You still need to consider variability, incoming stock, commitments, cash constraints and how the tool defines the quantity being monitored.

## Separate the alert from the purchase decision

Reaching the trigger should prompt a review, not necessarily an automatic order. Check current demand, open purchase orders, supplier changes and whether the product is being discontinued.

Avoid ordering twice because two people received the same alert. Record who owns the replenishment decision and the purchase reference once action is taken.

If your software supports an alert, test which quantity it uses. If it does not, a controlled manual review can still apply the rule. This guide does not claim that a particular oBizee automation exists.

## Decide the replenishment quantity separately

The point at which you reorder and the amount you order are different questions. A trigger of twenty-seven pieces does not mean the next purchase must be twenty-seven.

Consider storage, minimum order quantities, shelf life where relevant, supplier reliability and the resources tied up in stock. Avoid buying a large quantity only because the unit price is lower.

For significant financial commitments or regulated products, obtain appropriate professional advice. A simple stock formula is not a substitute for cash-flow planning or product-specific obligations.

## Review the rule when conditions change

Revisit the trigger after a promotion, a supplier delay, a product change or a sustained shift in demand. Keep the old assumptions in your notes so you can understand why the rule changed.

Track stockouts, emergency purchases and persistent excess stock. These outcomes help you judge whether the trigger and order quantity need adjustment.

Do not tune the rule after every single day's movement. Look for meaningful changes while responding promptly to known disruptions.

Use [the inventory guide](/blog/inventory-for-instagram-sellers/) to establish reliable quantities and [the discount guide](/blog/discounts-without-losing-margin/) before using promotions to solve excess stock. A good reorder routine turns a warning into a considered decision, with assumptions that somebody else can understand.

title: Keep bundle availability tied to its component items
description: Calculate bundle availability from the components it consumes, then record reservations, substitutions and returns without creating extra stock.
body:
A gift bundle can look like a separate product while drawing from the same items you also sell individually. If the bundle listing and individual listings each hold independent quantities without a reliable connection, you can promise the same piece more than once.

Begin with the bundle's contents. The selling name matters to the customer; the component list matters to availability and packing. Both need to describe the same offer.

## Write the contents as quantities and units

List every stock-managed component and the number required for one bundle. Include packaging if its availability limits whether the bundle can be supplied.

“Gift set” is not a usable stock specification. “One pouch, two scrunchies and one gift box” is. If the customer can choose colours, identify which component choices the order consumes.

Do not assume two similarly named components are interchangeable. Substituting a material, size or colour changes what the customer receives.

## Calculate the limiting component

For each component, divide the available quantity by the quantity needed per bundle and round down to whole bundles. The smallest result limits how many complete bundles can be offered.

Consider an illustrative set containing one pouch, two scrunchies and one box. With eight available pouches, thirteen scrunchies and ten boxes, the component capacities are eight, six and ten bundles respectively. The set is limited to six complete bundles.
