If the promised time cannot be met, arrange an honest update rather than letting the deadline disappear during the transfer.

Avoid making a fresh promise on behalf of another person without confirming that they can carry it out. Handover is coordination, not a way to pass an impossible deadline downstream.

## Use a compact structure

An illustrative private note could contain:

| Field | Example |
|---|---|
| Reference | Order or enquiry identifier |
| Verified state | Accepted; payment verification still open |
| Agreed choice | One small navy pouch; no personalisation |
| Remaining task | Check payment through the approved process |
| Next customer update | By the agreed working-day deadline |
| New owner | Person who acknowledged the handover |

The example is fictional and not a system-generated oBizee record. Use your actual workflow and appropriate access controls.

## Leave unnecessary private information out

Do not repeat full addresses, identity documents or payment details in a handover channel merely because they exist in the order. Point authorised staff to the protected record.

Avoid placing customer data in screenshots used for training or public progress reports. Prepare a fictional example instead.

When access is no longer needed, follow your business's access and retention procedures. A convenient shared note should not become a permanent uncontrolled archive.

## Confirm receipt and close the transfer

The receiving person should acknowledge the handover and understand the next action. Until then, the original owner should not assume responsibility has moved.

Check that the order record and any support queue show the current owner consistently. Otherwise two people may still act independently or both wait for the other.

If the handover repeatedly requires long explanations, inspect the underlying product and order records. The note may be compensating for missing structure.

Use [the stock guide](/blog/inventory-for-instagram-sellers/) for commitments and [catalogue preparation](/blog/product-page-checklist/) for product clarity. A good handover is brief because the facts are organised, not because important uncertainty has been omitted.

title: Separate production time, dispatch time and transit estimates
description: Explain production, dispatch and transit as separate stages so customers can understand an estimate without mistaking it for a guaranteed arrival date.
body:
“Delivery in five days” is a risky phrase when you actually mean that production takes five days before the parcel can be handed to a courier. The customer hears an arrival promise; the business intended a preparation estimate.

Separate the stages in your public information and order messages. Clear timing helps buyers decide whether the product suits their occasion and reduces avoidable follow-up questions.

## Define the three clocks

Production time covers making or customising the item. Dispatch time concerns preparing and handing over the parcel. Transit concerns the journey after the carrier receives it.

Your process may combine some work, but the customer's understanding still matters. Explain when an estimate begins and whether you mean calendar days or working days.

Do not add together vague numbers and present the result as a guarantee. Each stage can have its own dependencies and uncertainty.

## Distinguish ready stock from made-to-order work

A ready-made product may still need checking, packing and a collection slot. “In stock” does not automatically mean it leaves immediately.

A made-to-order item needs a production estimate based on the current queue and required approvals. The clock may depend on receiving the customer's final personalisation details.

Keep these product types clear in the catalogue. A single site-wide statement can mislead buyers if some products are ready while others require substantial work.

## State what starts the estimate

Identify the event your estimate depends on: acceptance, verified payment, approved customisation or another actual step in your process.

Do not quietly restart the clock after taking an order if the initial information implied a different starting point. If a missing detail prevents work, explain that dependency before agreement.

Record the relevant event so support can understand the timing later. A remembered promise is difficult to reconcile when several people help with orders.

## Write the sequence in plain language

An illustrative made-to-order explanation might be: “We normally need the stated production period after your design approval. Packing and courier handover follow; the carrier's transit estimate is separate.”

Replace “stated period” with a current, supportable estimate for the product. Do not copy another seller's timeline or use the shortest completion time you have ever achieved.

For a ready item, explain the dispatch window and then the available transit information. Keep uncertainty visible where the carrier provides an estimate rather than a guaranteed service.

## Ask about occasion dates before promising suitability

If the buyer needs the item for an event, compare the full sequence with that date. Include the work still needed, current capacity and relevant delivery coverage.

Do not promise arrival simply because the production stage fits. A parcel still needs to be handed over and transported.

Where the timing is uncertain, say so and let the customer decide. An alternative product or a declined request may be more responsible than accepting an unrealistic deadline.

## Update delays against the original expectation

When a stage slips, identify what changed and what remains known. “Still processing” is less useful than “production is complete, but the scheduled collection did not occur.”

Give a realistic next update time even when you cannot yet provide a reliable new arrival estimate. Avoid repeatedly moving the date without acknowledging the earlier commitment.

Keep the order and communication history aligned. A system status should not say dispatched while the parcel is still awaiting handover.

## Maintain timing information during busy periods

Review public estimates when your production queue, collection schedule or known carrier conditions change. A festival promotion can increase workload faster than an old product description reflects.

Check scheduled posts and saved replies too. They may continue making outdated promises even after the main policy page is corrected.

Use [the inventory guide](/blog/inventory-for-instagram-sellers/) to keep capacity and commitments distinct, and [the product-page checklist](/blog/product-page-checklist/) to place fulfilment information where buyers can find it.

The aim is not to make every estimate longer. It is to make the estimate mean what the customer reasonably thinks it means, with a clear beginning, stage and level of certainty.

title: Choose packaging around the item’s damage risks
description: Choose packaging by examining movement, impact, moisture and presentation risks, then test the finished parcel against your carrier’s requirements.
body:
A ceramic cup and a fabric scrunchie can weigh the same and still need very different packaging. Weight alone does not describe how an item may be damaged.

Start with the product's vulnerabilities and the handling it must tolerate. This guide provides an assessment method, not a certified packaging specification. Follow the current requirements for your actual product and carrier, especially for fragile, hazardous, perishable or regulated goods.

## Inspect the product before choosing the box

Identify parts that can break, bend, scratch, leak, tangle or stain. Consider whether several items in one parcel can damage one another.

For a set containing hard and soft components, the hard item may need separation even if the outer box looks sturdy. A polished finish may need protection from rubbing as well as impact.

Write down the risks. “Fragile” is less useful to the packer than “handle can strike the neighbouring cup; glazed surfaces must not rub.”

## Separate product protection from presentation

A branded sleeve can look attractive without providing meaningful transit protection. Tissue paper may improve presentation but may not control movement or protect a vulnerable component.

Decide what each material does. Use presentation materials where they add value, but do not assume they replace a protective layer.

Check that the packaging itself does not create a problem through colour transfer, adhesive contact or pressure on a delicate feature. Use materials suitable for the product.

## Control movement inside the parcel

Place the item in its intended packaging and assess whether it can shift or collide with another component. Do this safely and according to appropriate packaging guidance.

Do not compensate for the wrong outer size by adding random scraps without understanding their effect. The finished parcel needs a consistent method another person can reproduce.

Where a component requires a particular orientation or support, make that part of the packing instruction. A handwritten “handle carefully” note does not physically prevent movement.

## Consider the route and service

Check the carrier's accepted packaging, dimensional limits and any product restrictions. A package suitable for a local hand delivery may not suit a multi-stage courier journey.

Do not promise that an “upright” label ensures the parcel remains upright. Design and approve the packing method for the handling conditions required by the service.

If you cannot establish a safe method for an unusual item, obtain specialist packaging or carrier advice before offering that delivery option.

## Create a repeatable packing specification

Record the product or range, outer package, protective materials, separation method and final checks. Include photographs of your own approved packing example where helpful.

A useful specification lets a helper reproduce the method rather than interpret “pack nicely.” Keep material sizes or references identifiable.

For mixed orders, define when the standard method no longer applies. Adding one more item can change the space and pressure inside the parcel.

## Test before scaling

Use an appropriate controlled test for the risks and service involved. Inspect the product and packaging afterward, and record what the test actually establishes.

Do not claim that one successful shipment proves the method will never fail. Keep customer-reported damage and carrier observations connected to the packing configuration used.

If you change the box or protective material, reassess the method. A cheaper replacement with similar appearance may not behave the same way.

## Balance waste, cost and protection

Reducing unnecessary material is worthwhile, but removing a protective function can create replacements, extra transport and customer frustration.

Compare the complete outcome rather than only the cost of the box. Track damage patterns by product and packing method so you can make a more informed decision.

Avoid unsupported environmental claims about packaging. Describe verified materials or disposal instructions accurately rather than labelling every brown box sustainable.

Use [the product photography guide](/blog/product-photography-checklist/) to keep presentation honest and [the stock guide](/blog/inventory-for-instagram-sellers/) to isolate damaged goods. A dependable packing method is a documented response to the product's risks, not simply more layers or a more expensive carton.

title: Check an address before the parcel reaches the courier
description: Check delivery details privately and consistently before booking a parcel, with a clear process for incomplete addresses and last-minute changes.
body:
An incomplete address is easier to resolve before the parcel leaves than after a delivery attempt fails. The check should confirm the information needed for fulfilment without turning a routine order into unnecessary personal-data collection.

Use the current order record as the starting point. Do not reconstruct an address from several old messages or assume that a returning customer wants the same destination as last time.

## Ask for the details your delivery process needs

Use the address fields required by your actual shipping service and destination. Explain missing information clearly rather than repeatedly saying “send full address.”

Keep the conversation private. Do not ask a customer to post an address, phone number or order reference in a public comment.

Avoid requesting identity documents as a default address check. If a particular service requires additional verification, follow its legitimate process and explain the requirement appropriately.

## Check consistency, not just whether fields are filled

A filled form can still contain contradictory information. Review the city, region and postcode relationship through the tools and process you are authorised to use.

Do not guess the intended locality from a similar place name. Ask a concise clarifying question when something does not match.

Preserve meaningful building, unit or delivery-access information where supported. Removing it to make a label look shorter can make the address less usable.

## Confirm the current destination

For a message-led order, show the relevant delivery details back to the customer in the private confirmation process. Ask them to check the important fields before dispatch.

For a store-led process, use the accepted address in the order record. If the customer requests a change, treat it as a change request rather than silently replacing the history.

Check the order's stage before agreeing. An address edit after courier handover may require a carrier-supported process and may not be possible.

## Keep serviceability separate from address validity

An address can be genuine while a particular service does not cover it. Confirm coverage using your current carrier or shipping workflow before promising that option.

Do not assume cash collection, express delivery or another service is available everywhere the carrier delivers. Check the exact combination you intend to offer.

If the requested option is unavailable, explain the supported alternatives and any effect on price or timing before the customer agrees.

## Pass the correct version to the label

Compare the shipping record with the current approved destination before printing or attaching the label. A corrected order address is not enough if an earlier label remains in use.

Remove obsolete labels through the proper workflow rather than leaving two competing destinations visible.

Keep address information out of general campaign spreadsheets and public packing photographs. Only people who need the details for fulfilment or support should have appropriate access.

## Handle ambiguity without blame

If a detail is unclear, ask a specific question: the missing unit, an inconsistent postcode or the required locality. Do not imply that the customer caused a delivery failure before the facts are known.

Record the confirmed correction and its time. This helps distinguish an address issue from a picking, booking or carrier problem later.

Where the customer cannot be reached, follow your stated order process rather than dispatching to a guessed destination merely to meet an internal deadline.

## Learn from unsuccessful deliveries

When a parcel cannot be delivered, compare the actual reason with the address check. Some failures may involve access, availability, service conditions or carrier handling rather than a wrong address.

Do not label every returned parcel as a fake order. Use evidence-based categories and preserve uncertainty where the reason is unclear.

If the same field is repeatedly missing, improve the order form or confirmation message. A better collection process can prevent repeated manual correction.

Use [the catalogue checklist](/blog/product-page-checklist/) for clear delivery expectations and [the Instagram-to-store guide](/blog/instagram-to-online-store/) for a structured ordering route. The address check is complete when the approved details, supported service and label agree—not merely when every box contains text.

title: Keep shipping labels readable without exposing customer details
description: Prepare legible shipping labels, match them to the right parcel and handle discarded copies as customer information rather than ordinary scrap.
body:
A correct address on the wrong parcel is still a wrong delivery. Label quality and label matching are separate checks, and both matter.

Use the label generated or accepted by your actual shipping process. This guide covers the operating routine around it; dimensions, placement and barcode requirements must follow the current carrier instructions.

## Print from the current shipment record

Confirm the order and shipping details before generating the label. If the destination or service changes, check whether the previous label must be replaced through the provider's process.

Do not alter a generated label in a way that changes required information or interferes with its machine-readable elements. Use the supported correction route.

Keep the shipment reference connected to the order so support can investigate later without guessing which parcel belongs to the customer.

## Check legibility before packing is finished

Inspect text and machine-readable areas for fading, clipping, smudging or distortion. A label that looks acceptable at a glance may have a missing edge or unreadable reference.

Use suitable printer settings and material according to the carrier's guidance. Do not assume that shrinking a label to fit a smaller space is harmless.

If the print is faulty, replace it properly rather than relying on handwritten additions to repair essential data.

## Match one label to one completed order

Use a repeatable check between the order reference, contents and label. Printing a large stack first can save time but requires a reliable matching process.

For a small workspace, handling one order at a time may reduce confusion. For batch work, separate orders physically and verify each pairing before attachment.

Do not use customer names alone when names may repeat. The order or shipment reference provides a more dependable connection.

## Place it according to the service instructions

Follow the carrier's requirements for surface, visibility and protection. Avoid placement that makes the label difficult to scan or likely to be damaged during normal handling.

Remove obsolete labels and barcodes from reused packaging where appropriate. Multiple visible routing references can create confusion.

Do not assume that adding a second identical-looking label is always the correct solution. Check the specific service requirements rather than improvising.

## Keep customer details out of public content

A dispatch photograph can accidentally expose names, addresses, phone numbers and tracking references. Cover or exclude labels before creating marketing images.

Use fictional or safely redacted examples for training material. Check the full image, not just the most obvious address block.

Do not post a customer's label as proof that your shop is busy. Fulfilling an order does not automatically provide permission to publicise their personal information.

## Dispose of failed prints appropriately

Treat misprints, cancelled labels and old packing sheets as records containing customer information. Do not leave them in an accessible pile or use them as visible scrap packaging.

Follow the business's appropriate retention and disposal process. Keep what is legitimately needed for fulfilment or investigation in the protected system rather than collecting uncontrolled paper copies.

If another person helps with printing, include this handling rule in the task instructions. It is easy to overlook privacy when the immediate concern is a jammed printer.

## Reconcile labels with parcels at handover

Compare prepared shipments with the parcels actually leaving. A generated label does not prove that its parcel was packed or collected.

Record the available handover evidence and investigate labels with no corresponding parcel. This prevents premature dispatch messages and makes missing-parcel questions easier to trace.

If a label is unused, follow the provider's cancellation or correction process where applicable. Do not reuse it for a different order without explicit support for that action.

## Review recurring errors

Log common problems: wrong paper size, clipped prints, mixed batches, old labels or a mismatch between order and shipping records.

Fix the repeated cause instead of adding more last-minute checking to an already confusing process. A clear sequence can be more effective than asking a tired packer to inspect the same stack several times.

Use [the stock guide](/blog/inventory-for-instagram-sellers/) for order-to-item consistency and [catalogue preparation](/blog/product-page-checklist/) for unambiguous product choices. The finished parcel should have one correct, usable label and a traceable connection to the order it fulfils.

title: Record proof of courier handover for each parcel
description: Connect every dispatched parcel to the available courier handover evidence, keeping label creation, collection and tracking updates distinct.
body:
A label exists, a parcel is packed and the courier was expected this afternoon. None of those facts alone proves that the parcel left your possession.

Keep a record of the actual handover event and the evidence your service provides. That record helps you communicate accurately and investigate when tracking does not move as expected.

## Define what counts as handover

Use the process supported by your carrier: collection acknowledgement, accepted manifest, drop-off receipt or another valid record. The available evidence may differ by service.

Do not invent a scan or status because the driver usually collects at that time. Record what you can actually verify.

If the service provides limited evidence, acknowledge that limitation internally and seek a clearer process where appropriate. A missing record should not be replaced by an assumption.

## Prepare a parcel list before collection

Connect each packed parcel to its order and shipment reference. Check that the list reflects the parcels physically ready to leave, not every label generated that day.

Separate parcels with unresolved address, payment or packing issues. They should not appear ready merely because their paperwork exists.

Use references rather than unnecessary customer data in broadly shared operational lists. Keep full delivery details in the appropriate protected record.

## Reconcile the physical handover

At collection or drop-off, compare the parcels leaving with the prepared list. Record exceptions immediately where possible.

If one parcel remains behind, note it and update the order workflow. Do not let a batch-wide dispatch message tell that customer their parcel left.

For multi-parcel orders, track the relationship between the order and each parcel. One collected box may not represent the complete order.

## Retain the useful evidence

Keep the available handover acknowledgement connected to the shipment references and date. Store it in a location authorised staff can find when needed.

Do not rely on a photograph stored only on one person's phone if the business requires a shared record. Equally, do not circulate documents containing customer details to people who do not need them.

Follow appropriate retention rules and carrier claim requirements rather than keeping every document indefinitely without purpose.

## Send a message that matches the event

If handover is verified, communicate that event and provide the supported tracking route. Do not promise an arrival date beyond what the service and circumstances justify.

If only a label has been prepared, say that preparation is underway rather than calling the parcel dispatched.

A useful update separates the known fact from the estimate: the parcel was handed over on the recorded date; the carrier's transit information is the next source to check. Adapt the wording to your actual evidence.

## Investigate missing progress in sequence

When tracking has not changed, first confirm the correct reference, carrier and handover record. Then use the provider's official support or investigation process.

Do not repeatedly create new labels for the same parcel as a way to make the status appear active. That can complicate the record without moving the shipment.

Keep the customer informed with a realistic next update time. A tracking delay does not justify inventing a new location or promising that the parcel will arrive tomorrow.

## Close the daily dispatch loop

At the end of the session, identify parcels handed over, parcels left behind and any mismatch requiring follow-up. Assign each unresolved case an owner.

Compare the order system's dispatch state with the actual evidence. Correct premature statuses through the authorised process and retain the reason.

A short daily reconciliation can prevent a parcel from remaining unnoticed behind the packing table while everyone assumes it is in transit.

## Use the record to improve the process

Repeated missed collections, incomplete acknowledgements or mismatched lists are operational signals. Discuss the specific problem with the responsible service or improve the preparation routine.

Do not judge a carrier from one unexplained incident alone, but do not ignore a repeated pattern because most parcels eventually arrive.

Use [the inventory guide](/blog/inventory-for-instagram-sellers/) for the earlier stock movement and [the product-page checklist](/blog/product-page-checklist/) for truthful dispatch expectations. Handover evidence is the bridge between your packing work and the customer's delivery journey; keep that bridge traceable.

title: Explain a tracking number that has not moved yet
description: Explain early tracking gaps using verified preparation and handover facts, with a clear investigation and follow-up plan instead of invented reassurance.
body:
A customer opens a tracking link and sees no movement. Before replying that the parcel is “on the way,” check whether you have evidence of handover or only a generated label.

Tracking information and physical events do not always appear at exactly the same moment, but that does not make every delay harmless. Your job is to establish the known facts, use the carrier's process and keep the customer informed.

## Check the reference and destination first

Confirm that the customer received the correct tracking reference and official carrier link. A copied number from another order can make a normal shipment look like a problem.

Avoid asking the customer to enter personal or payment information into an unfamiliar tracking page. Use the legitimate route supplied by your shipping provider.

If the link was wrong, correct it clearly and check whether the order communication process needs repair.

## Establish the last verified event

Look at the packing and handover records. Was the parcel prepared, collected, accepted at a drop-off point or recorded at a later stage?

Do not treat a scheduled collection as proof that collection happened. If the parcel is still with you, explain that fact and arrange the appropriate next step.

If handover is confirmed, retain the evidence and compare it with the carrier's current record. Keep facts and assumptions separate.

## Describe uncertainty honestly

A useful response names the verified event and the action being taken. For example: “Our handover record shows collection yesterday. Tracking has not updated, so we are checking it with the carrier and will update you by the next agreed working-day deadline.”

Use only facts that apply to the order and a follow-up time you can meet. Do not copy a universal waiting period from another provider.

Avoid a confident explanation such as “the system is just slow” unless the carrier has actually established that cause.

## Open the appropriate carrier enquiry

Follow the service's current investigation process and supply the required shipment information through the authorised channel.

Record the enquiry reference, submission time and next expected response. A complaint sent without a follow-up owner can disappear as easily as the original tracking question.

If the carrier supplies a corrected reference, preserve the connection to the original shipment in your record. Send the customer the corrected official link and explain what changed.

Do not include unnecessary customer information in public posts asking the carrier for attention. Keep private details within the proper support process.

## Keep the customer update separate from the investigation deadline

The carrier may not answer immediately. You can still tell the customer what remains known and when you will check again.

If your promised update arrives before a resolution, send the update anyway. Silence after a commitment makes uncertainty harder to manage.

Do not repeatedly issue a new arrival estimate to replace the missing tracking event. A credible estimate needs a basis.

## Escalate according to the actual situation

If the parcel was never handed over, resolve the dispatch failure. If the carrier confirms a problem, follow the applicable remedy and investigation process.

Do not promise a refund, replacement or claim outcome before checking the relevant facts and authority. Do not use that caution as an excuse to avoid taking ownership of the customer case.

Keep the order state, support record and customer messages consistent as the investigation progresses.

## Learn from repeated early gaps

Look for patterns: labels generated too early, collections not reconciled, incorrect links or a particular service repeatedly lacking usable handover evidence.

A single tracking issue does not establish a universal carrier failure. A repeated process weakness deserves a specific correction.

Review saved dispatch messages so they are triggered or sent at the right stage. “Label prepared” and “parcel collected” should not be interchangeable.

Use [the stock guide](/blog/inventory-for-instagram-sellers/) to maintain the order-to-item record and [catalogue preparation](/blog/product-page-checklist/) to state fulfilment expectations clearly. The most helpful response to a quiet tracking page is a verified last event, an owned investigation and a dependable next update—not a more confident guess.

title: Resolve a missing item using the packing record
description: Investigate a reported missing item by comparing the agreed contents, packing record and parcel evidence before deciding the next action.
body:
A customer says one item is missing from the parcel. The order screen shows the complete set, but that only proves what was recorded—not necessarily what went into the box.

Treat the report as a case to investigate, not an accusation to reject. A clear sequence helps you find the facts and avoid asking the customer to repeat information that the business already holds.

## Confirm which item is reported missing

Locate the order through your normal private verification process. Ask the customer to identify the missing product or component clearly.

For a set, compare the report with the contents that were actually advertised and agreed. A styling accessory in a photograph may have created confusion, while a listed component may genuinely be absent.

Do not assume the customer misunderstood. If the listing is ambiguous, that is part of the problem to resolve.

## Check whether the order had multiple parcels

Look for separate shipment references or an agreed split dispatch. If another parcel is still in progress, explain that with verified information.

Do not invent a second parcel merely because it would explain the missing item. The shipment record should support the statement.

If the business failed to tell the customer that the order was split, acknowledge the communication gap and provide the relevant next update.

## Review the packing evidence

Compare the order contents, picking record and any legitimate packing checks you maintain. Identify whether the correct variant and quantity were prepared.

A photograph can help if it is clear and properly associated with the order, but it may not prove everything about the sealed parcel. Do not overstate its evidential value.

Check whether a component was left in the packing area or recorded as unavailable. A system marked “packed” is not sufficient reason to dismiss contradictory physical evidence.

## Ask only for information that helps

If useful and appropriate, ask about the parcel's condition and the items received. Explain why a photograph would help rather than making the customer guess what to send.

Do not ask for an unboxing video that was never reasonably required as an automatic barrier to investigating the complaint. Follow the applicable policy and law, and obtain professional advice for disputed obligations.

Keep addresses, payment details and customer photographs in the protected support record. Do not post them publicly to seek opinions on who is right.

## Keep an investigation note

Use a short structure that separates observation from conclusion.

| Question | Record |
|---|---|
| What was agreed? | Product, variant, quantity and set contents |
| What was received? | Customer's report, clearly attributed |
| What was packed? | Available business records and their limits |
| What happened in transit? | Verified parcel information, if relevant |
| What remains uncertain? | Specific unresolved point |
| Next action | Owner and update time |

This avoids turning a first impression into a fixed verdict.

## Agree the next action through the proper process

Once the facts are clearer, explain the supported remedy or further investigation. Do not promise a replacement before checking availability or a refund before confirming the authorised process.

If the business confirms a packing mistake, acknowledge it directly. Avoid making the customer negotiate over a mistake you have already established.

Record approval and completion separately. An agreed replacement is not dispatched until the relevant fulfilment event occurs.

## Repair the cause

A missing accessory may point to an incomplete packing checklist. Similar-looking variants may need clearer storage labels. An ambiguous set photograph may need revised product information.

Check other affected orders if the issue could be systematic, using an appropriately scoped review rather than assuming it is isolated.

Use [the catalogue checklist](/blog/product-page-checklist/) for contents clarity and [the stock guide](/blog/inventory-for-instagram-sellers/) for component movements.

Close the case when the agreed action is completed and the customer has a clear update. Preserve the useful learning without exposing their personal information. The goal is an accurate resolution and fewer repeated mistakes, not simply a support message that sounds decisive.

title: Handle a wrong variant without blaming the customer first
description: Compare the ordered, approved and delivered variant, then coordinate a remedy and stock correction without silently rewriting the order history.
body:
A customer receives the wrong colour or size. The first task is to establish the agreed choice and what was delivered, not to decide immediately who made the mistake.

Variant errors can begin in the product selector, a message handover, picking or labelling. Investigate the whole path and keep the customer informed while you determine the appropriate next action.

## Locate the approved choice

Use the accepted order record and any documented changes. A later message may have revised the selection, so do not rely only on the original request.

Check whether the public option names were clear. “Natural,” “ivory” and “cream” may describe one option internally but appear as different choices to the customer.

Preserve the history. Do not edit the original selection after the complaint to make it match the dispatched item.

## Identify what arrived

Ask for the minimum information needed to distinguish the received variant. A product label, measurement or appropriate photograph may help.

Explain the request and keep it private. Do not require the customer to publish personal details or perform an unnecessary public demonstration.

For colour concerns, remember that images and screens have limitations. That does not justify ignoring a genuinely different option or an inaccurate listing.

## Trace the handoff to packing

Compare the approved choice with the picking instruction and packing record. Did the correct variant reach the person preparing the parcel?

If the record contained an unclear internal code, inspect the mapping. If two storage bins were similar, check whether their labels or placement contributed.

A page can display the right option while a downstream record loses it. Do not assume the error happened at the shelf until you have checked the earlier steps.

## Separate the customer remedy from the internal cause

The customer needs a clear next action even if the business has not finished every internal investigation. Explain what is known and when you will update them.

Follow applicable policy and legal obligations. Do not treat this guide as a universal rule about who must pay return shipping or when a refund is required.

Avoid offering an unavailable replacement or silently substituting a different product of the same price. Ask for agreement where choices are involved.

## Coordinate any return or replacement carefully

If a return or replacement is arranged, record the references and responsibilities. Keep the original and replacement orders connected so the business does not accidentally dispatch twice.

Do not make returned stock available before it has been received and inspected through your normal process. A customer agreeing to return an item does not put it back on the shelf.

Send messages based on actual events: arrangement approved, pickup requested, parcel received or replacement handed over. Those events should not collapse into one vague “resolved” label.

## Correct the operational record transparently

Where a stock movement or order record needs correction, use the authorised procedure and retain the reason. Avoid deleting the evidence of the mistake.

Check whether the wrong variant's balance and the intended variant's balance both need attention. A single adjustment may leave the inventory inconsistent.

If several orders were packed together, check for a possible swap before preparing another parcel. Keep each customer's information private during that investigation.

Use [the inventory guide](/blog/inventory-for-instagram-sellers/) to distinguish physical stock from commitments during the resolution.

## Prevent the next version of the same error

A useful corrective action might be a clearer public label, a stable variant reference, a photograph showing the selected option or a packing check against the approved choice.

Test the change through the whole buying-to-packing path. Do not stop at a tidier product page if the downstream instruction remains ambiguous.

[The catalogue checklist](/blog/product-page-checklist/) helps identify missing option information, and [the photography guide](/blog/product-photography-checklist/) supports more representative images.

Close the case with the completed action and a concise learning note. Avoid blaming the customer for not interpreting an internal naming convention. The business's job is to preserve a clear choice all the way from selection to delivery.

title: Write a delayed-order update before the buyer has to chase
description: Send a delayed-order update that acknowledges the earlier expectation, states the verified position and gives a realistic next contact time.
body:
The most frustrating delay is often the one a customer has to discover by repeatedly asking. If you know an order will miss the expectation you set, prepare a specific update before the promised date passes where possible.

A useful delay message contains four things: the earlier expectation, the current verified position, the next action and the next update time. It does not need a long excuse.

## Check the order before explaining the delay

Find the current production, packing or shipment state and the promise already given to the customer. Do not write from an outdated status label.

Identify whether the problem is confirmed or still being investigated. “The supplier shipment is late” should not be used if nobody has checked the supplier.

Keep internal uncertainty visible in your notes so it does not become a confident but unsupported customer explanation.

## Acknowledge the expectation that changed

Refer to the relevant commitment plainly. If the shop said dispatch would happen by a particular day, acknowledge that it will not happen as expected.

Avoid changing the date silently in a system while pretending the original estimate never existed. Customers may have planned around the earlier information.

An apology can be brief and direct. It should not require the customer to reassure you or understand every difficulty inside the business.

## State what is known now

Explain the current stage in ordinary language. “Production is complete, but the parcel has not yet been handed over” is more useful than “your order is processing.”

Do not collapse production and transit into one explanation. If the parcel is still with you, do not tell the customer the courier is delivering it.

If the cause is unresolved, say what you are checking. Avoid inventing an arrival date to make the update feel more complete.

## Offer a realistic next action

The action might be completing a specific production step, confirming collection or opening a carrier enquiry. Name who is coordinating it internally.

Where the customer has options under the applicable agreement and law, explain them through the proper process. Do not hide a material delay behind repeated requests to wait.

Avoid promising a remedy you are not authorised or able to provide. Check stock before offering a replacement and use the correct process for any cancellation or refund discussion.

## Give a dependable update time

Choose a time you can honour even if the problem is not fully resolved. A promised update is different from a promised delivery.

An illustrative message is: “We expected to dispatch by Thursday. Packing is complete, but collection has not been confirmed. We are arranging the next step and will update you by Friday afternoon, even if the carrier has not replied.”

Use your actual facts and working schedule. Do not copy dates from an example.

## Keep the record aligned

Save the communication and next update time in the order or support workflow. A colleague should be able to see what was promised before replying.

If several tools send messages, check that an automated status does not contradict the manual update. The customer should not receive “dispatched” immediately after being told the parcel is still waiting.

Limit access to the private order details. A delayed-order queue does not need to become a public list of customer information.

## Follow through and learn

Send the next update when promised, including when there is no final resolution. Explain the action completed and the remaining uncertainty.

After the case closes, identify whether the original estimate was unrealistic, a handover failed or an exceptional event occurred. The corrective action should fit the cause.

If many orders are affected, update current public estimates and scheduled promotions rather than continuing to create the same expectation for new buyers.

Use [the stock guide](/blog/inventory-for-instagram-sellers/) for commitments and [the product-page checklist](/blog/product-page-checklist/) for fulfilment information. A delay message cannot undo the delay, but accurate timing and ownership can prevent uncertainty from becoming a second avoidable problem.

title: Turn repeated enquiries into clearer product information
description: Convert recurring support questions into precise catalogue or ordering improvements while keeping customer conversations private.
body:
When several customers ask whether a product is sold as a pair, the solution is not only a faster reply. The listing may need to say “one pair” more clearly.

Repeated enquiries are a useful source of content priorities. They show where the current buying information is not doing enough work. Use them carefully: a question is evidence of uncertainty, not proof that every customer wants the same feature.

## Record the question without the personal details

Keep a simple tally of the underlying topic: size, contents, care, delivery coverage, customisation or order status. Do not copy entire private conversations into a marketing sheet.

Use your own wording to summarise the information gap. “Cannot identify the set contents” is more useful than a screenshot containing an address and phone number.

Distinguish genuine repetitions from several messages in one unresolved case. Otherwise one difficult conversation can look like a widespread pattern.

## Find the intended answer

Check the product or operational facts before drafting a public response. A recurring question does not justify inventing an answer.

If the team gives different replies, resolve that disagreement first. Publishing one version while support continues using another creates more confusion.

Name the owner of the underlying information. Product specifications, dispatch estimates and remedy decisions may require different people or records.

## Choose the right location

Place the answer where the customer needs it. Set contents belong near the product description; general dispatch information may belong in a linked fulfilment guide.

Avoid adding every support question to a long site-wide FAQ. That can hide product-specific differences and force customers to search unnecessarily.

A private order-status question should not become public order information. Improve the update process rather than publishing customer-specific details.

## Rewrite the information, not the customer's message

Use a clear heading and a direct answer based on verified facts. Add an illustration or measurement where words alone caused the confusion.

For example, “What is included?” can be answered with an exact contents list and a note that styling props are excluded. A vague line saying “everything shown” may remain ambiguous if photographs differ.

Do not reproduce a customer's wording or story as a testimonial without appropriate permission. The operational lesson can be used without turning the person into marketing material.

## Check for contradictions elsewhere

Review the title, image captions, variant labels, saved replies and campaign copy. Fixing one paragraph is insufficient if another part of the journey still gives the old answer.

When a product fact changes, preserve the information needed to support earlier orders. A current page update should not erase what an existing customer was originally promised.

Use [the catalogue checklist](/blog/product-page-checklist/) to inspect the whole listing rather than treating the new answer as an isolated addition.

## Observe whether the question changes

After updating the information, keep the tally using the same categories. Do not declare success from one quiet day.

Look at the quality of the remaining questions. Buyers may now understand the set contents but need help choosing a size. That is useful progress and a different next task.

Do not assume that fewer enquiries always means a better experience. Check that customers can still find support and that the page has not simply become inaccessible.

## Build a small learning loop

At a regular review, choose a few recurring gaps, assign the factual check, make the public correction and note the result. Keep the process light enough to maintain.

Separate verified defects from requests for new capabilities. “The listing never says the dimensions” is a content repair. “I wish this came in another material” is a product idea requiring a different decision.

Use [the photography guide](/blog/product-photography-checklist/) for visual explanations and [the Instagram-to-store guide](/blog/instagram-to-online-store/) for the handoff from social content.

Support becomes a source of better content when you preserve the question, verify the answer and repair the right point in the journey. It should not become a reason to publish private messages or create dozens of pages that all answer the same uncertainty.

title: Handle a cancellation request while an order is being packed
description: Handle a cancellation request against the order’s actual fulfilment stage, coordinating support, packing and payment actions without promising an instant reversal.
body:
A cancellation request can arrive while somebody is sealing the parcel. If support says “cancelled” before checking with packing, the item may still leave. If packing stops but the order record remains active, another helper may restart the work.

Coordinate the request across the people and systems involved. The customer's rights and your obligations depend on the applicable law and agreement; this guide explains operational coordination, not a universal cancellation policy.

## Acknowledge the request accurately

Tell the customer the request has been received and that you are checking the order's stage. Do not call it completed before the necessary actions have happened.

Record the time and reference through your normal private support process. Verify authority to discuss or change the order appropriately.

Avoid collecting unnecessary sensitive information. The purpose is to locate and handle the order, not to build a new customer profile.

## Establish the real fulfilment stage

Check whether the order is awaiting work, in production, being packed, ready for collection or already handed over. Use actual records and people where needed.

A system label may lag behind the physical process. If the parcel is on the packing table, coordinate with the responsible person rather than relying only on an earlier status.

For custom work, establish what has actually been completed without assuming that every custom order has the same cancellation terms.

## Prevent an accidental dispatch where appropriate

If the request requires work or dispatch to pause while it is considered, communicate that clearly to the authorised fulfilment owner.

Identify the physical parcel or items and the operational reference. A message saying “hold that order” is unsafe if several similar orders are being packed.

Do not make unauthorised changes to carrier records or attempt to intercept a shipment outside the service's supported process.

## Decide and communicate through the proper policy

Apply the relevant agreement and legal requirements, escalating uncertainty to someone qualified or authorised. Do not invent a rule during the conversation.

Explain the outcome and remaining steps plainly. If the parcel has already left, say what process is available rather than pretending the earlier dispatch can be undone instantly.

Avoid using internal inconvenience as a substitute for the customer's actual rights. Where professional guidance is needed, obtain it.

## Keep money and stock actions separate

A cancellation decision does not itself prove that money has been returned. Record any authorised payment action and its actual status through the proper payment process.

Similarly, do not add stock back merely because the customer requested cancellation. Check whether the item is physically available, already consumed in production, dispatched or waiting for inspection.

Use [the stock guide](/blog/inventory-for-instagram-sellers/) to release commitments without creating phantom stock. A returned parcel needs its own receipt and inspection process.

## Update every affected handoff

Make sure the order record, packing instruction and relevant support note agree. Remove or cancel obsolete shipment preparation through the supported workflow where applicable.

Tell the person who paused the work when the decision is final. Otherwise an unresolved hold can become forgotten stock or a parcel nobody owns.

Preserve the history of the request and action rather than deleting the order to make the queue look tidy.

## Confirm completion with the correct wording

State what has actually completed and what remains in progress. “Cancellation approved; payment processing is pending” is different from “everything refunded,” and the customer should not have to infer the distinction.

Provide a realistic next update or tracking route for any remaining action. Do not promise a settlement time that your payment provider has not supported.

Review the case afterward for a handover improvement. If support and packing repeatedly miss each other's messages, establish a clearer stop-and-confirm procedure.

Use [catalogue preparation](/blog/product-page-checklist/) to make ordering terms easier to find and [the Instagram-to-store guide](/blog/instagram-to-online-store/) to reduce fragmented agreements. A well-handled cancellation keeps the customer informed while ensuring the physical order, money and stock records each reflect what really happened.

title: Choose a cover photo that represents the item actually sold
description: Select a product cover image that makes the offer identifiable, shows the relevant option and does not confuse props with included items.
body:
The cover image often becomes the customer's first impression of the product. It should help them identify what is being sold before it tries to create a mood.

Choose the photograph against the actual offer. A striking image that shows a different variant or an entire styled scene can attract attention while creating the wrong expectation.

## Identify the unit being sold

Start with a plain statement: one pouch, one pair of earrings, a four-piece set or another exact unit. The cover should not contradict that statement.

If several items appear in the image, make the relationship clear in the listing. A customer should not have to infer whether the price covers the whole arrangement.

Use a separate lifestyle image when the styled scene is useful but too ambiguous to serve as the primary product view.

## Show the product clearly at small sizes

Inspect the image as a small card, not only as a full-screen photograph. The product needs to remain recognisable when the catalogue displays several items together.

Avoid a composition where the item occupies a tiny corner or blends into the background. Decorative surroundings should not overwhelm the object the customer is choosing.

Check important edges and details after cropping. A strap, handle or set component disappearing outside the crop can change the perceived offer.

## Match the photographed option

Where a product has several variants, identify which one the cover shows and ensure the selection process does not imply a different default.

Do not use the most attractive colour as an unlabelled stand-in if the customer can only order another colour. Explain example imagery where exact appearance varies.

For handmade work, show representative differences in additional images rather than promising identical pattern placement through one carefully selected photograph.

## Keep editing faithful to the item

Adjust presentation without changing the product's essential characteristics. Removing a distracting background is different from changing the shape, finish or included parts.

If AI or compositing is used, inspect details that could misrepresent the item: closures, texture, print alignment, proportions and accessories. A plausible-looking image can still be false.

Do not claim a photograph is an unedited customer image when it is a constructed marketing asset. Use images you have the right to publish.

## Add supporting views for the unanswered questions

The cover does not need to answer everything. Use the remaining gallery for scale, interior, fastening, reverse side or another relevant detail.

A useful sequence might move from identification to evidence: overall item, size context, construction detail and included contents. Choose the sequence for the product rather than forcing every listing into the same number of images.

[The photography checklist](/blog/product-photography-checklist/) provides a broader preparation framework. Keep each additional view purposeful rather than repeating the same angle.

## Test the image beside the title and price

Look at the complete product card. Does the title clarify the contents? Does the price presentation relate to the item shown? Can the buyer distinguish it from nearby products?

A photograph of a large bundle beside an entry price for one small component needs especially careful presentation. Do not rely on a later paragraph to correct a misleading first impression.

Ask someone unfamiliar with the range what they expect to receive. Their answer can reveal ambiguity before customers encounter it.

## Maintain the cover when the product changes

Review the image when materials, components or packaging change materially. An old photograph may remain attractive while no longer representing the current offer.

Keep the previous product information needed for historical order support. Replacing the live image should not make it impossible to understand what an earlier customer saw.

If the cover is temporarily missing, use an honest unavailable-image state rather than an unrelated stock photograph that could be mistaken for the product.

Use [catalogue preparation](/blog/product-page-checklist/) to align the image with the description and [the inventory guide](/blog/inventory-for-instagram-sellers/) to keep the offered variant credible. The right cover earns attention by making the product understandable, not by making the offer appear larger or different than it is.

title: Make category names useful to someone new to your range
description: Create category labels and groupings that help first-time visitors find products without learning your internal collection names.
body:
A category is a browsing decision. When a customer chooses it, they expect the next page to contain a recognisable type of product or a useful selection.

Internal launch names can be meaningful to your team and confusing to everyone else. Build the catalogue's main grouping around customer language, then use creative collection names where they add context rather than replace it.

## Start with the range, not a menu template

List the products you actually sell and the differences customers use to choose between them. Product type, use or another clear distinction may provide a useful starting point.

Do not create empty categories merely because a template includes them. A small catalogue can be easier to browse with a few meaningful groups.

Keep planned products separate from current availability. A category title should not suggest a substantial range that does not yet exist.

## Use names that explain the contents

“Pouches,” “hair accessories” and “desk organisers” are clearer than unexplained codes or poetic names alone. You can combine a creative name with a descriptive label if the relationship remains obvious.

Avoid near-duplicates such as “gifts,” “gift ideas” and “gifting” unless each has a genuinely different role. Customers should not need to open all three to understand the distinction.

Use consistent language across the menu, page heading and product references. Switching terms halfway through browsing creates unnecessary uncertainty.

## Decide how overlapping products behave

A product can reasonably belong to more than one browsing group. A pouch may appear under accessories and gifts without becoming two separate stock items.

Keep the product's identity stable. Do not duplicate the listing solely to place it in another category unless your system requires a carefully managed alternative.

Check that overlapping groups do not produce contradictory descriptions, prices or availability for what is physically the same item.

## Choose images that represent the category honestly

A category image should help visitors anticipate the contents. If you use a product photo, choose one that belongs to the category and that you have permission to use.

Do not select a striking but unrelated image just to fill a tile. If the category includes a broader range than the image shows, let the title do clear descriptive work.

Keep an explicit category image separate from any automatic fallback your platform may provide. Verify the actual behaviour rather than assuming every tool chooses a stable or representative product image.

## Keep the first level manageable

A small shop rarely benefits from a complicated hierarchy that forces several clicks before showing products. Group only where the distinction helps a real buying decision.

If a category becomes large, consider whether supported filters or clearer subgroups would help. Do not invent a filter feature your current store does not have.

For a very small category, ask whether it belongs inside a broader group. One isolated item may not need a permanent top-level destination.

## Test findability with concrete tasks

Ask somebody unfamiliar with the range to find a particular type of item. Watch which label they choose and where they hesitate.

Use realistic tasks such as “find something to organise charging cables,” not instructions that already reveal the category name.

Do not treat one test as a complete audience study. Use it to identify obvious naming problems, then observe recurring customer questions after the change.

## Maintain categories as the range evolves

Review empty groups, discontinued products and seasonal collections. A temporary promotion should not leave a permanent dead end in the navigation.

Check links when renaming or retiring a category. Existing campaigns and saved product guides may still point to the old destination.

Keep historical or technical changes controlled through the tools and permissions available to you. This guide is about organising the range, not a promise of automatic redirects or import support.

Use [the catalogue checklist](/blog/product-page-checklist/) for item-level completeness and [the photography guide](/blog/product-photography-checklist/) for representative imagery. Category design succeeds when customers can predict what is behind a label and find the right products without understanding how your business files them internally.

title: Keep product references stable when public names change
description: Preserve a product’s internal identity while improving its public name, and check the effect on links, variants, records and active campaigns.
body:
You may want to rename a product because the original title was unclear. That does not necessarily mean the product itself has changed.

Separate the public wording from the identifiers that connect stock, orders and other records. A clearer title should not accidentally create a duplicate item or break the history of what customers bought.

## Identify which field you are changing

A product can have a display title, internal reference, supplier code, URL and system identifier. They serve different purposes and may not all change together.

Read the current tool's behaviour before editing. Do not assume that changing the visible title leaves the URL unchanged, or that editing a reference is harmless.

If the consequences are unclear, use an authorised test or ask the person responsible for the system. Guessing is not a safe migration method.

## Decide whether this is a rename or a new product

A spelling correction or clearer description may be a rename. A materially different size, construction or included set may require a distinct product or version.

Consider whether old and new stock coexist. If a customer can receive two different physical specifications under one record, the naming change may be hiding a product change.

Document the decision. Support and packing need to understand which description applies to historical orders.

## Keep a before-and-after mapping

Record the old title, new title, stable reference and affected destination where appropriate. Include the date and reason.

Do not rely on memory when several similar products are renamed together. A mapping also helps find old campaign references later.

Keep the record free of unnecessary customer information. Product history can usually be maintained without copying complete orders into the change sheet.

## Check variants and images together

A renamed parent product should still have understandable variant labels and representative photographs. Changing the title alone can leave contradictory information.

Inspect set contents, dimensions and care text for old names or assumptions. Search your authorised content files or use the platform's supported tools rather than manually guessing where the phrase appears.

Do not change physical specifications simply to make them fit the new marketing name. The description must follow the product, not the other way around.

## Verify links and references

Test the public product link used in your profile, posts, guides and messages. If the URL changes, follow the platform's supported redirect or link-update process.

Do not promise that old links will keep working unless you have verified that behaviour. A renamed page that produces a dead end can waste existing interest.

Check any external catalogue or manual record that depends on the old reference. Avoid silently creating a new listing when the intention was to update the existing one.

## Preserve order history

An existing customer's agreement should remain understandable after the public rename. The current title may be useful for navigation, but it must not erase what was actually ordered.

Where your system snapshots order information, verify that historical records remain intact. Where it uses current product data for display, understand and document that limitation.

Do not edit old orders merely to make the new branding look consistent. Changes to order records require their own legitimate purpose and authorised process.

## Test one controlled example

For a larger rename exercise, begin with a representative product in an appropriate environment. Check its public page, variant selection, internal reference, stock connection and an authorised historical record.

Record the result before repeating the procedure across the range. A successful title edit does not prove every connected surface was preserved.

Keep a recovery copy of the original product data appropriate to the operation. Do not call an export a complete backup unless you know what it contains.

Use [the catalogue checklist](/blog/product-page-checklist/) to improve customer language and [the inventory guide](/blog/inventory-for-instagram-sellers/) to preserve stable item references. Good product naming makes the shop easier to understand; good identity management ensures that clarity does not come at the cost of broken records.

title: Show what is included in a set, pair or bundle
description: Make the quantity, contents, options and exclusions of a set visible before purchase so customers and packers understand the same offer.
body:
A photograph of six objects beside the word “set” can leave several questions unanswered. Does the buyer receive all six? Are some props? Can colours be chosen? Does quantity two mean two pieces or two complete sets?

Answer those questions explicitly. A bundle can be attractive without making customers infer its contents from a styled image.

## Define one sellable unit

Write a sentence describing exactly what one order unit contains. For example, “One set contains two coasters and one storage pouch” is clearer than “coaster combo.”

Keep this unit consistent in the title, description, quantity control and order record. If the customer selects quantity two, the resulting contents should be understandable.

Do not mix packs and individual pieces in stock calculations without a documented relationship. [The inventory guide](/blog/inventory-for-instagram-sellers/) explains why counting units matter.

## List the contents in a scannable form

Use a short list or table for components and quantities. Include meaningful specifications where different components could be confused.

An illustrative contents table might look like this:

| Component | Quantity in one set | Choice |
|---|---|---|
| Fabric coaster | Two pieces | Selected colour family |
| Storage pouch | One piece | Fixed natural colour |
| Gift note | One card | Optional message if supported |

This is a fictional offer. Use only components and options you actually provide.

## Explain what the photograph does not include

Identify styling props that could reasonably be mistaken for part of the purchase. A vase, tray or gift box in the image may change the perceived value of the offer.

Place the clarification near the relevant content rather than burying it in a long policy page. The cover image and title should already make the main unit clear.

Do not rely on “for illustration only” as a blanket excuse for a misleading arrangement. Choose a more representative image where possible.

## Make option rules explicit

If buyers can choose colours or sizes, explain whether the choice applies to every component or only part of the set. “Blue” may otherwise mean different things to the customer and packer.

For mixed sets, state whether the selection is fixed, customer-chosen or an assortment. Do not describe an unknown assortment as the exact photographed combination.

If a component becomes unavailable, obtain agreement before substituting it. Equal price does not make two products equivalent.

## Show the complete price relationship

Present the price for the stated unit. Avoid showing a photograph of a full bundle beside a headline price that actually applies to one component without a clear explanation.

If options change the total, make that visible before agreement through the process your store supports. Do not add an undisclosed component charge later in a private message.

Use [the discount guide](/blog/discounts-without-losing-margin/) if the set is promoted as a saving. A comparison needs a legitimate basis, not an invented “usual price.”

## Carry the contents into fulfilment

Give the packer a component checklist connected to the order. A bundle name alone may not be sufficient when several versions look similar.

Check quantities and approved options before sealing the parcel. Include packaging or inserts when they are part of the customer-facing offer.

If the set is assembled from items also sold individually, keep availability tied to the real component stock through your verified process. A separate listing should not create extra physical stock.

## Test the customer's interpretation

Ask someone unfamiliar with the product what they expect to receive for one unit and for two units. Compare their answer with your intended contents.

If they misinterpret the offer, improve the title, image or list rather than assuming every future customer will read more carefully.

Review questions and complaints after launch. Repeated uncertainty about a particular component is a content signal that deserves a specific repair.

Use [catalogue preparation](/blog/product-page-checklist/) and [the photography checklist](/blog/product-photography-checklist/) to align the whole listing. A well-described set feels easy to choose because its value and contents are clear, not because the presentation leaves the buyer to imagine more than is included.

title: Explain made-to-order products before customers reach checkout
description: Explain the approval, production and fulfilment steps for made-to-order items before a customer commits, without treating unfinished capacity as ready stock.
body:
Made-to-order products ask the customer to agree to a process as well as an item. They need to know what will be made, what choices they must supply and what starts the production timeline.

Put that information into the listing and confirmation process before the order is accepted. A vague “custom orders welcome” message leaves too much to reconstruct later.

## State that the item is made after agreement

Use a clear label that distinguishes the product from ready-to-dispatch stock. Do not rely on a small note hidden below unrelated content.

Explain whether photographs show an example or the exact item. If appearance can vary, describe the relevant variation accurately.

Avoid presenting unfinished material as a finished product available for immediate dispatch. Production capacity needs its own check.

## Define the available choices

List the aspects the customer can select: size, colour, text or another supported option. State limits that materially affect what can be made.

Do not offer an open-ended choice if you only support a specific range. “Any design” can create expectations far beyond a small workshop's capacity.

For choices requiring a quote or feasibility check, say so before the customer assumes the displayed amount covers every possible request.

## Explain the approval checkpoint

Identify what the customer must confirm before work begins. This could be exact spelling, a measurement or a supported design choice.

Keep the approved version connected to the order. A later message should not silently overwrite it without checking whether production has started.

If a preview or sample approval is part of the process, describe what it does and does not represent. Do not promise a digital proof feature your workflow does not actually provide.

## Describe timing by stage

Separate waiting for customer information, production, packing and transit. Explain the event that starts the estimate and whether working days are used.

Base the estimate on the current queue and required materials. The shortest time you once completed an item is not a reliable promise for every new order.

For occasion-specific requests, check the whole sequence before accepting a deadline. A production finish date is not automatically an arrival date.

## Make changes and uncertainty understandable

Explain the process for requesting a change after approval. The practical options may depend on the stage reached and the applicable agreement and law.

Do not turn a general statement about custom work into an assumed exemption from all consumer rights. Obtain appropriate advice for policy wording.

If materials become unavailable or a significant delay appears, contact the customer with the actual options. Do not substitute something different because it is convenient.

## Keep the order total connected to the agreed scope

A displayed starting price should not conceal charges necessary for the advertised example. Make the basis of the quote clear.

Where custom choices affect the amount, confirm the final scope and total before agreement. Record the accepted version so payment, production and support use the same information.

[The handmade pricing guide](/blog/price-handmade-products/) can help with the internal calculation, but a customer's order should not become an open-ended bill for work they did not approve.

## Prepare the operational handover

Give production the approved choices, relevant reference and required checks. Keep customer information limited to what the task needs.

Track capacity separately from finished stock. One accepted custom order uses time and materials even if no finished item exists yet.

If one order combines ready-made and made-to-order pieces, explain whether they will travel together or separately. Confirm any effect on delivery charges and timing before agreement. The ready item should not create the impression that the whole order can leave immediately, and a split shipment should not be invented after the customer has accepted a different arrangement.

At completion, check the product against the agreement before packing. Do not assume that finishing the work proves every detail matches.

Use [the inventory guide](/blog/inventory-for-instagram-sellers/) for commitments and [catalogue preparation](/blog/product-page-checklist/) for the public listing. A good made-to-order page lets the customer understand the process before committing and gives the business a clear agreement to fulfil afterward.

title: Record damaged items so they cannot be sold again
description: Separate damaged goods from sellable stock, record the reason and prevent an adjustment from silently making an unsuitable item available again.
body:
A damaged item can remain physically on the shelf while no longer being available to sell. If your stock record only counts what is present, that piece may still be promised to a customer.

Create a clear state and location for goods that cannot be offered normally. The procedure should protect customer commitments while preserving enough information to investigate the cause.

## Identify the exact item and problem

Record the product, variant, quantity and counting unit. Describe the observed issue rather than using an unexplained “bad stock” label.

A scratched finish, broken fastening and stained fabric may need different decisions. Do not assume a cosmetic issue is harmless if it changes what the customer was promised.

For products with safety, hygiene or regulatory implications, obtain appropriate specialist guidance. This guide does not determine whether a particular damaged product can legally or safely be resold.

## Remove it from normal picking

Use a clearly marked location or controlled state so a helper cannot accidentally pack the item. Physical separation is useful when software labels alone are easy to overlook.

Do not place it beside similar sellable variants without a distinction. A note in a spreadsheet will not protect the customer if the packer never sees it.

Keep the quantity visible in the business's physical records while excluding it from ordinary availability through the supported process.

## Record the movement, not just a smaller balance

Create a traceable event showing when the item changed state, who recorded it and why. Keep any relevant receipt, inspection or order reference.

Do not silently reduce the total and discard the explanation. Without the reason, a later count cannot distinguish damage from a missed sale or missing receipt.

Avoid duplicating the adjustment. If an item was already removed from available stock by another process, check the current state before subtracting it again.

## Check open customer commitments

Determine whether the damaged piece was needed for an accepted order. Available stock and committed stock may be affected differently.

If a promise can no longer be fulfilled, inform the responsible person and handle the customer communication promptly. Do not continue promoting the variant while the shortage remains unresolved.

Do not substitute a visibly different or lower-quality item without agreement. The original order remains the reference for what the customer expected.

## Decide the next disposition deliberately

The next step could be supplier return, repair assessment, disposal or another authorised action. Keep the decision separate from the initial quarantine.
