Any return, alteration or service terms should be checked against your current policy and applicable requirements. This enquiry workflow is not a way to remove customer rights through a checkbox.

## Keep a change history

If the requested size changes, update the order specification and record the new confirmation. Do not leave the workshop working from the first screenshot while the sales conversation contains a later instruction.

Use a clear production status: waiting for measurement, waiting for confirmation, confirmed, or already in production. Only offer a change that the current production stage can accommodate.

The same principle appears in the [custom approval guide](/blog/set-a-custom-order-approval-checkpoint-before-production/): approval needs a stable object to approve.

## End with a practical next action

A good enquiry ends with either a complete, confirmed size specification or an explicit request for better measurement. It should not end with “probably fine.”

That small discipline protects both the customer and the maker from treating uncertainty as an order instruction. It also gives your team a clear record to consult without repeatedly asking the buyer to explain the whole conversation.

title: Photograph earrings as pairs with useful weight and closure details
description: Photograph earrings with pair quantities, individual weight, fastening and rear views that help customers understand the actual item.
body:
The front of an earring is only part of the product. A customer may also need to know whether the price includes a pair, how the fastening works, what the back looks like and what the stated weight represents.

Build the listing around those questions. Decorative photographs can attract attention, but the practical views should make the purchase understandable without a long message exchange.

## Make the selling unit unmistakable

State whether the product is one earring, a matching pair, an intentionally different pair or a multi-piece set. Do this near the price, not only at the end of the description.

A photograph of two earrings does not always settle the issue. Styling images can include several products, and replacement listings may sell a single piece.

If customers can choose left or right for an asymmetrical design, record that selection clearly. The packing check should use the same language as the product option.

## Report weight with a defined unit

If you provide weight, identify whether it is per earring or for the pair, and whether removable parts are included. Use an appropriate scale and record the measurement consistently.

Avoid translating that number into “comfortable for everyone” or “you will not feel them.” Comfort is personal, and a weight measurement is not a universal wearing guarantee.

If natural or handmade variation affects the measured sample, explain the variation honestly. Do not publish an exact-looking figure that your own process cannot reproduce.

## Show the fastening open and closed

Photograph the post, hook, clip or other fastening in a way that reveals its structure. Include the backs or other pieces supplied with the order.

Do not describe a closure as secure solely because it looks sturdy in a photograph. Use factual descriptions of the mechanism and check the actual finished pair before dispatch.

If a customer asks whether a fastening suits a particular need, answer from verified product information. Avoid medical or allergy assurances based on appearance, supplier shorthand or the word “hypoallergenic” without supporting evidence.

## Include front, side and rear views

The side view helps show depth and projection. The rear view can reveal construction, finish and the position of the fastening. Neither should be hidden because it is less decorative than the front.

Keep the pair together in at least one image so customers can compare symmetry and intentional differences. For a handmade pair, describe the variation you actually permit.

A close-up should not replace a dimensioned full view. Include length and width using a consistent method, especially where a hanging element moves or changes position.

## Keep worn photographs specific

A worn photograph can communicate scale, but identify the actual product and avoid editing its size. Hair, angle and cropping can all make the same earring appear larger or smaller.

Where the model wears several ear pieces, label what the customer receives. Do not allow an ear stack to look like the included set if only one pair is sold.

Keep the [material description](/blog/describe-jewellery-metals-and-finishes-without-blurring-the-difference/) alongside these images. A picture cannot establish the composition of a post or decorative coating.

## Build a pair-matching check

Before packing, compare the two pieces against the intended design. Check the selected finish, orientation, decorative components and supplied backs.

If you sell mixed pairs, use a component record rather than asking the packer to remember which combinations belong together. A photograph of the packed pair can support your internal check without replacing inspection.

Keep customer-identifying information out of any process photographs used publicly.

## Review the listing from a first-time buyer's view

Ask five questions: how many pieces arrive, how large are they, what does the weight refer to, how do they fasten, and what materials are confirmed?

If one answer requires guessing, add a direct line or a useful photograph. Resist adding more lifestyle copy when the missing information is operational.

A strong earring page does not have to promise effortless comfort or universal suitability. It helps the customer compare a real pair with their own preferences and makes the order easy for your team to assemble correctly.

title: Keep gemstone descriptions tied to supplier evidence
description: Keep gemstone identity, treatment, origin and report references separate so jewellery descriptions do not outrun the available evidence.
body:
A gemstone description can become more confident each time it is copied: a supplier's informal colour name becomes a stone identity, then an origin claim, then a promise about value. Stop that progression by recording exactly what is known and where it came from.

This guide is a documentation workflow for a jewellery seller. It is not a method for identifying stones from photographs or replacing a gemological assessment.

## Separate identity from appearance

Colour, shape and cut are observable listing details. A claim about the stone's identity needs an appropriate basis. Do not infer identity from a familiar colour or from a product name used elsewhere online.

Keep the supplier's exact description in your internal record. If it is ambiguous, ask for clarification before translating it into stronger customer-facing wording.

A red decorative stone is not automatically a ruby. A clear stone is not automatically a diamond. When the identity is unverified, resolve that question or describe the item without an unsupported gemstone claim.

## Record treatment and manufacture information

Ask what the supplier knows about treatment and whether the material is natural, laboratory-grown, an imitation or another specified category. Do not collapse these distinctions into the word “real.”

GIA's [introduction to gem treatments](https://www.gia.edu/gem-treatment) explains why treatment information and related care considerations matter. Use that as a reason to seek evidence, not as a basis for declaring your own stock untreated.

If the supplier does not know, record the uncertainty. “No treatment disclosed to us” is not the same statement as “untreated.”

## Link a report to the actual item

Where a laboratory report exists, record the report reference and check what it covers. A document for one stone should not be used to imply that an entire batch has been assessed.

Verify the issuing organisation and use its available verification process where appropriate. Match the product details rather than assuming that a convincing-looking PDF establishes identity.

Do not call a supplier invoice a laboratory certificate. Both can be useful records, but they serve different purposes.

## Treat origin claims as separate evidence

A geographic origin can be an important part of a buying decision. It should not be inferred from the supplier's address, shipping location or the name of a cutting style.

If an origin is asserted, retain the supporting documentation and understand its scope. Where the evidence does not establish origin, leave that claim out.

The same caution applies to ethical, sustainable or traceability claims. A pleasant brand story does not substitute for information about the particular supply chain.

## Write the listing in layers

Start with the product's observable design and confirmed materials. Then state supported gemstone information in plain language. Place any relevant limitations close to the claim they qualify.

Avoid a confident headline followed by a contradictory note far below it. The customer should not need to decode abbreviations or scroll through unrelated care text to discover an important distinction.

If you sell different stone options under one design, maintain separate evidence records. Do not copy the strongest description across every option.

## Keep care guidance specific

Cleaning and care can depend on the stone, treatment and setting. GIA's [jewellery care guidance](https://www.gia.edu/gia-news-research-tips-caring-jewelry) notes that these differences matter.

Use instructions appropriate to the confirmed item and seek qualified advice where needed. Do not recommend a single chemical, heat process or cleaning device for every gemstone in your catalogue.

When a repair or cleaning enquiry involves uncertain material, say that inspection is needed rather than guessing from a customer photograph.

## Set a publication checkpoint

Before a gemstone listing goes live, have one person compare every identity, treatment, origin and certification statement with the record behind it. Remove claims that cannot be supported.

Keep the record connected to the stock batch and update it when the supplier changes. A previous delivery's paperwork does not automatically describe the next one.

The result is not timid copy. It is a product description that can answer a customer's reasonable questions without escalating from evidence into speculation.

title: Prepare an artificial-jewellery catalogue for everyday buying questions
description: Organise an artificial-jewellery catalogue around materials, dimensions, included pieces and practical buying questions.
body:
Artificial jewellery often sells through a striking photograph, but the questions that determine whether someone orders are more practical. What is the base material? Is it a pair? How long is the chain? Does the set include the earrings in the styling image?

A useful catalogue answers those questions consistently across the range. It does not need to imitate the language of precious jewellery or promise a level of durability you have not established.

## Choose categories that reflect buying decisions

Start with recognisable product types: earrings, necklaces, bracelets, rings and sets. Add a more specific grouping only when there are enough genuinely different products to make it useful.

Avoid creating five nearly identical categories simply because a product could suit five occasions. A buyer should be able to compare alternatives without repeatedly meeting the same item under different labels.

Use occasion styling as secondary guidance. Keep the product's factual identity stable wherever it appears.

## Give every listing the same core fields

Prepare fields for the selling unit, confirmed materials, finish, dimensions, fastening, included components and care information. Mark missing information internally before writing attractive copy.

For a necklace-and-earring set, describe both parts. A necklace length alone does not explain the earrings, and a set photograph does not establish which pieces are included.

Where weight is measured, state whether it refers to one piece or the complete set. Follow the more detailed [earring photography guide](/blog/photograph-earrings-as-pairs-with-useful-weight-and-closure-details/) for pairs and closures.

## Separate appearance from performance

Words such as gold-tone, textured, floral or geometric can describe appearance. Claims such as waterproof, anti-tarnish or allergy-safe describe performance or suitability and need a different level of evidence.

Do not add those promises because a competitor uses them. If the supplier cannot support a claim for the actual item, leave it out and provide accurate material and care information instead.

A clear limitation is more useful than a confident slogan that your support team will later have to qualify.

## Make options visibly different

If a design comes in two finishes, use the correct photograph for each. If stones or decorative components vary, show the actual available options and name them consistently.

Do not use a colour selector for an entirely different construction without explaining the difference. A customer selecting one finish should not accidentally receive a different clasp, size or component count.

Keep option names short enough to appear in an order summary without being cut into indistinguishable fragments.

## Photograph the less glamorous details

Include the back, clasp, extension, post or attachment where it helps a buyer understand the item. A polished front image should not conceal an unfinished rear surface.

Use a neutral scale view alongside styling photographs. Keep edits focused on accurate presentation, not changing the apparent colour, stone size or finish.

For sets, make one plain contents photograph showing every included piece separately. It doubles as a useful reference for the packing team.

## Plan a small catalogue audit

Choose a handful of active products and pretend you are buying them without sending a message. Can you identify the material, size, selling unit and included parts?

Record each missing answer as a field problem, not merely a copywriting problem. If ten listings lack clasp details, improve the product-information collection process rather than fixing ten sentences in isolation.

Do the same check when a new supplier batch arrives. Similar appearance does not guarantee identical specifications.

## Keep after-sale information connected

Make the care note and support route easy to find. If repair, replacement parts or an adjustment service is available, describe the actual scope instead of promising general lifetime support.

When a customer reports a problem, use the product and batch record to understand it. Do not assume that every item under the same design name came from the same construction run.

A strong artificial-jewellery catalogue makes ordinary questions answerable before purchase. That is a more durable advantage than repeatedly adding “premium” to descriptions that still leave the important details unknown.

title: Record jewellery sets and their individual components accurately
description: Use a component record to sell and pack jewellery sets accurately, including mixed pairs, detachable parts and replacement requests.
body:
A jewellery set is a promise about several objects arriving together. A necklace, two earrings and a detachable charm may be photographed as one look, but your stock and packing process still need to recognise each component.

When the components are vague, mistakes are difficult to detect. A missing earring back can disappear inside a product description that only says “complete festive set.”

## Define the contents before naming the set

Write an explicit contents list with quantities. Distinguish a pair of earrings from two pairs, and a detachable pendant from a second necklace.

Include small supplied parts where they matter to use, such as backs, an extension or a separate tie. Do not assume that the packing team knows which accessories accompany the design.

Give the set its own identifier, then connect it to the component identifiers you actually manage. A spreadsheet can perform this role if your current system does not support component inventory.

## Separate styling props from included items

Photograph the set alone in at least one image. If a styling photograph includes another necklace, a tray or a gift box that is not supplied, label that clearly.

A decorative box can look like part of the purchase when it appears in every image. State the actual packaging rather than relying on customers to distinguish props from contents.

Where premium packaging is an option, give it a separate selection and record it with the order.

## Keep matched characteristics visible

Record the intended finish, decorative colour and size combination. If a set deliberately combines different motifs, describe that rather than calling it a matching set without explanation.

For handmade components, define which variation is acceptable within the design. The word handmade should not hide a wrong colour or an unintended missing piece.

Use the [materials guide](/blog/describe-jewellery-metals-and-finishes-without-blurring-the-difference/) for evidence behind composition claims. A set-level description should not imply that every component has the same material if that has not been confirmed.

## Calculate availability from components

If the same earrings are sold individually and inside a set, both sales draw from the same physical stock. Keep that connection visible.

For example, eight necklaces and five earring pairs can support at most five complete sets when each set needs one of each. That illustrative count assumes none are reserved, damaged or committed to individual orders.

Do not publish eight available sets merely because eight necklaces exist. The limiting component determines how many complete promises you can fulfil.

## Handle substitutions as a new decision

A similar earring pair is not automatically an acceptable replacement for an unavailable component. Show the difference and ask for approval before changing a confirmed set.

If the replacement changes the price, materials or delivery timing, explain that as part of the choice. Keep the approved contents attached to the order.

When no suitable alternative exists, follow your actual cancellation or resolution process. Do not quietly complete the visual impression while changing the purchased product.

## Make packing a component check

Lay out the contents against the order record before closing the package. Check quantities, finish, fastenings and the selected packaging.

A checklist should name the parts rather than simply ask “set complete?” The more specific prompt makes it easier to catch a missing small item.

If you retain an internal packing photograph, avoid exposing customer addresses or contact details. It is a process record, not material for an unapproved social post.

## Prepare for later questions

A customer may request a replacement earring, an extra extension or a repair to one component. A component record lets you identify what they originally received without guessing from the collection name.

Do not promise that every part will remain available indefinitely. Explain what you can currently supply and whether a replacement may differ from the original batch.

The benefit of a well-defined set is consistency: the listing, stock decision, parcel and support conversation all refer to the same group of objects. That is what makes a coordinated product feel thoughtfully assembled rather than loosely bundled.

title: Handle a jewellery repair enquiry without promising the wrong service
description: Collect the right information for a jewellery repair enquiry while keeping inspection, quotation and approval separate.
body:
A customer sends a photograph of a broken clasp and asks, “Can you fix this?” It is tempting to answer yes immediately, especially when the repair looks familiar. But a photograph may not reveal the material, hidden damage or whether the replacement will suit the construction.

Treat the first conversation as an enquiry. A repair promise should follow the checks your workshop actually needs.

## Identify the item and requested outcome

Ask which product the customer has, when it was purchased from you if relevant, and what has happened. Let them describe the issue before deciding what repair it requires.

Record whether they want the original appearance restored, a functional replacement or an alteration. Those are different jobs.

If the item was not sold by your business, explain whether you assess outside pieces. Do not accept it automatically if your service is limited to your own products.

## Request useful photographs without diagnosing from them

Ask for an overall image, a close view of the affected area and any detached parts. Explain that photographs help with initial assessment but may not establish the full repair scope.

Do not tell the customer to bend, heat, glue or dismantle the item to improve the picture. A risky home intervention can make the condition harder to assess.

Where the item is valuable or its materials are uncertain, direct the customer towards a suitably qualified professional rather than offering a remote guess.

## Separate assessment from quotation

Explain whether inspection is required, whether there is an assessment charge and how the customer should approve the next step. Use your actual service terms, not an assumed industry practice.

An initial estimate should be labelled as such. If inspection changes the scope, provide the revised proposal before carrying out additional work.

The proposal should identify the repair, parts, finish limitations, price and expected timing. Avoid a broad “repair and polish” line when the customer has only asked about a clasp.

## Record condition at handover

When the item arrives, note the components received and visible condition. Compare that with the enquiry and tell the customer about material differences before beginning.

Keep stones, detachable charms and spare parts individually identified. An intake record should make it possible to distinguish two similar items on the same workbench.

Photographs can support the record, but keep them private unless the customer separately permits their use for marketing.

## Confirm appearance and material limitations

A replacement may not match an old finish perfectly. A repair may alter how a component moves or sits. Explain relevant limitations with a clear example or photograph.

Do not claim an invisible repair, original strength or permanent result unless the service can support that claim. Equally, do not use vague disclaimers to avoid describing the work.

For uncertain gemstone or treatment information, refer to the [gemstone evidence workflow](/blog/keep-gemstone-descriptions-tied-to-supplier-evidence/) and obtain the appropriate assessment before proposing a process.

## Keep approval tied to the job

Store the customer's approval beside the final repair proposal. If they later request a different alteration, update the proposal and timing.

A message saying “go ahead” is only useful when it clearly refers to a particular scope and price. Avoid relying on a long conversation containing several incompatible options.

Use statuses such as awaiting inspection, quotation sent, approved, in progress and ready. These are operational labels you can maintain manually; they are not a claim about any particular software feature.

## Close the job with a factual summary

At completion, explain what was done, which parts were replaced and any care or service information relevant to the repaired item. Check that the returned components match the intake record.

Invite the customer to raise a specific concern if the result differs from the agreed scope. Follow your actual policy and applicable obligations rather than inventing a universal repair warranty.

A disciplined enquiry does not make service feel cold. It helps you give a reliable answer and avoids turning a helpful first response into a promise the workshop cannot safely fulfil.

title: Present precious-metal verification information without inventing certification
description: Present verified precious-metal information clearly, with official checking routes and no borrowed certification claims.
body:
Precious-metal information should be easier to inspect than a promotional banner. A customer needs to know what claim applies to the item, what evidence supports it and how to check the relevant details.

This page is about organising that information. It is not a substitute for current hallmarking requirements or professional compliance advice for your product and business.

## Start with the actual product category

Do not apply gold-jewellery language to gold-coloured costume jewellery. Identify the confirmed material and product before deciding which verification information belongs on the page.

Different products and circumstances can have different requirements. Check the current official rules relevant to what you sell rather than copying a competitor's certification paragraph.

If you cannot establish the material or the evidence behind a claim, do not publish it as verified.

## Use official references for official marks

BIS provides [hallmarking FAQs](https://www.bis.gov.in/hallmarking-overview/hallmarking-faqs/hallmarking-faq/?lang=en) and [consumer verification guidance](https://www.bis.gov.in/hallmarking-overview/consumer-protection/?lang=en). Its guidance explains the gold hallmark information and the HUID verification route through BIS Care.

Link customers to the relevant official resource rather than recreating a verification service in a graphic. Check the current guidance when preparing the listing.

Do not display an official logo in a way that implies your entire store or every product has a certification that has not been established.

## Match evidence to the item

Maintain the product identifier, relevant verification details and supporting purchase records together. A certificate or record associated with one item should not be used as a general badge for unrelated stock.

If the listing photograph shows a mark, make sure it is from the actual item or a clearly explained representative example. Do not retouch a mark into a product image.

A customer-facing statement should be specific enough to check without revealing unrelated private business or customer information.

## Distinguish different kinds of documents

An invoice, a supplier declaration, a laboratory report and a hallmarking reference are not interchangeable. Name each document accurately.

Explain what you are providing with the purchase and what it establishes. Avoid the loose phrase “fully certified” if the customer cannot tell who issued the evidence or what was assessed.

For gemstones within a precious-metal piece, use a separate [gemstone record](/blog/keep-gemstone-descriptions-tied-to-supplier-evidence/). A metal verification claim should not silently become a claim about the stone.

## Keep price explanations factual

Where a quotation contains several components, explain them in the format your business actually uses. Identify the product and quotation date, and avoid implying that an old quote remains current indefinitely.

Do not invent investment returns, resale guarantees or future metal-price predictions to strengthen a product description. A jewellery purchase should not be promoted through unsupported financial promises.

If a customer needs valuation or investment advice, direct them to an appropriately qualified source rather than treating your sales copy as that advice.

## Prepare the support response in advance

Customers may ask how to verify a mark or why a detail differs from what they expected. Give staff a factual response based on the item record and official checking route.

If a discrepancy appears, investigate it. Do not reassure the customer with “all our products are genuine” instead of checking the specific concern.

Keep any correction visible in the relevant listing and order communication. Removing an inaccurate sentence silently does not resolve an existing customer's question.

## Recheck information when stock changes

A new supplier, altered design or different material specification should trigger another evidence check. Do not reuse an old product page merely because the new item looks similar.

Maintain a dated internal record of the information checked and the person responsible. This is especially useful when several people upload products or answer enquiries.

The standard is not how many assurance badges fit on the page. It is whether a buyer can understand the precise claim, inspect its basis and receive a consistent answer from your team. Keep the official compliance decision with current authoritative guidance, not with a copied marketing template.

title: Pack delicate jewellery with a final component check
description: Build a jewellery packing check around components, movement, surface protection and the exact order contents.
body:
A jewellery parcel can look beautifully presented and still contain a tangled chain or a missing back. Presentation and protection are related, but they are not the same job.

Start with the finished item and its weak points. Then choose a packing arrangement that keeps the correct components together without putting unnecessary pressure on delicate parts.

## Inspect before wrapping

Match the product, finish, size and selling quantity to the order. For a set, use the [component checklist](/blog/record-jewellery-sets-and-their-individual-components-accurately/) rather than relying on the collection name.

Check the fastenings and visible condition using your normal product-inspection process. Packaging should not become the stage where an unfinished repair or missing part is hidden.

If the item fails inspection, resolve that before preparing the parcel. A gift deadline does not make the wrong component acceptable.

## Control movement inside the presentation pack

Think about how the necklace, pendant or earrings can move when the package is turned. Separate parts that may tangle, rub or strike each other.

Avoid fixing a piece so tightly that removing it requires force against a delicate joint. The customer should be able to understand how to release it.

Test the arrangement with a sample of the actual product. A box that works for a flat pendant may not suit a projecting stone setting or a long pair of earrings.

## Keep small supplied parts accounted for

Backs, extensions, spare components or care cards should have a defined place. Do not drop a small part loose into decorative filler.

If several pieces look similar, identify them in a way that does not require the customer to guess which belongs where. Keep the contents note consistent with the product listing.

Do not add unlisted extras that could confuse the material or care information. A surprise accessory still needs to be suitable and accurately described.

## Separate gift presentation from transit packaging

The attractive inner box may need a separate protective outer package. Select the outer arrangement for the product and the delivery conditions you actually use.

Follow your carrier's current packaging and item-acceptance requirements. Do not assume that a fragile sticker changes handling or replaces adequate internal protection.

This guide does not establish insurance, carrier liability or suitability for high-value shipping. Check those matters directly with the provider before offering the service.

## Record the final contents

A final check can be short: item and option correct, components present, condition checked, movement controlled, customer-facing information included.

An internal photograph may help document the arrangement. Keep addresses, telephone numbers and other personal information out of images used for training or public content.

The photo is not proof that every later problem must be the carrier's fault. Use it as one part of an investigation, alongside the customer's report and the actual packaging.

## Include useful opening and care information

If the fastening or mounting card needs a particular release step, explain it simply. Avoid packaging that makes the customer pull against a thin chain because the attachment is hidden.

Care guidance should match the confirmed materials and components. Do not include one generic cleaning recipe across every stone and finish in the shop.

A concise product-specific note is more useful than a large insert filled with unsupported durability promises.

## Learn from damage patterns

When a parcel arrives with a problem, record what moved, bent, rubbed or went missing. Look for repeated patterns by product and packing method.

Change one part of the arrangement and test it on a sample before applying it across the range. Keep the new method documented so the next packer does not revert to the old habit.

Also check whether the listing made the contents clear. Sometimes a “missing item” enquiry begins with an ambiguous styling photo rather than an actual packing omission.

The goal is a parcel that opens logically: the customer sees the item they selected, finds every included component and can remove it without damaging the piece. Good presentation should make that experience easier, not conceal the checks behind it.

title: Build gift-hamper options from a controlled contents list
description: Define hamper contents, quantities, packaging and substitution rules before offering several gift options.
body:
A hamper is not a photograph of several attractive things. It is a specific collection of products that must be available, packed together and delivered as described. If the contents change casually, the customer cannot know what they are buying.

Build the contents record first. Then create the photograph, price and occasion description around that record.

## Define each hamper as a list of items

Give every included product a name, quantity and relevant option. “Three little surprises” may sound appealing, but it is not a useful packing instruction or a clear buying description.

State whether the basket, box, wrapping and message card are included. If a styled photograph contains flowers or props that do not arrive, identify them.

This guide focuses on ordinary non-food gifts. Food, cosmetics and other regulated or perishable contents need their own suitability, labelling and handling checks; do not assume this checklist covers them.

## Limit choices to combinations you can maintain

A customer may appreciate a few clear options more than an unrestricted “build anything” promise. Start with a defined base and a small number of supported additions.

For each option, check that the packaging still fits and that the contents remain identifiable. A larger mug or framed piece can change the whole packing arrangement.

Keep the option names meaningful: describe what changes rather than relying only on labels such as classic, deluxe and ultimate.

## Calculate availability from the limiting item

If each hamper requires one notebook and two keychains, stock has to support both quantities. Ten notebooks and twelve keychains allow at most six complete hampers before other commitments are considered.

That is an illustrative calculation, not a demand forecast. Subtract reserved, damaged or separately committed stock before deciding how many you can offer.

If components are also sold individually, keep their shared availability visible. Selling a keychain separately should not leave a confirmed hamper impossible to complete.

## Photograph an actual finished version

Make one sample using the contents and packaging you intend to sell. Photograph the packed view and a clear layout of the individual items.

If the customer chooses between colours or messages, show representative options without implying that every photograph is included in one hamper.

Keep the description connected to the photographed version. When the contents change, update the image or clearly identify the new contents before accepting orders.

## Set the substitution boundary

Decide what happens when an item becomes unavailable. A similar price is not enough to make a replacement equivalent to the customer.

Use the [hamper substitution workflow](/blog/handle-unavailable-hamper-components-without-silent-substitutions/) to offer an explicit choice. Do not hide a broad “contents may vary” sentence under a highly specific photograph and treat that as permission for any change.

For a surprise assortment, define the boundaries honestly: the number of items, relevant categories and exclusions should still be clear.

## Keep personalisation separate from the contents list

A name on a card and a name engraved on a product are different production tasks. Record each personalised element separately with its exact text and approval status.

Do not let a late message change hold up a hamper that has already been packed without telling the buyer. Explain the current stage and what can still be changed.

The [wording approval guide](/blog/approve-personalised-gift-wording-before-making-the-item/) provides a more detailed process for text that becomes part of the product.

## Test one complete fulfilment cycle

Before promoting the range, assemble a sample from the stock record, check it against the contents list and pack it for the delivery method you actually use.

Record the time and materials required. Include those costs when setting the price rather than counting only the individual products.

Finally, ask someone to compare the parcel with the listing. They should identify every promised item and understand the packaging without an explanation from the person who designed it. That is the foundation of a hamper range you can repeat reliably.

Keep one approved contents version for each live hamper so sales, assembly and photography all refer to the same offer.

title: Approve personalised gift wording before making the item
description: Create a clear text-proof and approval process for names, dates and messages on personalised gifts.
body:
A personalised gift can be beautifully made and still be wrong because one letter, date or line break was misunderstood. The mistake often begins before production, when the intended wording is scattered across messages and screenshots.

Give the customer one final text proof to inspect. Make that proof the instruction used by the maker.

## Collect the text in a defined field

Ask for the exact name, date or message, including spelling, capitalisation and punctuation. Explain any character or line limits that genuinely apply to the product.

Do not ask the customer to “send details” without saying what details are required. A structured prompt reduces missing information and makes it easier to distinguish the recipient's name from the buyer's name.

If the customer supplies handwriting or another image, explain what the production process can reproduce and what needs assessment.

## Separate wording from design choices

Record the text, font or lettering option, position and colour as distinct decisions. A customer may approve the words without realising that a particular layout has been selected.

For a multi-part gift, label each placement. A name on the outside of a box and a message inside the lid should not be treated as one unstructured paragraph.

If a language or character is not supported by your process, say so before accepting the order. Do not silently replace it with a visually similar character.

## Produce a proof that shows the actual arrangement

The proof should make line breaks, alignment and placement understandable. Identify the product and version so the customer knows what they are approving.

A digital preview may not represent every texture or production variation. Explain its limits, but make it accurate enough to reveal avoidable spelling and layout problems.

Do not use a low-resolution screenshot that makes important letters hard to distinguish. The proof exists to make checking easier.

## Ask for a specific confirmation

Invite the customer to check spelling, dates, punctuation, placement and the selected design. Ask them to approve the identified version or list corrections.

Avoid asking only “okay?” beneath several competing mock-ups. A useful approval says which version is final.

For example, “Please check proof B for the name, date and two-line message. We will use this version after your confirmation.” Replace the example with the real proof reference and production process.

## Keep corrections in one revision trail

When the customer changes something, create a new proof and mark the earlier one superseded. Do not leave both versions looking equally current.

If production has already started, explain what can still be changed and any genuine effect on timing or cost. Do not promise an effortless change before checking the workshop.

The approved proof should travel with the job. A maker should not have to search a chat history to decide which spelling is current.

## Check the finished item against the proof

Before packing, compare the actual text and placement with the approved version. Customer approval does not remove the need for your own production check.

If your team made an error, follow the appropriate resolution process. Do not use approval language to excuse a mismatch between the proof and the finished item.

Keep your personalisation, cancellation and returns information accurate and consistent with applicable obligations. This workflow is about preventing mistakes, not creating a blanket exemption from responsibility.

## Protect private messages

Gift messages can contain personal information. Limit access to the people who need it for production and fulfilment, and do not reuse a customer's message in marketing without appropriate permission.

If you photograph the finished item for your portfolio, obtain permission or use a separate sample. Blurring a name may not be enough when the remaining message is distinctive.

## Make the next order easier

Track the kinds of corrections that occur repeatedly. If customers often omit the year or confuse recipient and sender names, improve the initial form.

A good process does not demand more messages. It replaces several uncertain exchanges with one clear specification, one inspectable proof and one final check before the gift leaves your workshop.

title: Plan a corporate gifting enquiry around quantities and delivery groups
description: Plan a corporate gift enquiry with product quantities, personalisation, approvals and delivery groups kept separate.
body:
A request for fifty gifts can sound like one order while behaving like fifty small fulfilment jobs. Names may differ, packages may go to several offices, and one person may approve the design while another supplies the addresses.

Before quoting, separate the product decision from the delivery and approval decisions. That makes the work visible instead of hiding it inside a single quantity.

## Establish what is being requested

Ask for the product or hamper type, quantity, intended use and required delivery window. Find out whether the client wants a standard product, a branded version or an individually personalised item.

Avoid treating “corporate gifting” as a complete specification. A single-office welcome pack and a multi-city appreciation campaign have different assembly and dispatch requirements.

State which parts of the enquiry remain provisional. Do not reserve production capacity indefinitely against an unconfirmed number.

## Divide the order into delivery groups

Record whether everything goes to one address or to several recipients. For each group, identify quantity, location information needed for a quote and the intended dispatch arrangement.

Do not collect a full recipient list before it is needed merely because a large order feels important. Start with enough information to assess feasibility, then use a controlled handover for confirmed delivery details.

Keep the group totals reconciled with the order total. An address spreadsheet should not quietly increase the quantity beyond what was approved.

## Define branding and personalisation

Ask who will provide the artwork and who has authority to approve its use. Record the print or placement method your business can actually offer.

If each item has a different name, establish a final data format and a correction deadline. Do not accept a mixture of screenshots, voice notes and handwritten lists as the production source.

For wording, follow the [personalisation approval process](/blog/approve-personalised-gift-wording-before-making-the-item/). A corporate contact should approve a clearly identified version, not a vague description of the intended result.

## Quote the work in understandable parts

Distinguish products, customisation, packaging and delivery where relevant to your actual pricing. Explain assumptions behind the quote, such as one approved design or a defined number of delivery groups.

Any tax or invoicing treatment should be checked through your normal accounting process. Do not invent a tax rule to make the quotation appear complete.

Give the quote a clear validity and confirmation process. Availability and production capacity can change while a client gathers internal approvals.

## Identify one final approver

Record who can confirm the design, quantities and recipient data. Other people can contribute, but the workshop needs one authoritative version.

If the client changes the decision-maker, update the record rather than treating every new message as an instruction. Conflicting feedback should be resolved before production continues.

A short sign-off sheet can connect the approved sample, quantity, delivery groups and schedule without requiring an elaborate system.

## Build a staged production plan

Consider a sample approval before the full run when the customisation warrants it. Then plan material preparation, production, inspection, packing and dispatch.

Do not count only making time. Sorting personalised items into recipient groups can be a substantial part of the work.

For example, forty gifts split across four offices may need four labelled dispatch batches. Forty individually addressed gifts require a different checking process even though the product quantity is identical.

## Check data and parcels together

Before dispatch, reconcile the recipient or group list with the packed items. Keep personalisation and address records linked carefully so one recipient does not receive another person's gift.

Protect the list as private operational information. Do not place client recipient names or addresses in public progress photographs.

After dispatch, provide the agreed tracking or status information and a clear route for exceptions. Avoid promising a consolidated report or automated notification feature unless your current workflow can actually deliver it.

A well-run corporate enquiry turns a large, vague request into a finite set of approved decisions. That clarity is what lets a small gifting business accept larger work without losing control of the details.

title: Design a gift guide around recipient needs rather than stereotypes
description: Build gift-guide categories around interests, practical constraints and the information a buyer needs to choose.
body:
A gift guide becomes less useful when every suggestion is based on a broad label such as “for her” or “for him.” The buyer may know much more relevant things: the recipient likes plants, has limited desk space, prefers useful objects or needs something easy to carry.

Organise the guide around those needs. Keep demographic labels from doing the work that product information should do.

## Begin with a real choosing problem

List the questions buyers ask before selecting a gift. They may need a small parcel, a personal message, a low-maintenance object or a gift that does not require knowing a clothing size.

Use those questions to define guide sections. “Small gifts for a work desk” gives a clearer comparison than “gifts everyone will love.”

Do not claim universal appeal. A guide can reduce uncertainty without pretending to know the recipient personally.

## Choose products for a stated reason

Each recommendation should explain why it belongs. A compact keychain may suit a small-parcel constraint; a personalised notebook may suit a buyer who knows the recipient's preferred name.

Keep the reason factual. Avoid assigning interests or preferences to an age, gender or profession without evidence.

If the fit depends on something the buyer must check, say so. For example, a framed print may require available wall or desk space, and a personalised item requires confirmed wording.

## Include practical limits near the recommendation

Show dimensions, included items, customisation timing and relevant delivery information. A beautiful suggestion is not useful if the buyer discovers too late that it cannot meet the occasion.

Distinguish ready-to-dispatch products from made-to-order work. Link to the actual product information rather than copying a delivery promise that may change.

For date-sensitive purchases, direct readers to the [gift deadline guide](/blog/separate-a-gift-deadline-from-a-dispatch-promise/) before they rely on an arrival date.

## Use budgets without manufacturing value claims

If you group by price, keep the prices current and explain whether delivery or optional personalisation is additional. Do not call a range affordable for everyone.

Avoid fake original prices or exaggerated savings to make a recommendation attractive. The guide should help compare current choices, not create urgency through unsupported discounts.

A “within this budget” section should contain products that actually fit the stated conditions at the time it is checked.

## Offer a small number of meaningful alternatives

Too many similar suggestions can make the guide feel like a catalogue dump. Choose a few different answers to the same need and explain the trade-off.

For instance, a ready-made gift may be quicker, while a personalised option may allow a more specific message but need approval time. Neither is automatically better.

Keep sponsored, preferential or commercial relationships transparent where relevant. Recommendations should not appear independent when they are not.

## Write for the uncertain buyer

Include a short “check before choosing” prompt. Ask whether the recipient has space for the object, whether the buyer knows the required personalisation and whether the delivery arrangement is suitable.

Do not ask for unnecessary personal information about the recipient. The guide can help someone choose without collecting a profile of another person.

Where a product has specialist suitability or safety considerations, do not cover them with a casual gift-guide sentence. Use the appropriate product-specific information and qualified guidance.

## Maintain the guide as stock changes

Review linked products, prices and availability. Replace unavailable suggestions deliberately rather than letting half the guide lead to dead ends.

Keep the original choosing problem intact when replacing an item. A large decorative object is not an equivalent replacement for a compact travel-friendly gift simply because both are in stock.

A strong gift guide earns its usefulness through the explanation behind each choice. It helps a buyer make a thoughtful decision with the information they actually have, while leaving room for the recipient's individual preferences.

Ask your support team which comparisons buyers actually struggle with. Those questions are a better starting point for the next guide than adding another generic recipient label.

title: Separate a gift deadline from a dispatch promise
description: Separate making, approval, dispatch and delivery estimates when customers need a gift for a particular date.
body:
“Needed by Friday” is not the same instruction as “dispatch on Friday.” A gift buyer cares about the date the recipient can use the item, while your workshop and carrier operate through several earlier stages.

Write those stages separately. Otherwise a customer may interpret a production estimate as an arrival promise that you never intended to make.

## Ask for the occasion date and destination

Find out when the gift is needed and where it is going. Check whether it must arrive before the event or can arrive on the day.

Use only the information needed to assess the request. A postcode or service area may be enough initially; the full address can follow when the order is confirmed.

Do not promise a date before checking the product's readiness, personalisation requirements and available delivery service.

## Separate four time periods

Think in terms of information collection, approval, production and delivery after dispatch. A customer delay in approving a proof can affect the making schedule.

Show which period your estimate describes. “Three working days to make after approval” should not appear beside a button as though it means delivery in three days.

If an item is already made, say what still needs to happen before dispatch, such as personalisation, final inspection or gift packing.

## Use a schedule with explicit assumptions

For a custom gift, explain the latest approval time that supports the proposed dispatch date. Identify weekends or business closures according to your actual operation.

Do not invent a guaranteed carrier transit time from one previous parcel. Use the current service information and state whether the delivery date is an estimate or a service commitment you can genuinely offer.

Where uncertainty makes the deadline unrealistic, say so early. Offering a ready-made alternative is more useful than accepting an order that depends on everything going perfectly.

## Keep urgency from bypassing checks

A rush request still needs accurate wording, an available product and a correct address. Skipping the approval step can create a gift that arrives quickly but is unusable.

If you offer a rush service, define what it accelerates. Faster production does not automatically mean faster transport.

Explain any extra charge before confirmation and do not imply that paying it removes every delivery risk.

## Record the promise in the order conversation

Summarise the item, approval requirement, planned dispatch date and delivery expectation. Use the same terminology on the product page and in the confirmation.

For example, a hypothetical order may be planned for dispatch after a proof is approved by a stated time. The arrival estimate should remain a separate line based on the selected service.

Avoid saying “confirmed” when only the enquiry has been received. Confirm the actual commitments your team has checked.

## Respond quickly when the schedule changes

If production falls behind or approval arrives late, explain the effect before the original expectation becomes impossible. Offer the choices your business can genuinely support.

Do not silently switch to an unapproved product to preserve the date. The [hamper substitution guide](/blog/handle-unavailable-hamper-components-without-silent-substitutions/) illustrates why timing and contents need separate consent.

If the carrier reports a delay, share the known status without guessing a new guaranteed arrival date. Follow your current resolution policy and applicable obligations.

## Review deadline enquiries after the occasion

Look at where misunderstandings arose. Did customers read dispatch as delivery? Did the proof deadline appear too late? Did your team promise a date before checking stock?

Use those observations to improve the listing and enquiry prompt. Do not manufacture a conversion claim from a few successful urgent orders.

A well-explained deadline can still disappoint a buyer when an unexpected delay occurs, but it avoids creating false certainty at the start. The goal is a feasible, clearly stated plan that respects both the occasion and the work required to fulfil it.

Keep a record of the final agreed schedule with the order, so a different team member can answer a status question without reconstructing the whole enquiry.

title: Manage surprise-gift addresses and recipient communication
description: Keep surprise-gift delivery practical by separating purchaser instructions, recipient contact and the limits of secrecy.
body:
A surprise gift has two audiences: the person paying and the person receiving it. Their needs overlap, but they are not identical. The buyer may want secrecy, while the delivery process may need someone to answer a call or confirm an address.

Explain that tension before accepting special instructions. Do not promise a completely silent delivery process you cannot control.

## Distinguish purchaser and recipient details

Use separate fields or clearly labelled notes for the buyer and recipient. Confirm which name belongs on the parcel and which contact is appropriate for delivery.

A common mistake is to copy the buyer's saved address into the recipient field or use the recipient's name in the payment conversation. A simple read-back of the final delivery details can catch this.

Collect only the information needed to fulfil the order. Do not ask for unrelated personal details to make the surprise feel more elaborate.

## Ask what must remain a surprise

The buyer may want the contents hidden, the sender's name omitted or the timing kept private. These are different requests.

Record the specific instruction rather than a general note saying “surprise.” Explain which requests you can support and which depend on the delivery provider.

If the parcel requires recipient contact, do not imply that the carrier will never call. Share the actual service limitations before the buyer relies on them.

## Check the outer and inner information separately

Review the delivery label, packaging, gift message and any required documents. Determine what the recipient will see when the parcel arrives and when it is opened.

Do not remove information that must accompany the shipment merely to preserve a surprise. Where a legal or carrier requirement is relevant, check it through your normal process.

If your packaging identifies the shop or product category, say so. A plain-box request should not be accepted if you have no suitable packaging available.

## Handle gift messages as exact content

Ask the buyer to provide the message and sender wording exactly. “From us” may be meaningful to the buyer but confusing to the recipient.

Use the [personalised wording workflow](/blog/approve-personalised-gift-wording-before-making-the-item/) when the text is printed, engraved or otherwise difficult to change.

Keep private messages out of public packing videos. A surprise for the recipient is not permission to share the order with an audience.

## Confirm availability at the destination

Ask the buyer to consider whether someone can receive the parcel at the intended address. Do not assume an office, hostel or apartment reception accepts every kind of delivery.

If there are delivery instructions, record them accurately and explain that acceptance by the carrier or building is not guaranteed merely because a note exists.

Avoid promising a precise arrival time unless the service genuinely supports that commitment. For occasion dates, use the [deadline guide](/blog/separate-a-gift-deadline-from-a-dispatch-promise/).

## Prepare an exception contact plan

Decide who should be contacted if the address is incomplete, delivery fails or the parcel is refused. Usually that requires a clear route back to the purchaser, but the actual arrangement should be confirmed.

Do not share the recipient's information beyond what the fulfilment process needs. If a correction is requested, verify it through the appropriate order contact rather than accepting any unsolicited message.

Keep address changes attached to the order so the packing team does not use an earlier version.

## Close the loop without exposing more than necessary

Provide the buyer with the delivery status available through your process. Do not claim that “delivered” proves the recipient personally opened or liked the gift.

If a problem occurs, investigate it as a delivery issue rather than blaming the surprise instruction. Use the agreed details and actual service information to decide the next step.

A successful surprise order is not built on secrecy at all costs. It is built on clear boundaries: who receives the parcel, who can answer questions, what information travels with it and what the business can realistically keep private.

title: Price gift wrapping as a defined service rather than a vague add-on
description: Define gift wrapping by materials, item coverage, message handling and packing time before setting an add-on price.
body:
“Gift wrap available” can mean anything from a ribbon around one item to a box, tissue, card and carefully arranged presentation. If the offer is vague, customers and packers may imagine different services.

Define the wrapping unit first. Then price the materials and work needed to deliver that unit consistently.

## State what the option covers

Explain whether the charge applies per item, per box or per order. If three products can be wrapped together, show that option separately from three individually wrapped gifts.

List the included materials in plain language. Identify whether a message card, premium box or decorative element is included or optional.

Do not use a photograph of an elaborate sample if the standard add-on provides something simpler. The image should represent the service being purchased.

## Check which products are eligible

Some shapes fit your standard wrap; others require a different arrangement. Record those limits before making the option available across the whole catalogue.

A large framed item, fragile ceramic piece and soft accessory may not suit the same wrapping method. Gift presentation must not interfere with protection during delivery.

If the service is unavailable for a product, explain that before checkout or confirmation rather than removing it after the customer has paid.

## Count materials and time

Measure a sample job using the actual paper, box, card and fastening materials. Include waste and the time spent preparing, writing and checking the presentation.

For a hypothetical example, materials of ₹45 plus fifteen minutes of work valued internally at ₹120 per hour create ₹75 of direct cost before other expenses. That is an arithmetic illustration, not a suggested selling price.

Use the broader [handmade pricing guide](/blog/price-handmade-products/) to consider the rest of your cost structure. Do not treat an attractive round add-on price as proof that the service pays for itself.

## Show choices without creating endless variations

Offer a manageable range of paper, ribbon or message options that you can keep available. Photograph the combinations honestly.

If colours may vary, define the range and ask for approval when the difference matters. Do not use “subject to availability” to replace a specifically chosen colour without discussion.

Keep names consistent across the product page, order note and packing materials shelf.

## Keep the message workflow separate

A gift message needs exact wording and a clear character or space limit. Do not squeeze an unexpectedly long message onto a small card without checking the result.

Confirm whether the sender's name should appear. If the buyer leaves it blank, ask rather than inventing a sign-off.

Treat the message as private fulfilment information. Do not photograph it for marketing without appropriate permission.

## Make the packing instruction visible

The packer should know which items belong in each wrapped group, which message accompanies it and which option was selected.

For an order with several recipients, label the internal packing plan carefully. Two identical wrapped boxes can be difficult to distinguish once closed.

Perform a contents check before wrapping and a presentation check afterwards. Wrapping should not make it impossible to verify whether the right item went into the box.

## Explain changes and limitations early

If a requested wrap is unavailable, offer a specific alternative before doing the work. State any effect on price or timing.

Do not promise a flawless presentation after a long delivery journey. Use protective outer packaging and describe the gift service accurately without implying that it replaces transit protection.

If the customer reports damage, assess the actual issue and follow your normal resolution process.

## Review the service as a small product

Track material usage, common requests and the time taken for different item shapes. Improve the offer when those observations show a recurring mismatch.

A well-defined wrap service is easier to buy, easier to pack and easier to price. The customer knows what the add-on changes, and your team can deliver that change without interpreting a vague promise differently on every order.

title: Create a custom photo-gift proof that customers can inspect
description: Prepare photo-gift proofs that reveal cropping, placement and resolution concerns before production begins.
body:
A customer may love a photograph that does not fit the shape of the gift they have chosen. A wide group photo can lose people when cropped into a small circle, while a screenshot may look clear on a phone but contain too little detail for the intended print.

Use the proof stage to make those differences visible. Do not treat receiving an image as receiving a complete production instruction.

## Ask for the best available source file

Explain the file information your process needs without promising a universal resolution threshold. The appropriate file depends on the output size and production method.

Encourage the customer to supply the original image where available rather than a screenshot of a social post. If the file is unsuitable, explain the observed issue and request a better version before proceeding.

Do not claim that editing can restore detail that is not present in the source.

## Confirm permission to use the image

Ask the customer to provide an image they are entitled to use for the requested product. Do not assume that an image found online is free to reproduce.

WIPO's [copyright FAQs](https://www.wipo.int/en/web/copyright/faq-copyright) explain that photographs and artwork can be protected and that permission questions depend on the use. For uncertain commercial or third-party imagery, obtain appropriate advice rather than treating a customer upload as proof of rights.

Keep this check practical and respectful. It should not become an unsupported legal declaration about every possible image.

## Show the actual crop

Place the image within the real printable area or an accurate representation of it. Show which edges will be removed and where important faces or details sit.

If the product has a curved or interrupted surface, explain the relevant limitation. Do not present a flat mock-up as an exact photograph of the finished object.

Offer a different crop or product format when the requested composition cannot fit without losing important content.

## Keep text and image approvals distinct

If a name or date is added, include it in the proof and ask the customer to inspect both elements. An approved photograph does not automatically approve a misspelled caption.

Identify the proof version and the selected product. Keep earlier versions clearly superseded.

Use the [wording approval guide](/blog/approve-personalised-gift-wording-before-making-the-item/) for the text portion so the final production record contains one coherent instruction.

## Explain colour limits honestly

A screen preview is not a guarantee of an identical physical colour under every light. Explain relevant production limitations without using that fact to excuse avoidable errors.

Work from a consistent process and inspect a sample where the product warrants it. Do not apply a filter that makes the proof more attractive than the output you can produce.

If a particular colour match is essential to the customer, clarify whether your service can support that requirement before accepting the job.

## Check the finished result against the proof

Compare placement, crop, orientation and wording before packing. Look for a mirrored image, clipped face or text shifted into an edge.

Customer approval does not replace your own quality check. If production differs from the approved version, resolve the discrepancy rather than treating the approval as a blanket defence.

Keep the proof and final job reference together so another team member can understand the agreed result.

## Protect personal photographs

Limit access to the files to the people who need them for the order. Explain your actual file-retention approach and do not reuse private photographs in examples without separate permission.

For a public portfolio, use your own licensed sample images or approved customer work. A beautiful finished gift does not automatically become promotional material.

A useful proof process helps the customer see the product they are choosing, not just the photograph they supplied. That is how it prevents disappointment before the irreversible production step.

Keep the approved file name and proof version in the production record, so a later upload cannot accidentally replace the image already agreed.

title: Handle unavailable hamper components without silent substitutions
description: Offer explicit hamper substitutions with updated contents and pricing instead of quietly replacing unavailable items.
body:
One component of a confirmed hamper becomes unavailable. The replacement costs the same and looks similar, so it may seem harmless to swap it. But the buyer may have chosen the hamper because of that exact item, colour or personal meaning.

Treat the change as a new customer decision. Price similarity alone does not make two products equivalent.

## Identify what changed

Record the unavailable component, affected orders and the reason it cannot be supplied. Check whether the shortage is temporary, a stock-record error or a supplier change.

Do not alter the public contents list and assume existing orders have changed with it. Those customers bought the earlier version.

Keep the original contents record available while you resolve the exception.

## Describe a specific alternative

Offer the replacement by name, quantity and relevant option. Show a photograph where appearance matters.

Explain differences in materials, size, function or personalisation. Avoid saying only “equal or higher value,” because that does not tell the customer whether the new item suits the intended recipient.

If no suitable replacement exists, say so. An honest cancellation or revised plan can be better than a hamper assembled from whatever remains.

## Recheck the whole package

A different component may change the box size, weight or arrangement. Check whether the existing packaging and delivery quote still work.

If the replacement affects the message or occasion, explain that too. A floral accessory and a practical desk item may occupy similar space while serving very different gift intentions.

Use the original [controlled contents list](/blog/build-gift-hamper-options-from-a-controlled-contents-list/) as the reference for the updated version.

## Present the customer's choices clearly

Offer only choices you can actually fulfil: accept the named replacement, wait for the original if a credible date exists, choose another available hamper, or use the applicable cancellation or resolution route.

State any price or timing change before approval. Do not make the customer discover a revised delivery charge after agreeing to the item.

Avoid pressure based on the approaching occasion. A short deadline makes clarity more important, not less.

## Obtain approval before assembly

Record which option the customer chose and update the order's contents version. The packing team should see the revised list, not a separate message that can be missed.

If the customer has not replied, do not interpret silence as approval for a materially different product. Follow your actual order-management and customer-contact process.

Where an assortment was sold with defined variation, check whether the proposed change genuinely fits those stated boundaries. A general disclaimer does not make every substitution expected.

## Correct the live offer

If the original component will remain unavailable, update the current listing, photographs and price as necessary. Keep the revised offer distinct from the version already purchased.

Do not continue promoting an old photograph that centres the missing item. A note at the bottom may not be enough to explain a visually different hamper.

If the replacement becomes a permanent version, give it a stable contents record so future orders do not depend on remembering an exception.

## Learn from the shortage

Check whether the component was shared with another product or sold individually without reducing hamper availability. A repeated substitution problem can indicate a stock-planning issue.

For example, a decorative keychain used in three hampers should not be counted independently in each offer. The same physical stock cannot fulfil all three commitments at once.

Adjust the availability process rather than relying on customer approval to repair every shortage.

## Close the conversation with the final specification

Send a concise confirmation of the approved contents, any price adjustment and the expected next step. Keep the wording factual.

Before dispatch, compare the parcel with that final specification. The customer should receive the replacement they approved, not another last-minute variation.

A careful substitution process protects the meaning of the gift as well as the order. It recognises that customers buy particular combinations, not simply a box that reaches a stated monetary value.

title: Prepare a small gift collection for an occasion-based launch
description: Launch an occasion-based gift range with a small coherent selection, complete specifications and realistic fulfilment capacity.
body:
An occasion can help organise a gift collection, but it should not become a reason to launch every product you can make. A range with too many unfinished options can create more questions than orders.

Start with a small collection you can photograph, specify and fulfil consistently. The occasion gives the range context; the individual products still need to make sense.

## Choose one clear buying situation

Define what the buyer is trying to do. They may want a small thank-you, a personalised keepsake or several matching gifts for a group.

Do not combine every recipient, budget and delivery urgency into one launch. A narrower range is easier to explain and easier for your team to prepare.

Use the [recipient-needs guide](/blog/design-a-gift-guide-around-recipient-needs-rather-than-stereotypes/) to describe the purpose without assuming preferences from gender or age.

## Select products that differ meaningfully

Choose a few options with clear distinctions: ready-made versus personalised, one item versus a defined set, or compact versus larger presentation.

Avoid creating several names for almost identical bundles. Buyers should understand why one option suits their situation better.

Check that every chosen product has complete material, dimension, contents and care information before writing campaign copy.

## Build a sample of each offer

Make or assemble the actual version you intend to sell. Photograph it alone and, where useful, in an occasion setting.

Keep decorative props separate from the included contents. If the launch includes gift wrapping, use the same service shown in the listing.

A digital mood board can help planning, but it is not a substitute for checking that the physical combination fits the box and looks as described.

## Establish the production boundary

Count available finished items, components and making capacity. Include personalisation, inspection and packing time rather than only assembly.

Set a realistic limit for custom work. Do not offer unlimited orders until a date if the workshop can only produce a finite number.

Where stock is shared across offers, calculate the limiting component. A successful promotion should not create several confirmed orders competing for the same final piece.

## Publish timing in separate stages

Explain the time needed for approval, making and dispatch. Keep delivery estimates separate and check the current service for the destination.

Use a clear cutoff only when it reflects your actual process. Avoid a countdown that resets or implies a guarantee you cannot support.

For a customer who arrives after the custom deadline, identify a genuine ready-made alternative if one exists. Do not accept the original promise and hope to recover the schedule later.

## Prepare enquiry answers before promotion

Write short factual answers for the questions most likely to arrive: what is included, how personalisation works, whether the price includes wrapping, and what delivery information is needed.

Keep those answers aligned with the listing. A promotional message should not promise an option that the order process cannot record.

If the range is sold through an enquiry rather than a fully configured checkout, explain the next step honestly. Do not imply an automated capability your current store does not have.

## Run a small operational rehearsal

Place a sample instruction through the same internal steps a real order will follow. Check the contents, approval record, packing materials and dispatch information.

Time the process and note where clarification was required. Fix those points before sending more traffic to the collection.

This rehearsal is not a conversion forecast. It is a way to discover whether your own team can fulfil the promise without relying on the founder's memory.

## Review the launch by product and question

After the occasion, compare which products were requested, which enquiries stalled and which fulfilment tasks took longer than expected. Keep the observations separate from assumptions about why customers did not buy.

Use the findings to improve the next range rather than automatically expanding it. A smaller collection with clearer information may serve customers better than a larger one with repeated uncertainty.

The aim is an occasion offer that feels considered because it is considered—from the selection and photographs to the last packing check.

title: Build garment measurement tables from the actual clothing
description: Create product-specific clothing measurements with clear units, measurement points and a distinction between body and garment size.
body:
A size label is a useful identifier, but it is not a measurement. Two garments marked medium can have different shapes, lengths and intended fits. A boutique that publishes only the label leaves customers trying to translate their usual size into an unfamiliar product.

Build the chart from the garment and explain what the numbers mean. This is more useful than copying a generic chart into every listing.

## Distinguish body measurements from garment measurements
