A body chart describes the person the garment is intended to fit. A garment chart describes the finished item. Label the chart clearly so customers do not compare the two as though they are identical.

If you provide both, explain how your maker intends them to be used. Do not invent a universal allowance between body and garment measurements.

Baymard's [apparel research](https://baymard.com/research-articles/apparel-5-best-practices) supports providing measurement information relevant to the product type. A trouser buyer needs different details from someone choosing a top.

## Choose useful measurement points

For each product, identify the measurements that help explain its shape. A shirt may need chest width, shoulder, sleeve and length; trousers may need waist, hip, rise and inseam.

These are examples, not a universal production standard. Use points appropriate to the construction and explain where each starts and ends.

Avoid including a column simply because it appeared in another brand's chart. Every number should be traceable to a defined measurement.

## Show the method visually

A simple original diagram or clearly marked photograph can explain a flat measurement. State whether a width is measured across one side or represents a full circumference.

Do not label a flat waist width as waist circumference. If you calculate a derived value, identify it rather than letting the customer assume it was directly measured.

Keep units visible in the table heading. Do not mix centimetres and inches without clear labels and checked conversions.

## Measure the finished product

Use the actual finished sample or stock according to your quality process. Record the method and compare more than one piece where production variation is relevant.

Do not publish a level of precision your process cannot maintain. If a reasonable manufacturing tolerance applies, establish it from the product and explain it clearly.

Avoid using a broad tolerance note to excuse a chart that was never measured.

## Keep sizes and variants connected

If one colour uses a different fabric or construction that changes the dimensions, check it rather than assuming the first chart covers every option.

When the supplier or pattern changes, review the chart. A product name can remain familiar while its fit changes between batches.

Maintain a version reference internally so customer support can identify which chart applied to a particular order.

## Test the chart as a customer would

Ask someone to compare the listed garment with a similar item they own using the stated method. They should understand what to measure without asking the person who created the chart.

If they confuse width with circumference or cannot identify the length point, improve the explanation.

A chart cannot guarantee personal fit, but it can make the available evidence clearer and reduce avoidable guessing.

## Put the chart where the decision happens

Keep the measurement link or table close to the size choice and product information. Do not hide it in a general policy page.

Ensure the table remains readable on a phone. Long headings can be shortened with an explanation beside the chart rather than leaving the numbers detached from their meaning.

Use the [fit-photography guide](/blog/show-clothing-fit-with-model-and-garment-context/) alongside the chart; measurements and photographs answer different questions.

## Maintain the same language in support

When someone asks for sizing help, refer to the product-specific chart and its method. Avoid promising that a size will definitely fit based only on a familiar letter label.

Record recurring questions and improve the chart where they reveal ambiguity. The goal is a measurement resource customers can actually use, not a decorative table added only to make the page look complete.

title: Show clothing fit with model and garment context
description: Give clothing photographs enough context to show the selected size, garment shape and styling changes honestly.
body:
A model photograph helps someone imagine a garment, but it can also hide information. Pinning a loose shirt at the back or showing only a tightly cropped pose may make the item look different from the piece a customer receives.

Use styling to present the garment, not to change its apparent construction. Add enough context for the customer to understand what they are seeing.

## Identify the size shown

State the size worn in the photograph. Where the model has consented to sharing relevant measurements, provide the information you actually collected and verified.

Do not invent measurements to complete a template. If they are unavailable, still identify the garment size and provide a reliable product chart.

A model's clothing size is not a substitute for the dimensions of the item being sold.

## Show more than one posture

Include a straightforward front view, a side or rear view where useful, and a view that reveals the garment's natural shape. Highly posed images can supplement these rather than replace them.

For a flowing item, show how the fabric hangs when it is not being held out. For a fitted item, avoid cropping away the areas customers need to inspect.

Keep the product visible. Accessories and scenery should not make it difficult to understand sleeve length, hem shape or closure.

## Disclose changes made for the photograph

If the sample is pinned, tucked, rolled or otherwise styled in a way that changes the apparent fit, explain it. Better still, include an unaltered view as well.

A tucked shirt can be useful styling inspiration, but the customer also needs to see its actual length. A rolled sleeve does not establish the sleeve's full measurement.

Do not retouch the garment into a different silhouette or remove construction details that will be present on delivery.

## Link visual fit with measurements

Use the [garment measurement table](/blog/build-garment-measurement-tables-from-the-actual-clothing/) to explain dimensions that a photograph cannot establish.

Baymard's [apparel usability research](https://baymard.com/research-articles/apparel-5-best-practices) identifies model imagery and relevant sizing information as complementary shopping information. Neither should be treated as a universal fit guarantee.

If you describe a fit as relaxed or close-fitting, define it through the garment's actual design and chart rather than relying on the label alone.

## Keep colour and variant identity accurate

Photograph the selected variant where possible. If a detail differs between variants, do not imply that one photograph represents them all.

A black garment may conceal seams that are visible in a pale version. Add detail images where the main image does not answer the question.

Keep editing consistent and avoid promising identical colour across every screen. That limitation does not justify using an obviously inaccurate image.

## Show included and excluded pieces

A co-ordinated look may contain several products, but the listing may sell only one. Label the included garment clearly.

If the belt, inner layer or accessory is not supplied, say so near the styling image. Customers should not need to infer the selling unit from a shortened title.

For sets, use the [co-ordinated clothing guide](/blog/show-the-contents-and-sizing-of-a-coordinated-clothing-set/) to describe each included component.

## Review the page without the shoot team

Ask a colleague who was not present at the photograph session what size is shown, what arrives and how the garment is worn in the image.

If they assume a styling adjustment is part of the construction, the page needs clarification. Fix the information before adding more campaign photographs.

## Avoid turning representation into a promise

Showing a garment on more than one person can be useful when you have the resources and permissions, but no photograph can predict every customer's fit.

Keep the language respectful and factual. Do not label one body type as the correct one for the product or promise that a garment will solve a personal insecurity.

The strongest fit presentation lets customers compare the garment with their own preferences using honest images and clear measurements. It does not ask them to trust a pose as a specification.

title: Keep a boutique size-and-colour matrix understandable
description: Keep boutique stock organised by the exact size-and-colour combination customers can order.
body:
A boutique may have twenty pieces of a design and still be unable to fulfil a request for medium in blue. Total stock hides the combinations that matter to the buyer.

Build the range around exact variants. The same names should appear in your stock record, product options, photographs and packing instructions.

## Define the variant before counting it

A variant is the specific combination you sell: design, size, colour and any other meaningful difference. Give it a stable identifier.

Do not use “blue medium” as the complete internal identity if several designs share that description. A short product code can prevent confusion without appearing in the main customer-facing title.

Keep the manufacturer's label and your displayed size name connected where they differ.

## Create a matrix that shows gaps

List sizes along one dimension and colours along the other. Record the available quantity for each combination rather than entering one total for the style.

A simple spreadsheet can work if it is maintained consistently. The important feature is not the tool but the ability to see that blue medium is unavailable while blue large remains in stock.

Do not fill an unavailable cell with the nearest size merely to keep the product selectable.

## Separate physical stock from available stock

Set aside items reserved for confirmed orders, under inspection or damaged. They should not appear available simply because they are still on the shelf.

Use the existing [inventory guide](/blog/inventory-for-instagram-sellers/) for the general stock workflow. The boutique-specific task is to keep every adjustment attached to the correct size-and-colour cell.

A return should also be checked before re-entering availability. The parcel arriving back does not automatically make the garment saleable.

## Connect photographs to the variant

Use the correct colour image and identify any design difference. If one colour has a different lining or fabric specification, do not treat it as a purely visual switch.

Check that the option label matches the photograph. Names such as beige, cream and off-white can drift between the supplier sheet and the product page.

Retain one approved naming convention so support staff do not create new names while answering messages.

## Make unavailable combinations understandable

Show only choices your current store can accurately represent. If the interface cannot disable a combination cleanly, use a clear enquiry process rather than accepting impossible orders.

Do not promise automatic stock synchronisation unless that capability has been verified in your actual setup. Manual controls should be described and operated honestly.

If you accept preorders, separate them from ready stock and explain the confirmed timing and terms. An empty stock cell is not automatically a preorder offer.

## Check the size chart against the design

A consistent variant matrix does not mean every design shares one size chart. Link the appropriate [garment measurements](/blog/build-garment-measurement-tables-from-the-actual-clothing/) to each product.

When a new batch changes the cut, review both the chart and the stock identity. Mixing old and new fits under one indistinguishable variant can make support difficult.

Keep the batch distinction internally even if the customer-facing product name remains the same.

## Give packing an exact instruction

The order should identify the design, colour and size without relying on a photograph alone. Check the garment label and appearance against that instruction before sealing the parcel.

Where two colours look similar under indoor lighting, use the stock identifier rather than memory. Do not ask the packer to infer the selection from a chat screenshot.

## Audit the combinations that cause enquiries

Review repeated questions and fulfilment errors by variant. If customers regularly choose unavailable combinations, the problem may be how options are displayed rather than low demand.

If one size is repeatedly missing, that is a stock-planning observation—not proof that every customer wants it. Use your own order and enquiry records before expanding the next purchase.

A clear matrix turns a vague quantity into a set of promises your boutique can actually keep.

Keep sold-out cells visible in your internal record so a later restock does not accidentally create a second name for the same combination.

title: Describe fabric opacity, lining and finish with useful evidence
description: Describe clothing fabric, lining and opacity through observable details and confirmed specifications rather than vague quality claims.
body:
“Soft premium fabric” leaves many clothing questions unanswered. A buyer may need to know whether a garment is lined, how much light passes through it, whether the surface is textured and what fibre information is confirmed.

Replace broad praise with useful evidence. The description should help someone understand the garment, not merely suggest that it is good.

## Start with confirmed composition

Use the composition information supported by the product or supplier record. Do not identify a fibre by touch alone or borrow the composition from a similar design.

If a garment has a lining, trim or panel made from a different material, keep that information separate where relevant. One main-fabric sentence may not describe the whole item.

When a supplier changes, recheck the information rather than carrying the previous batch's description forward automatically.

## Describe the surface in plain language

Explain whether the fabric is smooth, textured, ribbed, brushed or otherwise visibly distinctive. Use close-up photographs to support the words.

Avoid turning a sensory description into an unsupported durability claim. A fabric that feels substantial is not automatically long-lasting, and a soft surface does not establish suitability for every skin type.

Keep adjectives specific enough that the customer can recognise what you mean in the photograph.

## Show opacity under stated conditions

Opacity can change with lighting, stretch and the layers worn underneath. Do not promise that a garment is never see-through based on one flattering image.

Photograph the item in a useful, reasonably consistent setting and explain relevant observations. If an inner layer is used for styling, identify whether it is included.

Where the product needs a lining or separate layer for the look shown, make that clear before purchase. Do not hide the information in a general care note.

## Identify lining coverage

State which parts are lined and, where useful, show the inside. A fully lined body with unlined sleeves should not be described simply as fully lined.

For skirts or dresses, explain the lining length relative to the outer garment. Use measured or clearly photographed information rather than an ambiguous phrase such as “proper lining.”

If the lining differs by colour variant, attach the correct detail to that option.

## Explain stretch without inventing a fit range

A fabric may stretch, but that does not make the finished garment suitable for every measurement. Construction, lining and seams also affect how it behaves.

Use the product's measured dimensions and a maker-supported description of the intended fit. Do not assign a broad body-size range solely because you can pull the fabric by hand.

The [measurement guide](/blog/build-garment-measurement-tables-from-the-actual-clothing/) helps keep the chart separate from an unverified stretch promise.

## Inspect finishing details

Show hems, seams, closures and any intentional raw edges. If the design includes a distressed or unfinished-looking feature, identify it so the buyer can distinguish intention from damage.

Do not use “handmade variation” to cover loose construction that falls outside your quality standard. Define what your business considers acceptable before writing the listing.

Photographs of the inside can be especially helpful when finishing is part of the product's value.

## Keep care information attached to the actual garment

Use instructions appropriate to the complete product, including trims and lining. A care suggestion for the main fibre alone may not cover every component.

Do not invent a washing temperature or cleaning method to complete a template. Obtain the relevant product guidance or qualified advice.

If care information changes between batches, update the listing and the information supplied with the item.

## Test the description against a real question

Ask whether a buyer could answer: what is confirmed about the material, where is it lined, what do the images show about opacity, and what care information applies?

If the answer still depends on “premium quality,” add the missing fact. A useful fabric description earns confidence through specificity and honest limits, not by repeating assurances that cannot be checked.

Keep a retained reference sample or supplier specification where practical, so future copy changes can be checked against something more reliable than memory.

title: Prepare made-to-measure clothing enquiries for a fitting discussion
description: Prepare made-to-measure clothing enquiries with a clear design brief, measurement process and fitting responsibilities.
body:
Made-to-measure work begins with more than a set of numbers. The maker needs to understand the design, intended use, measurement method and what fitting process is available.

An enquiry page should help collect that information without implying that every request can be quoted or guaranteed from a short message.

## Define the service you actually offer

Explain whether you adapt an existing pattern, create a custom design or make a standard design to supplied measurements. These are different services.

State which garments and changes are within your scope. Do not use “fully custom” when the customer can only choose length and colour.

If an in-person fitting is required, make that visible before someone assumes the order can be completed entirely remotely.

## Collect the design brief before measurements

Ask for the garment type, desired details and intended occasion or use where relevant. Reference images can help explain preferences, but they should not become a promise to copy another designer's work.

Identify which parts are essential and which are open to discussion. A neckline, sleeve and closure choice can affect the construction and measurement requirements.

Do not quote a complex request as though it were a standard product before the maker has reviewed it.

## Use the maker's measurement method

Provide the specific instructions or fitting arrangement used by your workshop. Avoid combining several online measurement guides into one form.

Record units and the method used. If a measurement appears inconsistent, ask for clarification rather than silently correcting it.

Where reliable measurement cannot be established remotely, recommend the appropriate fitting step. A deadline should not turn uncertain information into a supposedly exact specification.

## Discuss fabric and construction together

The requested silhouette may depend on the fabric, lining and fastening. Confirm those decisions as part of the brief.

Do not promise that changing the fabric will preserve every detail of the original look. Explain relevant limitations and offer a sample or swatch process if your business supports one.

Use the [fabric-information guide](/blog/describe-fabric-opacity-lining-and-finish-with-useful-evidence/) to keep composition and finish claims accurate.

## Separate quotation from final approval

A quotation should identify the agreed scope, materials, fitting stages, expected timing and what is not included. Make assumptions visible.

If the brief changes, revise the quotation before proceeding. A new sleeve construction or additional fitting should not be hidden inside an old approval.

Any payment, cancellation or alteration terms should reflect your actual policy and applicable obligations. Do not invent a blanket rule merely because the product is custom.

## Record the fitting and change process

Explain how the customer can raise a fit concern and what the next assessment step is. Avoid promising unlimited alterations unless that is a service you genuinely provide.

Keep fitting notes connected to the garment and version. A change approved during a fitting should reach the person doing the work, not remain in one staff member's notebook.

If a customer changes their preference after approving a stage, distinguish that from correcting a production error.

## Build a realistic schedule

Include consultation, material sourcing, measurement, making, fittings and final checks. The sewing time alone is not the whole lead time.

For occasion wear, clarify the date the customer needs the finished garment, not only the event date. Travel or an earlier fitting may matter.

Do not accept a schedule that depends on skipping checks your own process requires.

## End the enquiry with a defined next step

The result may be an appointment, a request for more information or a reviewed quotation. It does not have to be immediate payment.

Summarise the current decisions and unresolved points so the customer understands what happens next. This also gives the workshop a reliable starting record.

A strong made-to-measure enquiry makes the service feel considered because the process is considered. It replaces a vague promise of perfect fit with a clear route for specifying, making and checking the actual garment.

Give the final approved brief a version date, and make sure both the customer-facing contact and the workshop are using that version.

title: Show the contents and sizing of a coordinated clothing set
description: Describe every piece in a clothing set, including separate measurements and whether mixed sizes are available.
body:
A co-ordinated outfit can look like one product in a photograph while containing several different fit decisions. A top may fit comfortably while the trousers do not, and the belt shown in the image may not be included at all.

Make the contents and sizing of the set explicit. A shared colour or fabric does not make the components interchangeable.

## List what arrives

Name each included garment and accessory. State quantities and identify styling items that are not supplied.

If the listing is for a two-piece set, do not let a jacket in the photograph imply a third piece. Use a plain contents image alongside the styled outfit.

Keep the product title and price description consistent with the contents list. “Co-ord look” is not a clear selling unit.

## Measure each garment separately

Provide relevant measurements for the top and bottom, or for every substantial component. One chest measurement cannot describe the fit of the whole outfit.

Use the [garment measurement method](/blog/build-garment-measurement-tables-from-the-actual-clothing/) consistently and label units. Distinguish body guidance from finished-garment dimensions.

If the set is sold under one size label, explain what that label means for both pieces. Do not assume that a customer's usual top size determines their preferred trouser fit.

## State whether mixed sizes are possible

Some businesses can supply different sizes for the top and bottom; others sell fixed combinations. Explain the actual offer before the customer reaches confirmation.

If mixed sizing is available, record both selections in the order. A general note saying “medium set” should not remain the packing instruction after a custom combination is approved.

Do not promise split sizing unless stock and pricing can support it.

## Explain variant differences

Check whether all colour options use the same fabric, lining and construction. If they differ, attach the relevant information to the selected option.

A printed set may also have pattern-placement variation. Describe the variation you genuinely expect without using it to excuse a different print or missing motif.

Where matching between pieces matters, inspect the finished combination rather than assuming two items from the same design name will coordinate identically.

## Photograph the components on their own

Show the complete outfit, then provide views of each piece. Customers may want to understand the top's length or the trouser waistband without visual overlap.

If a garment is tucked, rolled or pinned in the styled image, include an unaltered view. The photograph should not conceal the actual shape.

Use the [fit-context guide](/blog/show-clothing-fit-with-model-and-garment-context/) for model size and styling disclosures.

## Make exchange questions understandable

Explain where the customer can find your current set-related exchange or return information. Do not invent a universal rule that all sets must always be handled in one way.

If your process requires an assessment of the complete set, state the next step clearly. Keep the response consistent with applicable obligations and the policy presented at purchase.

A customer asking about one poorly fitting component should receive a factual answer, not an automatic assumption that the whole order is ineligible.

## Pack against a component record

Check the size, colour and identity of each garment. Two similar tops can be confused when several sets are being assembled together.

If the set has a supplied belt, tie or other removable piece, give it a specific check. Small accessories are easy to omit when the instruction only says “set complete.”

Keep the packing record connected to any approved mixed-size selection.

## Review the promise as a whole

Read the listing as though the customer has never seen the collection. They should know exactly how many pieces arrive, how each is measured and which options can be changed.

A co-ordinated set is useful because it simplifies a buying decision. It should not simplify away the information needed to choose the right combination.

When the page and the packing process share the same contents record, the outfit becomes easier to understand and easier to fulfil accurately.

title: Check clothing photos against the exact variant being sold
description: Audit clothing photographs against the real colour, size, print and construction variant attached to each listing.
body:
A customer selects the sage shirt shown on the page, but the dispatched shirt has different buttons and a shorter cuff. The team may regard it as the same style, while the buyer sees a different product.

Variant photography is not only about colour swatches. It is about keeping the visual promise attached to the item that can actually be ordered.

## Identify the sample before shooting

Record the product, variant, size and batch of the photographed garment. Keep that information with the image files.

Do not rely on a photographer remembering which of several similar shirts was used. A simple shot list can preserve the connection.

If the sample differs from sale stock, resolve that before using it as the main product image.

## Check construction as well as colour

Compare buttons, pockets, cuffs, hem, lining and print placement with the current stock. A supplier may change a detail without changing the style name.

Decide which differences require new photographs or explicit information. Do not treat every visible change as an insignificant batch variation.

For genuine handmade or print-placement variation, show and describe the expected range honestly.

## Keep file names operational

Use a naming convention that connects images to the product and variant. Avoid a folder containing several files called final-new-edit.

The person uploading the page should be able to select the right image without opening every file and guessing from its colour.

Retain an original image and a documented edited version. That makes it easier to identify whether an inaccurate appearance came from the sample, lighting or editing.

## Check editing against the garment

Use a consistent reference when reviewing colour and detail. Do not change a pale garment into a richer shade simply because the edited image looks more attractive.

Screen differences are real, but they do not justify avoidable misrepresentation. Keep the [fabric description](/blog/describe-fabric-opacity-lining-and-finish-with-useful-evidence/) aligned with what the images show.

Avoid retouching away seams, texture or construction features that remain on the delivered item.

## Test the option-to-image connection

Select every available option in the actual listing or preview. Check that the relevant photograph and text agree.

If the current interface cannot attach images to combinations, explain the photographs clearly instead of implying a capability that is not present. A labelled image sequence may be more honest than an inaccurate automatic switch.

Do not use a sold-out colour's hero image as though it represents the only available option.

## Show sizes without changing apparent proportions

A garment photographed in one size does not necessarily show the proportions of every size. Identify the sample size and provide the measurement chart.

Do not digitally reshape the image to simulate another size. If proportions change meaningfully across the range, consider additional real photographs.

Use model imagery as context, not as a replacement for the [product-specific chart](/blog/build-garment-measurement-tables-from-the-actual-clothing/).

## Recheck when stock is replenished

A restock is a useful checkpoint for image accuracy. Compare a new piece with the approved visual record before reusing the old page.

If the product has changed, update the images, details and internal variant identity as needed. Keep existing order expectations in mind rather than silently rewriting the past offer.

Do not wait for a customer complaint to discover that the new batch is visibly different.

## Use a short release checklist

Before publishing, verify the sample identity, colour, construction, selling unit, option labels and included accessories. Confirm that styling items are not mistaken for contents.

Have someone other than the uploader perform the option check where practical. They are more likely to notice a mismatched image than someone who knows what the page was intended to show.

The aim is not a technically elaborate photo system. It is a reliable chain from physical garment to image to selection to parcel, so the product a customer chooses remains the product your team sends.

Keep the audit result with the product record. When an image is replaced, note which variant and batch the replacement represents so later uploads do not restore the outdated version.

title: Prepare a clothing size-exchange enquiry without assuming eligibility
description: Collect clothing size-exchange information clearly while keeping assessment, availability and policy decisions separate.
body:
A customer says a garment does not fit and asks for another size. The useful first response is not an automatic yes or no. You need to identify the order, requested size and the process that applies.

A clear enquiry helps the customer understand the next step without promising eligibility or stock before either has been checked.

## Identify the exact garment

Confirm the order reference, product, colour and size received. If the order contains several garments, ask which one is involved.

Do not ask the customer to repeat information you already have in the order record. Use the enquiry to fill actual gaps.

Keep personal information limited to what is needed for the request and use your normal verification process.

## Understand the requested change

Ask which size the customer is considering and what aspect of fit was unsuitable. The purpose is to provide relevant product information, not to challenge their experience.

Refer to the [garment measurement chart](/blog/build-garment-measurement-tables-from-the-actual-clothing/) and explain its method. Avoid guaranteeing that the next size will fit.

If the chart or listing appears inaccurate, investigate that as a product-information issue rather than treating it as an ordinary preference change.

## Check the applicable process

Review the policy presented with the purchase and any applicable obligations. Do not invent a blanket rule that worn, discounted or custom goods always receive the same treatment in every situation.

Explain what information or assessment is needed. If photographs are relevant, ask for specific useful views rather than an excessive set of personal images.

Keep the enquiry distinct from a final eligibility decision.

## Verify replacement availability

Check the exact colour-and-size combination requested. Total stock for the design is not enough.

If the replacement is unavailable, explain the choices your process supports. Do not accept the return on the promise of a size that is not actually available unless a clear alternative arrangement has been agreed.

Use the [boutique variant matrix](/blog/keep-a-boutique-size-and-colour-matrix-understandable/) to avoid reserving the wrong combination.

## Explain logistics before the customer acts

Tell the customer the authorised next step for sending or handing over the item. State any approved charges or arrangements before they incur them.

Do not instruct them to use a random carrier or address without checking your receiving process. Keep the return reference connected to the order.

Avoid promising a replacement dispatch date before the required assessment and stock checks are complete.

## Record the outcome and reason

When the request is assessed, provide a clear explanation and the available resolution. Keep it factual and respectful.

If the item or listing was wrong, do not hide that behind a generic size-exchange response. Different causes may need different handling.

Update the inventory status carefully. A returned garment should not become available for another buyer until it has passed the appropriate inspection.

## Learn from repeated fit questions

Group enquiries by product and issue. Several customers reporting the same measurement mismatch may indicate a chart or production problem.

Do not assume every exchange means poor photography or that one successful exchange proves the chart is correct. Look at the actual records.

If a chart is corrected, make sure support staff use the new version and understand which orders were placed under the earlier information.

## Close the conversation clearly

Confirm the final arrangement, current status and what the customer should expect next. Avoid leaving a thread at “we will check” after a decision has been made.

A good exchange enquiry does not make policy disappear. It makes the process understandable while the relevant facts are established.

The customer should know whether the request is awaiting information, under assessment, approved or resolved—and your team should be able to find the same answer without reconstructing the entire message history.

If the customer asks about a set, check the component arrangement separately. A top-and-trouser order may involve two measurements and a stock combination that cannot be resolved by changing one generic size label.

title: Launch a small clothing drop with complete product information
description: Launch a small clothing collection only after variants, measurements, photographs and fulfilment information are ready.
body:
A clothing drop can attract attention before the product information is ready to support it. Customers arrive, ask about length or lining, and wait while the team searches for answers.

Treat the launch as the release of a complete offer, not just a set of photographs. A smaller range with reliable information can be easier to operate than a larger unfinished one.

## Define the collection's purpose

Choose the products that belong together and explain the connection. It might be a fabric, silhouette or practical use rather than a vague seasonal label.

Do not add unrelated stock merely to make the collection look larger. Every extra design adds measurements, photographs, options and support questions.

Keep the range manageable enough that your team can inspect each listing before promotion begins.

## Finalise the saleable variants

Record the exact sizes and colours available for each design. Distinguish finished stock from products that will be made after ordering.

Do not call an item ready to ship if it still needs a substantial production step. Explain the actual process and timing.

Use the [size-and-colour matrix](/blog/keep-a-boutique-size-and-colour-matrix-understandable/) so availability reflects the combination a customer selects.

## Complete the measurement information

Measure the finished garments using a consistent method. Provide relevant dimensions for each design rather than one generic chart for the collection.

Check that size names match the product options and labels. A chart that says large while the selector says size three creates unnecessary translation.

Where the fit differs from a previous collection, say so with useful measurements rather than assuming repeat customers will know.

## Audit the images and descriptions together

Confirm that every photograph represents the current variant and that the description identifies fabric, lining, closures and included pieces.

Show the full garment as well as useful details. If a styling image contains a belt or inner layer that is not supplied, make that visible in the information.

The [variant-photo audit](/blog/check-clothing-photos-against-the-exact-variant-being-sold/) provides a focused check before upload.

## Prepare fulfilment information

Check packing materials, inspection steps and the dispatch process for the expected order volume. Include the time needed to sort similar variants.

Keep delivery estimates separate from making and dispatch time. Do not use urgency in the promotion to imply a faster service than you can provide.

Make the current support and size-exchange process accessible. Customers should not have to search social comments for the rule that applies.

## Test one order path per important variation

Walk through selecting a size and colour, reading the chart and confirming the item. Use a test or preview process that does not create unintended live orders.

If your store is enquiry-led, test the information handover instead: can staff identify the requested variant and give a consistent answer?

Do not claim automated stock or payment features unless they are verified in your actual setup. The launch plan must fit the system you are using.

## Keep the launch message specific

Explain what is new, what is available and where to find the details. Avoid unsupported scarcity, reset countdowns or claims that every product is a bestseller before it has been sold.

If quantities are limited, base the statement on the actual available stock. Do not confuse a small first production run with evidence of high demand.

Use direct links to the relevant collection or product rather than sending every interested buyer through an unrelated homepage.

## Review the first enquiries as information feedback

Watch for repeated questions about the same missing fact. Add a clear answer to the listing instead of sending the same private reply indefinitely.

Also record stock mismatches and packing confusion. These are operational signals, not merely marketing results.

A successful drop is not only the moment people see the collection. It is the period in which they can understand, choose and receive the garments accurately. Prepare that whole journey before increasing the audience.

Keep a dated release checklist for the collection. When a late product joins the launch, run the same checks rather than assuming the original collection approval covers the new listing.

title: Keep alteration requests separate from standard clothing orders
description: Keep clothing alterations as a reviewed specification with clear feasibility, approval and production status.
body:
A request to shorten a sleeve can look like a small note on a standard clothing order. In practice, it changes the product your workshop must deliver and may affect timing, appearance and the customer's expectations.

Treat an alteration as a specific service decision. Do not hide it inside an ordinary size selection.

## Identify the requested change precisely

Ask what the customer wants changed and how they are describing the result. “A little shorter” is not a production measurement.

Use the maker's measurement method and confirm units. Where the request depends on personal fit, explain whether an in-person assessment or fitting is needed.

Do not infer an alteration from a customer's height alone.

## Check whether the design supports it

A change may affect pockets, closures, decoration or proportions. Have the appropriate person assess feasibility before promising the result.

Do not assume that every garment can be shortened or expanded by the same amount. The available construction and material matter.

If the request is outside your service, say so and offer only alternatives you can genuinely provide.

## Separate standard options from custom work

A standard length offered in the product selector is different from a one-off alteration. Keep those paths distinct in the order record.

If an alteration changes the price or making time, explain it before approval. Do not add the cost after the customer believes the standard product is confirmed.

Avoid advertising a custom option that the current order process cannot record reliably.

## Create a clear alteration specification

Record the product, original size, requested finished measurement, method and any agreed limitations. Identify the person who approved it.

A sketch or marked photograph can help where words are ambiguous, but it should support rather than contradict the written measurement.

Keep one current version. If the customer changes the request, mark the earlier instruction superseded before work continues.

## Explain the effect on the schedule

Include assessment, work and final inspection in the timing. Do not count only the minutes spent sewing.

If the garment is needed for an occasion, clarify the required completion date and whether a fitting is part of the process. Use a feasible schedule rather than an optimistic promise.

The [made-to-measure enquiry guide](/blog/prepare-made-to-measure-clothing-enquiries-for-a-fitting-discussion/) covers broader custom work when the request goes beyond a bounded alteration.

## Apply the actual service terms

Explain the relevant payment, cancellation, fit-assessment and resolution process. Check those terms against your policy and applicable obligations.

Do not assume that the word altered removes every responsibility for a production error. The finished garment still needs to match the approved specification.

If the customer asks to change an instruction after cutting or sewing has begun, assess what is possible and communicate it clearly before proceeding.

## Check the finished measurement

Inspect the result using the agreed method. Compare the garment with the alteration record rather than relying on how it looks on the workbench.

Check that related details still function and that the finish meets your normal standard. A correct length alone does not establish a complete job.

If there is a discrepancy, resolve it before packing or presenting the garment as complete.

## Keep the standard listing accurate

Do not change the public product measurements to reflect one customer's alteration. Future buyers still need the dimensions of the standard product.

Likewise, do not use an altered sample in the main photograph without explaining the difference. The visual promise should remain aligned with the item most customers order.

A separate alteration record lets your business offer flexibility without making the standard catalogue unreliable. It gives the customer a clear specification and the workshop a defined task, rather than asking either side to remember what “just a small change” was supposed to mean.

For collection or delivery, identify the altered garment separately from unmodified stock. An otherwise identical standard piece should not be packed by mistake after the workshop has completed the custom measurement and inspection.

title: Sell cushion covers without leaving insert and closure details unclear
description: Make cushion-cover listings clear about covers, inserts, dimensions, closures and pattern placement.
body:
A full-looking cushion in a styled photograph can make a cover-only listing appear to include an insert. The customer may not discover the difference until the parcel arrives.

State the selling unit first. Then explain the dimensions and construction that determine whether the cover suits the customer's existing cushion.

## Put cover-only information near the price

If the insert is not included, say so clearly in the title or immediate product information. Do not rely on a note at the bottom of the page.

If an insert option is available, identify it as a separate choice and describe what is supplied. Keep the photograph and selected option aligned.

A styled sofa image can remain useful, but it should not be the only explanation of the contents.

## Measure the cover consistently

State the finished cover dimensions and the method used. Identify whether measurements refer to the flat cover rather than an insert recommendation.

Do not promise compatibility with every insert carrying the same nominal size. Explain any maker-supported guidance relevant to your construction.

For a handmade cover, establish the actual variation your process allows. Avoid an exact-looking number unsupported by inspection.

## Show the closure and reverse

Photograph the zip, envelope opening, buttons or other closure. Show the back as well as the decorative front.

If the reverse uses a different fabric or colour, describe it. A single front image should not imply that the design continues around the whole cover.

Check that the closure is accessible and that the description reflects the finished product, not an earlier sample.

## Explain pattern placement

A patterned fabric may produce different motif positions across covers. Show representative variation where it genuinely occurs.

Do not use that explanation to send a different print or colourway. Keep the named fabric and intended design consistent.

If the customer is buying several covers for a coordinated arrangement, explain whether exact pattern matching is offered. Do not promise a matched set unless you can assemble one.

## Describe materials and care accurately

Use confirmed composition and product-specific care information. If trims, piping or embroidery require different treatment, account for them in the guidance.

Avoid unverified claims such as stain-proof, outdoor-safe or fade-proof. A fabric's appearance alone does not establish those properties.

For broader material wording, refer to the [materials and care guide](/blog/describe-materials-and-care-without-unsupported-claims/).

## Photograph scale without disguising the product

Use a plain view and, if helpful, a room setting that makes the dimensions understandable. Identify other cushions and props that are not included.

Do not digitally enlarge the cover to make it fill more of a sofa. The written measurement and visual impression should support each other.

If several sizes share one page, label the photographed size and ensure the customer can identify the selected one.

## Keep sets and singles distinct

A pair of covers should state the quantity and whether both designs are identical. A photo of four cushions should not represent a single-cover purchase without explanation.

If customers can mix colours, record each selected cover in the order. A general “two-piece set” label may be insufficient for packing.

Check quantities and variants before sealing the parcel, especially when similar colours are stored together.

## Answer fit enquiries with evidence

When a customer asks whether the cover will suit an existing insert, explain your measurements and ask them to compare using the stated method. Avoid guaranteeing a result from a vague description such as a standard cushion.

If the requested arrangement needs a custom size, use a separate confirmed specification rather than changing the standard listing.

A good cushion-cover page answers the basic question immediately: what exactly arrives? It then gives the customer enough information to compare that item with the insert, furniture and style they already have, without pretending that one photograph can settle every fit decision.

Before restocking a familiar design, compare the new closure and reverse fabric with the existing page. Small supplier changes can make an otherwise unchanged photograph incomplete.

title: Show wall décor dimensions without inventing installation advice
description: Present wall décor with accurate size, weight and supplied hardware information while leaving installation decisions to appropriate guidance.
body:
Wall décor can look small in a close-up and enormous in a room mock-up. It can also appear ready to hang when the listing does not actually include any mounting hardware.

Make the physical product clear before discussing how it might look in a room. Do not turn a decorative listing into unsupported installation advice.

## State the outer dimensions

Measure the complete item, including a frame or projecting edge where relevant. If the artwork area is smaller than the outer size, identify both.

For irregular shapes, explain the longest and widest points. A single diameter is not useful for a shape that is not circular.

Use consistent units and show the orientation. A customer should not have to guess whether the first number is height or width.

## Identify weight and supplied parts

If weight is relevant, measure the finished item and state what is included in that figure. Do not estimate from a similar product.

List any supplied hanging attachments or hardware accurately. Distinguish an attachment on the item from fixings for the customer's wall.

Do not claim that included hardware suits every wall type. Installation suitability depends on circumstances beyond a product photograph.

## Use room images honestly

A room setting can help with scale, but the item must be represented at a plausible size. Label a digital room visualisation if that is what it is.

Do not enlarge the product to create a more dramatic composition. Keep a dimensioned plain view available so the buyer can check the physical size.

Show how a multi-piece arrangement is laid out without implying that every object in the scene is included.

## Explain sets and spacing separately

For a group of wall pieces, list the size of each component. If you show an overall arrangement, explain that the total span depends on the spacing chosen.

Do not present one arrangement width as though it were the fixed size of a single product. The customer may choose different gaps.

A simple layout reference can show what was photographed while leaving installation decisions appropriately separate.

## Describe surface and finish

Show texture, edges and the reverse where useful. Identify reflective, raised or delicate elements that may not be obvious in a front view.

Keep material claims tied to evidence. Do not call a printed surface hand-painted unless that describes the actual process.

For artwork and reproductions, use the [catalogue distinction guide](/blog/separate-original-artwork-from-reproductions-in-the-catalogue/) to avoid blurring the type of product.

## Set an installation boundary

Provide the manufacturer's or maker's verified instructions where available. If your business does not provide installation, say so.

Do not recommend a load rating, adhesive, drill fixing or wall attachment from guesswork. Direct customers to suitable professional or manufacturer guidance when their wall or situation requires assessment.

A statement such as “easy to install anywhere” can create a promise the product information cannot support.

## Check the delivery offer

Large or fragile pieces may require a specific packing and delivery arrangement. Confirm the service for the actual dimensions rather than treating the item like a small accessory.

Explain what arrives assembled and what, if anything, remains to be done. Do not imply that a frame is included when the listing is for the artwork alone.

Keep delivery limitations and any genuine additional charges visible before confirmation.

## Review the page as a planning tool

A customer should be able to measure their available space, understand the supplied item and identify what installation information remains to be checked.

If they still need to guess the outer size, contents or mounting arrangement, add the missing fact. More room photographs will not solve a missing measurement.

Accurate wall-décor information helps someone decide whether an object belongs in their space without making your store responsible for installation promises it has not assessed.

Keep a separate field for the framed size when both framed and unframed options exist. The customer's available wall space should be compared with the selected option, not the smallest number in the description.

title: Prepare a ceramic décor listing around shape, finish and fragility
description: Describe decorative ceramics through measured shape, visible finish, intended use and careful packing information.
body:
A ceramic object may be sold for decoration, but customers can infer other uses from its shape. A bowl-like piece may be assumed suitable for food, and a vase-like object may be assumed watertight.

Do not let appearance create an unsupported function claim. State the intended use and provide the physical information a buyer needs.

## Identify the intended product

Describe the item as it is offered: decorative vessel, sculptural object, planter cover or another confirmed category. Do not add food-contact, heat or water-use claims without appropriate evidence.

If a function has not been established, do not stage the photograph in a way that implies it. Decorative use should be clear rather than hidden in a footnote.

This guide does not establish testing or compliance for functional ceramic ware.

## Measure the shape usefully

Record height, widest width and any opening dimension that matters to the intended use. For an irregular object, explain where the measurement is taken.

An overall width does not tell a customer the usable opening. Keep those figures separate.

If the object is handmade, inspect the actual range of variation and describe it honestly. Avoid treating every difference as acceptable merely because no two pieces are identical.

## Show the finish from several angles

Photograph the surface, base, rim and interior where relevant. A single front image may conceal the most useful details.

Explain intentional glaze variation or texture using the actual product range. Do not describe chips or unintended damage as natural variation.

If each piece is materially different, consider showing the exact item being sold or defining the selection process clearly.

## Keep colour representation consistent

Use lighting that shows the glaze without excessive reflection or colour shifts. Include a plain view alongside styled images.

Do not promise identical colour on every screen, but do not use that limitation to justify an image that is noticeably unlike the object.

Where several glaze options share a listing, attach the correct images and names to each selection.

## Clarify what is included

A flower arrangement, stand or plant in a photograph may be a styling prop. State whether it arrives with the ceramic piece.

For a set, list the number and dimensions of the objects. A trio photograph should not represent a single-item purchase without explanation.

Use the [home-décor set guide](/blog/create-a-home-decor-set-without-confusing-the-individual-pieces/) when several pieces are sold together.

## Pack for the actual shape

Identify protruding parts, narrow necks and contact points that need attention. Choose packaging based on the object rather than its product category alone.

Follow the carrier's current requirements and test your packing arrangement on representative samples. A fragile label does not replace adequate protection.

Do not claim a package is unbreakable or guaranteed damage-free because one test parcel arrived safely.

## Record condition before dispatch

Check the selected piece for the intended finish and any unintended damage. Match it to the order and retain a clear internal record where useful.

If photographs are kept, avoid customer information in images used outside fulfilment. The record supports investigation; it does not automatically disprove a later customer report.

Provide a straightforward route for reporting an arrival problem and follow your actual resolution process.

## Use enquiries to improve the listing

If customers repeatedly ask whether the piece holds water, what the opening size is or whether the flowers are included, answer those questions prominently.

Do not add a function just because people want it. The right improvement may be a clearer limitation or a different product that has been assessed for that use.

A strong decorative-ceramics page combines an appealing image with disciplined information. It lets the customer appreciate the object while understanding its dimensions, variation and intended role, without turning visual similarity into an unverified promise.

When photographing a batch, identify which piece appears in each file. If the customer chooses a particular glaze pattern, that selection needs to remain connected to the piece inspected and packed.

title: Photograph rugs with dimensions and room-scale context
description: Show rug dimensions, edge details and room-scale context without making a small rug look larger than it is.
body:
A rug photograph can make almost any size look generous when the camera is close enough. That may create interest, but it does not help a customer decide whether the rug fits their room.

Build the page around the actual dimensions and the way the product is represented. Room styling should support the measurement, not compete with it.

## Define the measured area

State the rug's length and width using a consistent method. Explain whether fringes are included when they affect the overall size.

For round or irregular rugs, identify the relevant diameter or longest dimensions. Do not force an irregular shape into an unexplained rectangular measurement.

Keep size names such as small and large secondary to the actual numbers.

## Show the whole outline

Include a plain view that reveals the rug's shape and edges. A close texture image is useful, but it cannot establish the overall design.

If the pattern has a directional element, show its orientation. Customers may need to understand how it will look relative to furniture.

Avoid cropping the main image so tightly that the buyer cannot see whether the rug is rectangular, rounded or irregular.

## Use room context at an honest scale

Photograph the actual rug in a room where possible. If a digital visualisation is used, label it and keep the scale consistent with the dimensions.

Do not enlarge the rug to reach under furniture it would not cover in reality. A customer should be able to reconcile the styled image with a tape measure.

Show the selected size or identify which size appears in the room image when the listing offers several.

## Describe the surface and reverse

Provide confirmed material information and close views of the surface, edge and backing. Explain construction details that affect the product's appearance.

Do not claim non-slip, stain-proof or suitable for every surface without appropriate evidence. A visible backing texture does not establish a tested safety property.

If an additional underlay is recommended by verified product guidance, identify whether it is included rather than implying it arrives automatically.

## Keep care information product-specific

Use the care instructions appropriate to the actual rug and its components. Do not infer a washing method from fibre content alone.

If professional cleaning or a particular process is required by the maker's guidance, communicate it clearly. Avoid inventing a simple cleaning recipe to make the product seem easier to own.

The [materials and care guide](/blog/describe-materials-and-care-without-unsupported-claims/) provides a broader claim-checking framework.

## Explain natural and handmade variation carefully

If size or pattern placement varies, establish the expected range from the product. Do not use a vague variation note to cover a substantially different item.

For one-of-a-kind pieces, show the exact rug or define how the customer selects it. A representative image may not be sufficient when the pattern is the main reason for buying.

Keep the variant record connected to the photographed piece.

## Check delivery and opening information

State the actual delivery arrangement and packaging information relevant to the product. Large dimensions can affect handling, so confirm the service rather than assuming a standard small-parcel process.

Provide maker-supported opening or settling guidance where available. Do not promise that every crease or shape issue will disappear after an invented number of hours.

If an arrival issue occurs, use the normal support process and assess the actual product.

## Help the customer compare their space

Encourage measuring the intended area and comparing it with the listed rug dimensions. Avoid prescribing a universal room layout as though it suits every home.

A useful product page lets the customer make that comparison without decoding a lifestyle photograph. The plain outline, dimensions and room context should tell the same story.

That consistency is what makes a rug listing trustworthy: the object in the parcel occupies the amount of space the page led the customer to expect.

Record whether the customer selected a size or a specific one-off piece. That distinction helps prevent a similar-looking rug from being treated as an interchangeable packing substitute.

title: Create a home-décor set without confusing the individual pieces
description: Define decorative sets with clear quantities, component dimensions and a packing record that matches the styled arrangement.
body:
A styled shelf can contain several products, props and pieces of furniture. If the listing sells a home-décor set, the customer needs to know which of those objects actually arrive.

Start with the contents. A coordinated appearance is not enough to define the purchase.

## Name every included component

List the items and quantities in the set. Use product names that your packing team can identify, not only mood-based labels.

If the photograph includes a plant, books or a tray that is not supplied, label them as styling props. Do not assume the customer will recognise which objects belong to your catalogue.

Keep the selling unit visible near the price: one set with a defined number of pieces.

## Give each piece its own measurements

A set-level size can be misleading because the arrangement depends on spacing. Provide the dimensions of each object.

If you show an overall display footprint, explain that it describes the photographed arrangement rather than a fixed assembled product.

For nested or stackable pieces, distinguish the stored arrangement from the individual dimensions. Do not imply a function that has not been established.

## Explain the relationship between pieces

Say whether the objects share a finish, material or design motif. If variation is intentional, show it.

Do not describe a set as matching when the components are only broadly similar and the differences matter visually. A customer may be choosing the group precisely for coordination.

Where handmade variation affects the set, inspect the actual combination before packing rather than pairing pieces at random.

## Separate functional claims

A decorative bowl, candle holder and vessel may each have different intended uses. Do not apply one broad safety or suitability statement to the whole set.

Only describe functions supported for the actual components. This guide does not establish heat, food-contact, electrical or load-bearing suitability.

If a component is decorative only, make that limitation visible rather than allowing the styled scene to imply another use.

## Keep stock linked to components

If the items are also sold separately, availability for the set depends on all required parts. A complete set cannot be promised simply because its largest piece remains in stock.

Use a component record and account for reservations or damaged items. A manual record is acceptable if it accurately reflects the physical stock.

When a component becomes unavailable, do not substitute a similar object without explaining the change and obtaining the appropriate agreement.

## Photograph contents and arrangement

Include one plain image of all supplied pieces and another showing a possible arrangement. The first explains the purchase; the second offers context.

Keep the scale honest and identify props. Do not use image editing to make the set appear larger or more numerous.

For specific product types, link to relevant details such as [ceramic finishes](/blog/prepare-a-ceramic-decor-listing-around-shape-finish-and-fragility/) or [wall dimensions](/blog/show-wall-decor-dimensions-without-inventing-installation-advice/).

## Pack each component deliberately

Check the complete contents before wrapping. Protect pieces from contacting one another and choose packaging suitable for their shapes.

A set may need more than one internal compartment even when it fits inside one outer box. Test the arrangement with representative samples and follow the delivery provider's requirements.

Keep a clear internal record of the final contents where useful, without exposing customer information.

## Handle support at component level

If a customer reports an issue with one piece, identify it accurately. A set name alone may not tell your team which object needs assessment.

Explain the available resolution through your actual process and applicable obligations. Do not assume that every component can be replaced independently or that the customer must always accept a different finish.

A well-defined home-décor set simplifies selection without hiding the objects inside it. The buyer understands what they receive, and your team can check the parcel against the same precise promise rather than recreating a styled photograph from memory.

If customers can choose a colour combination, record each component's selection separately. One set-level colour name may not capture a mixed arrangement that has been agreed during the enquiry.

title: Describe a handmade bag through usable internal measurements
description: Describe a handmade bag with opening, internal space and handle measurements rather than relying only on its outer size.
body:
A bag can be wide on the outside but narrow at the opening. It may look spacious in a photograph while a lining, curved base or internal pocket reduces the usable space.

Give customers measurements that answer what they can actually place inside. Outer dimensions remain useful, but they are only part of the specification.

## Measure the finished bag in a defined state

State whether the bag is measured flat, lightly filled or standing in its normal shape. A soft bag can produce different numbers depending on how it is arranged.

Record height, width and depth where those dimensions are meaningful. Explain irregular shapes rather than forcing them into an unexplained box.

Use the finished product, including lining and closure, rather than the unfinished outer panel.

## Show the opening separately

Measure the usable opening or describe its practical shape. A wide body with a short zip may not accept an object as wide as the bag itself.

Photograph the opening with the closure fully open in its intended use. Do not stretch or force it to create a more generous impression.

If the bag has a frame or rigid mouth, include that construction in the description.

## Demonstrate contents honestly

A contents photograph can help, but identify the items used for scale and state that they are not included. Use ordinary objects whose dimensions you can report where needed.

Do not claim that every laptop, tablet or bottle fits because one sample does. Device and container dimensions vary.

If you name a particular item used in a demonstration, make clear that it is a measured example rather than a universal compatibility promise.

## Record internal space and obstructions

Show the lining, dividers and pockets. A pocket can be useful while also affecting how a larger object sits.

For a structured bag, give useful internal measurements if you can measure them consistently. For a soft irregular bag, explain the limits of a precise capacity claim and rely on clear dimensions and representative contents.

Avoid inventing a litre capacity from a rough rectangular calculation when the bag does not retain that shape.

## Include handle and strap measurements

State the handle drop or strap length using a defined method. For an adjustable strap, provide the usable range and explain what the measurement includes.

Show the attachment points and whether the strap is removable. Do not let a photograph imply that an optional strap is supplied as standard.

Use the [custom strap specification guide](/blog/record-custom-bag-strap-requests-as-an-exact-specification/) for non-standard requests.

## Avoid unsupported load promises

A bag holding several props in a photograph is not evidence of a tested load rating. Do not publish a maximum weight unless it is supported for the finished construction.

Describe intended use factually and keep safety or durability claims within the evidence you have. A strong-looking handle is not a substitute for assessment.

If a customer asks about a use outside your confirmed specification, say what is unknown rather than reassuring them from appearance.

## Keep measurements tied to variants

Different sizes, linings or closures may change usable space. Check each meaningful variant instead of copying the first sample's measurements.

If handmade variation affects dimensions, establish the expected range from your process. Do not use a broad variation note to excuse a substantially different size.

Maintain the current record when a pattern or supplier component changes.

## Finish with a customer comparison

Encourage the customer to compare the listed opening and internal dimensions with the objects they want to carry. The decision should not depend on the word roomy.

Before publishing, ask someone to identify the opening size, overall shape, strap arrangement and included items from the page. Add the missing fact wherever they have to guess.

That is how a handmade bag listing becomes useful: it helps the buyer understand the space and construction they will receive, while leaving unsupported capacity and load claims out of the sales promise.

title: Show bag pockets, closures and lining before the customer asks
description: Show the inside of a bag with pocket dimensions, closures and lining details that match the selected product.
body:
The outside of a bag attracts attention; the inside often determines whether it suits daily use. A customer may care more about a zipped pocket or a secure opening than the styled photograph suggests.

Build an interior image set and description that makes those practical details visible. Do not leave them as answers available only through messages.

## Open the bag properly for the photograph

Show the main compartment in a way that reveals its shape without distorting it. A dark image taken through a narrow opening may technically show the lining but answer very little.

Use enough light to identify pockets, seams and closures accurately. Do not digitally add brightness that changes the lining's colour beyond recognition.

Include one overall interior view and closer details where the construction needs explanation.

## Name each pocket by its actual structure

Distinguish an open slip pocket from a zipped compartment. State how many there are and where they sit.

If you describe a pocket as suitable for a particular object, check the actual dimensions. “Phone pocket” should not imply that every phone fits.

A measured example can help, but the pocket's usable width and depth are more useful than a broad compatibility label.

## Show how the main closure works

Photograph the zip, magnet, drawstring, flap or other closure in relevant positions. Explain whether the bag closes fully or retains an open gap.

Do not describe a closure as theft-proof or completely secure without appropriate evidence. State the mechanism and let the customer understand its design.

If the closure is optional or differs by size, keep that information attached to the selected variant.

## Describe the lining accurately

Use confirmed material information and show the actual colour or pattern. If lining fabric varies, define the selection process rather than letting the customer expect the photograph exactly.

A contrast lining can make the interior look different from the outer product. Show that difference deliberately instead of hiding it.

Do not claim waterproof protection because the lining has a coated appearance. Performance claims need evidence for the finished bag.

## Include attachments and removable parts

Key loops, detachable pouches and dividers should be named and counted. State whether they are included or shown as optional accessories.

If a removable insert changes the usable space, explain both arrangements. Do not photograph the bag with an organiser and omit that it is sold separately.

Use a plain contents image where several parts could be confused.

## Keep the exterior and interior records connected

A change to the lining, pocket layout or zip can occur without changing the outer silhouette. Review the product page when production changes.

Do not let an old interior photograph describe a new batch. The customer may have chosen the bag specifically for that pocket arrangement.

The [usable-measurement guide](/blog/describe-a-handmade-bag-through-usable-internal-measurements/) complements these images with the dimensions a photograph cannot establish.

## Test the information with a packing scenario

Choose a representative set of ordinary items and check how they sit in the actual bag. Photograph the arrangement without overfilling or forcing the closure.

Explain that the contents are illustrative and not included. Avoid presenting the demonstration as a load test or a guarantee for every similarly named object.

If the demonstration reveals that a pocket is difficult to access, improve the description rather than concealing the limitation.

## Turn repeated questions into product information

If customers repeatedly ask whether the bag has a zip, a lining or an inside pocket, make those answers prominent. Do not keep important buying information in a private reply template only.

Before publishing, compare every interior claim with the finished product. A small feature can be a decisive reason to buy.

An honest interior presentation makes the bag easier to choose and reduces the gap between an attractive exterior photograph and the practical object the customer receives.

Include the interior view in the same update checklist as the hero image. Replacing the outer fabric should not accidentally leave an unrelated lining photograph attached to the product.

title: Record custom bag strap requests as an exact specification
description: Record custom bag straps by length, width, attachment and compatibility before agreeing to make or replace one.
body:
A customer asks for a longer strap, but the maker receives no clear answer to longer than what. Another customer requests a replacement for a bag bought elsewhere, without showing the attachment.

Treat a strap request as a specification, not an adjective. The length is only one part of the decision.

## Identify the bag and current attachment

Ask whether the strap is for your own design or another product. Obtain the relevant product reference or clear photographs of the attachment points.

Do not assume that clips, loops or rings are interchangeable because they look similar. Check dimensions and construction through the appropriate maker assessment.

If you cannot establish compatibility, explain that before accepting the request.

## Define how length is measured

State whether the length includes clips or other hardware and whether it refers to the shortest, longest or fixed wearable configuration.

Ask the customer to use the same method. A number measured from end to end should not be compared silently with one measured between attachment points.

For an adjustable strap, record the requested usable range rather than one ambiguous total.

## Record width and material separately

A longer strap may also need a particular width, colour or material. Confirm those choices and the evidence behind the material description.

Do not promise that a replacement will match an older bag perfectly when the original fabric or hardware is unavailable. Show the proposed difference.

If the customer is asking for a different construction, have the maker assess it rather than treating it as a simple length change.

## Check attachment and intended use

Record the clip or fastening type and the bag-side connection. Ask about the intended use where it affects feasibility, but do not infer a load rating from the answer.

A custom strap is not automatically stronger than the original. Avoid unsupported weight-capacity or safety claims.

If the proposed combination is outside your confirmed design, decline or seek the appropriate assessment instead of reassuring the customer from a photograph.

## Prepare one final specification

Summarise the bag reference, measurement method, length or adjustment range, width, material, colour and hardware. Include any agreed limitation.

A marked drawing or sample photograph can help clarify the arrangement. Keep it connected to the written version.

Use the [custom approval checkpoint](/blog/set-a-custom-order-approval-checkpoint-before-production/) so the maker works from one approved instruction rather than several messages.

## Confirm price and timing before production

Explain the actual work and materials involved. A replacement hardware request may require sourcing time even if the sewing is brief.

If the requested specification changes, update the quote and approval. Do not silently substitute a clip or shorten a range to use available materials.

Keep any service, cancellation or resolution terms consistent with your actual policy and applicable obligations.

## Inspect the finished strap against the record
