**Delivery information should be easy to find at the point where it affects the purchase.** Putting every condition in the header can crowd the page without helping the customer understand what applies.

Use a short, truthful summary where useful and provide the relevant detail beside the product or delivery choice.

## Separate universal and conditional facts

A statement applying to every order may suit a compact announcement area. A charge that depends on destination or basket value needs more context.

Do not present a conditional offer as universal merely to shorten the wording.

List the delivery facts first, then decide where each belongs. Layout should follow the meaning.

## Keep the header focused

The header primarily supports identity and navigation. A delivery message should not make the menu, search or bag difficult to use.

Check the combined height on a phone, including any sticky behaviour. Several short strips can consume a large part of a small screen.

Remove repeated statements that do not add new information.

## Put product-specific timing near the decision

Made-to-order preparation time may differ from courier transit time. Explain the distinction on the relevant product page.

Do not use a general shipping estimate to imply that every item is ready immediately.

If the customer selects a date, clarify whether it is a request, dispatch date or supported delivery commitment.

## Make the full explanation reachable

Link a concise summary to a clear delivery-information page or section. Use descriptive wording rather than an unexplained icon.

The destination should contain the actual conditions, not a generic placeholder.

Do not make the customer search through a long footer to understand a charge already affecting the basket.

## Update the total at the right stage

When delivery depends on an address or option, show the applicable amount before commitment. Explain what is still unknown if a quote is required.

A banner cannot substitute for the calculated result.

Check that the product page, bag and checkout do not make contradictory promises about free delivery or timing.

## Test boundary cases

Use a basket below and above any threshold and an address inside and outside the intended coverage. Inspect the wording as well as the amount.

If the offer excludes a product or location, make that understandable before the customer reaches a dead end.

Use safe test data and avoid creating real shipments.

## Avoid decorative assurance claims

Do not add guaranteed delivery, insured shipping or similar badges unless the business can substantiate the exact claim.

A simple accurate sentence is stronger than a row of impressive but unsupported icons.

Keep operational facts sourced from the people who actually fulfil the orders.

## Review the phone view

Check whether long delivery wording wraps over controls, whether a sticky message hides a field and whether the complete information remains readable.

A desktop banner that fits one line can become an intrusive block on mobile.

Do not reduce the text to an unreadable size merely to preserve the desktop shape.

## Maintain one factual source

Identify who updates delivery rules and which pages repeat them. A change in charge or lead time should not leave old copy elsewhere.

Keep a short inventory of the affected surfaces so updates can be checked systematically.

The design should make accurate maintenance easier, not require manually correcting the same promise in ten unrelated places.

## Check the shared-link entry

A visitor may arrive directly on a product rather than through the homepage. Open that route and confirm that the relevant delivery information is still discoverable. Do not make a header announcement the only place where an important condition is explained, especially if the message rotates or can be dismissed.

## Choose clarity over volume

The customer needs to know what applies to their order, not every internal detail of your logistics process.

Use the header for a limited relevant summary, the product for preparation context and checkout for the applicable choice and amount.

A useful delivery design answers the question at the right moment. It does not make the whole storefront smaller by placing every condition above the products.

title: Give product options enough space on a small screen
description: Design product-option controls for small screens so choices, availability, errors and the final selected item remain clear.
body:
**Product options need enough room to be read, selected and corrected on a phone.** Compressing them to preserve a decorative layout can create the wrong order.

Design around the longest ordinary labels and the actual combinations the business sells, not only short demo values.

## Name the choice clearly

Use a visible label for each option, such as size or finish. Do not expect the customer to infer the meaning of an unexplained row of circles.

If a choice needs a measurement or guide, make that information reachable near the control.

Keep the terminology consistent with the product description and the merchant's order record.

## Use real label lengths

Test the longest legitimate option name and more choices than the ideal demo shows. Check wrapping and spacing.

Do not abbreviate important differences until the labels become ambiguous.

A multi-line control can be preferable to tiny text if the selection remains clear and the layout stays usable.

## Distinguish selected and available

The customer should be able to tell what is chosen and what cannot currently be selected. Do not rely on colour alone.

An unavailable combination is different from an unselected available option. Use meaningful state presentation.

Avoid silently switching to another option when the requested combination is unavailable.

## Keep touch and focus practical

Ask the implementer to check the controls against relevant accessibility requirements and test them with keyboard navigation as well as touch.

Do not let a decorative swatch become the only means of identifying a colour or finish.

A visible focus state and understandable label support people using different input methods. One phone screenshot cannot establish the full result.

## Show price changes clearly

If a selection changes the price, keep the current amount near the decision and update it consistently.

Do not leave the product-level minimum appearing as though it is the selected amount.

Before adding to the bag, the buyer should understand the item and price they are choosing.

## Handle missing selections

If a required choice has not been made, explain what is needed without clearing other valid inputs.

The error should be near the relevant control and visible after activation. A message hidden above the current scroll position can leave the shopper unsure why nothing happened.

Do not use a default selection simply to avoid validation unless that default is genuinely appropriate and clearly shown.

## Protect the selection during navigation

Open a size guide, inspect another image and return. Check whether the selected option remains understandable.

If the page reloads or the customer returns from the bag, the behaviour should not silently create a different specification.

The exact persistence rules depend on the implementation, but the customer-facing result must be honest.

## Inspect the bag line

After a safe add-to-bag action, confirm the option appears in the line item. A selected control that disappears from the summary creates uncertainty.

Check quantity changes and removal too. The design should keep the item identity clear throughout.

Do not approve the product page in isolation from the next screen.

## Test the awkward combination

Use one unavailable choice, one long label and a product with more than one option group. This reveals whether the small-screen layout handles ordinary complexity.

A template that works only for a single short selector may not fit a variant-heavy range.

Keep the test data for later design changes.

## Check the instruction hierarchy

Keep the option label, supporting explanation and error visually distinct. If all three use the same small style, the customer may not know which is the current problem. A clear hierarchy helps the buyer correct a choice without rereading the entire product description or guessing which field blocked progress.

## Preserve the buying task

Give the options enough space even if that moves decorative content lower on the page. The product photograph and brand style still matter, but they should not prevent an accurate selection.

Choose the layout that makes the current state and next action obvious. The goal is not the smallest selector; it is the correct item reaching the bag and, eventually, the fulfilment record.

title: Keep cart and checkout visually connected to the store
description: Keep cart and checkout visually consistent with the storefront while preserving clear totals, correction controls and functional trust cues.
body:
**Cart and checkout should feel like part of the same store, not an unrelated page reached by accident.** Consistency helps orientation, but it must not obscure the practical information needed to complete an order.

Carry the brand through typography, colour and structure while giving totals, options and errors a clear hierarchy.

## Identify the shared design elements

Use a small set of consistent tokens or rules for text, buttons, borders and spacing. The same action should not change appearance arbitrarily between product and bag.

Keep the merchant identity recognisable. A customer should know they are still dealing with the intended store.

Do not copy a decorative homepage treatment into every functional control if it reduces readability.

## Preserve item identity

The bag should show the product, selected options, quantity and relevant image clearly. Long names must remain distinguishable.

A missing or loading image should not remove the textual identity of the item.

Check that a variant change is reflected in the summary rather than leaving an old label beside a new price.

## Make correction controls obvious

Quantity changes, removal and returning to shopping should be understandable on both phone and desktop.

Do not style a destructive action as the primary next step or hide it behind an unlabeled icon.

The customer should be able to correct the bag before commitment without losing unrelated information unnecessarily.

## Establish a total hierarchy

Distinguish item subtotal, delivery and the final amount. Show uncertainty honestly if delivery has not yet been calculated.

Do not make an estimated amount look like the final accepted total.

Use consistent monetary formatting, including meaningful fractional amounts. Visual simplification should not alter the apparent price.

## Keep checkout progression clear

If the flow has steps, show the current task and the next action. A button label should describe what happens, especially when it submits an order or initiates payment.

Do not use the same vague continue label for materially different commitments without surrounding context.

When returning to an earlier step, preserve valid information where the actual implementation supports it and explain any reset.

## Design errors as part of the theme

An error should be visible and readable without looking like an unrelated system failure. Keep its meaning more important than decorative consistency.

Show the relevant field and preserve valid entries. Do not rely only on a colour change.

If the outcome of a submission is uncertain, the message should not falsely say that nothing was recorded.

## Check sticky elements

A sticky header or summary can be helpful, but it must not cover focused fields, error messages or confirmation controls on a small screen.

Inspect the settled viewport while entering information, not only a full-page screenshot.

A visually coherent page can still be unusable if a persistent element occupies the wrong space.

## Avoid invented trust decoration

Do not add payment, security or delivery badges that imply unsupported certifications or guarantees.

Use actual provider identity and verified business information where relevant. Keep external payment handoffs understandable.

A polished badge row does not substitute for correct order and payment state.

## Test the complete journey

Use a safe route from product to bag to checkout and back. Check reload, correction and unavailable states where appropriate.

Inspect the merchant record after an authorised test submission; stop before submission when that is outside the test scope.

The visual review should be paired with functional verification rather than treated as proof of it.

## Retain the practical support route

If a customer cannot complete the process, provide a clear way to ask for help without implying that the order is already accepted. Keep private details out of public links and explain which reference is useful. Support access should remain recognisable even when the checkout uses a reduced navigation layout.

## Keep the design connected and calm

The customer is making a commitment, so clarity should increase as the flow progresses. Reduce irrelevant promotions and competing actions.

A consistent cart and checkout preserve the store's identity while making the selected items, amount and next step easier to understand. That is a stronger design result than simply applying the homepage's colours to a generic form.

title: Design honest empty, loading and unavailable states
description: Design clear empty, loading and unavailable storefront states without confusing missing content, slow data and genuine stock limitations.
body:
**Empty, loading and unavailable are different states and should not look like the same blank panel.** A customer needs to know whether to wait, choose another item or take a different action.

Treat these states as part of the storefront design from the beginning. They are not temporary developer screens that can be ignored after launch.

## Distinguish the causes

An empty bag contains no selected items. A loading bag is waiting for information. An unavailable service cannot currently provide the result.

Use language that matches the cause. “No products” is misleading when the catalogue failed to load.

The implementation must identify the state accurately; design cannot repair a false underlying classification.

## Give empty states a useful next step

An empty bag can link back to a relevant collection. A category without products can explain the situation and offer broader browsing.

Do not fill the space with invented products or unsupported restock promises.

Keep the action proportionate. The customer should understand the state without being forced into a promotional popup.

## Reserve layout during loading

Use stable space for images and key content so the page does not jump repeatedly as information arrives.

A placeholder should not resemble a purchasable product or a confirmed amount.

Do not show an old price as current merely to avoid an empty area while data is loading.

## Keep waiting feedback honest

If an operation is pending, explain that it is in progress without claiming success. Avoid endless animation with no route to understand a prolonged delay.

A retry may be appropriate for a read, but uncertain order or payment submissions require more care.

Do not invite repeated commitment actions before checking whether the original attempt was recorded.

## Explain unavailable products

Show whether an item or a particular option cannot currently be ordered. Preserve useful product information where appropriate.

Do not silently select a substitute. The customer should make any changed choice.

If the business offers a genuine enquiry or notification process, describe it accurately. Do not promise a feature that the store does not provide.

## Design service outages separately

A temporary inability to load the store should not appear as a permanently empty catalogue.

Use a concise explanation and a safe next step. Keep technical details and secrets out of public error text.

Avoid a fallback to fictional demo content that could be mistaken for the merchant's live range.

## Make controls match the state

A disabled action should be visibly and functionally disabled where appropriate, with an understandable reason. Do not rely only on a faded colour.

A retry action should indicate what it retries. A contact route should provide useful context without exposing private information.

Check keyboard access and focus behaviour as part of the implementation review.

## Keep brand treatment consistent

Use the store's typography, spacing and colour rules while preserving the message's clarity. An unavailable page should not look like an unrelated unfinished application.

At the same time, do not decorate an error so heavily that the explanation becomes hard to find.

The state should be calm, recognisable and useful.

## Test transitions

Move from loading to content, empty to populated and unavailable to recovered in a safe environment. Check that old messages and controls do not remain.

A screenshot of each state is not enough to prove the transition works.

Use representative content and a phone-sized view, including a focused field if the state occurs within checkout.

## Distinguish stale from confirmed information

If earlier data remains visible during a refresh, make sure the customer is not encouraged to rely on an amount or availability that the system cannot currently confirm. The appropriate treatment depends on the operation, but the interface should not disguise uncertainty simply to avoid a visual gap.

## Keep the state inventory

Record the expected message and action for the important states. Revisit it when integrations or workflows change.

A good fallback does not pretend the system succeeded. It tells the truth about what is known and helps the customer take the next safe step without losing the store's identity.

title: Decide whether a paid theme solves a demonstrated layout problem
description: Decide whether a paid theme solves a demonstrated layout problem by comparing real-content results, extra work and long-term maintenance.
body:
**A paid theme is worthwhile when it solves a real layout need better than the available alternatives.** Its price, popularity or polished demo does not establish that fit.

Begin with the problem and test the theme against it. Keep the same content in the comparison so the decision is about structure rather than photography quality.

## State the problem precisely

Examples include a product gallery that cannot show useful detail, a collection layout that obscures long names or a mobile header that consumes too much space.

Avoid a vague requirement such as make the shop luxurious. Translate the visual direction into specific choices and constraints.

A clear problem makes it possible to tell whether the theme actually helps.

## Check the current template first

Try ordinary configuration and content improvements before assuming replacement is necessary.

A better crop or clearer title can solve some problems without a new theme. A genuine structural limit may justify changing it.

Do not spend weeks forcing the current template beyond its reasonable capabilities, but obtain evidence before discarding it.

## Test the paid candidate with real content

Use the same products, images and wording. Include the awkward cases that exposed the original problem.

Inspect both desktop and phone layouts. A theme that solves the desktop gallery may create a difficult mobile selection area.

Do not approve from the supplier's demo alone.

## Identify what is actually included

Check whether the needed feature belongs to the theme or an additional app, custom modification or demo-only setup.

Read the current licence and support scope. Do not assume photographs or brand copy are included for reuse.

The complete arrangement may still be suitable, but its cost and dependencies should be explicit.

## Compare implementation effort

List content re-entry, configuration, custom work and testing needed for each option.

A paid theme can save development time if its standard structure fits. It can also create rework if the merchant's content does not suit it.

Use supplier estimates where necessary rather than inventing a time saving from the purchase price.

## Protect functional continuity

Check product options, bag behaviour, delivery information and the merchant record after any theme change.

A layout purchase does not prove those flows remain correct.

Keep a working version and an appropriate rollback process. Do not publish the new theme solely because the editor preview loads.

## Consider future edits

Try changing a product image, rearranging a section and updating a practical notice. Determine which work the merchant can perform.

If ordinary edits require technical help, include that arrangement in the decision.

The theme should support the business's maintenance capacity, not just the launch design.

## Separate appearance from performance claims

A clearer layout may be worth choosing without claiming a measured sales uplift. Do not repeat a vendor's conversion promise as your own result.

If you want to test a behavioural effect, design an appropriate experiment and keep other changes visible.

For the distinction, see [visual refresh versus conversion experiment](/blog/separate-a-visual-refresh-from-a-conversion-experiment/).

## Review update responsibility

Ask who applies future theme updates and how custom modifications are retained or rechecked. A purchase can solve today's layout problem while creating an ongoing maintenance obligation. Record that obligation before choosing, and keep the relevant custom changes documented. The merchant should know whether an update is a routine supported action or a piece of work requiring technical review and a safe test environment.

## Make the purchase evidence-based

Record the original problem, the candidate's demonstrated result and the remaining work. Compare the full cost with keeping or adapting the current template.

If the needed capability remains unverified, the theme has not yet justified the purchase.

The right paid theme is a useful component in a complete store, not a shortcut around content preparation and functional checking.

Retain the representative test cases after implementation. They help ensure that later updates preserve the specific improvement you paid to obtain, rather than gradually reintroducing the original problem.

title: Check theme support and update responsibilities before buying
description: Check theme support, update scope and customisation responsibilities before buying a storefront design that the business must maintain.
body:
**A theme purchase includes a particular product and support arrangement—not necessarily indefinite design labour.** Understand who keeps the theme compatible and who checks your custom changes before buying.

This is a practical procurement guide. Read the current licence and support terms for the specific theme rather than assuming all suppliers operate alike.

## Identify the supported product

Record the theme version, platform compatibility and included layouts. Ask whether the advertised demonstration uses additional tools.

Do not assume a feature shown in a screenshot belongs to the theme itself.

Keep the purchase and licence details with the business's records so a future maintainer can identify what was obtained.

## Read the support boundary

Determine whether support covers installation questions, defects, configuration or custom modifications. These are different services.

A supplier may reasonably exclude bespoke changes, but that boundary should be clear before you depend on them.

Do not treat a friendly pre-sale answer as a promise of unlimited future work.

## Ask about updates

Check how updates are delivered and whether access depends on a continuing subscription or licence condition.

Do not assume an update automatically applies safely to a customised store. Ask what the merchant or maintainer must do.

Keep a record of significant custom changes so the next version can be assessed against them.

## Separate custom code ownership

If a developer modifies the theme, identify where the changes are recorded and who maintains them. The original theme supplier may not support those modifications.

A small visual change can still affect several page states.

Require enough documentation for another authorised developer to understand the purpose and recheck it later.

## Test before publishing updates

Use the provider's supported preview or staging process where available. Check the important product, bag and checkout routes with real content.

Do not treat a successful installation message as proof that the store remains usable.

Keep an appropriate recovery plan and avoid changing the live store during an important campaign without considering the operational risk.

## Include content compatibility

An update may alter section settings, crop behaviour or text layout. Inspect long names, unavailable states and your actual photographs.

Do not review only the demo homepage after an update.

The theme's purpose is to present the merchant's content, so the acceptance set should contain that content.

## Check account and licence control

The business should know who owns the theme purchase and whether the licence can be used or transferred as intended.

Do not leave the only purchase record in a contractor's private account without understanding the consequences.

Use legitimate licences and obtain clarification for multiple stores or other non-standard use.

## Budget the ongoing work

Include the time or service cost of applying and checking updates. A low theme price does not necessarily imply low maintenance.

Conversely, do not assume a paid theme requires constant expensive work. Evaluate the actual arrangement and customisation level.

Keep routine maintenance separate from a future redesign.

## Prepare a support request well

When a problem occurs, provide the relevant version, affected page and safe reproduction steps. Avoid sharing secrets or unnecessary customer information.

Ask which supplier owns the issue if an app is involved.

A clear evidence record can reduce repeated explanation and make the support boundary easier to navigate.

## Check a discontinued-version scenario

Ask how the business is informed when an older version is no longer supported. Record the migration or update options without assuming a supplier will maintain every version indefinitely. Knowing this boundary helps you budget future work and avoids treating a one-time purchase as an unlimited compatibility promise.

## Buy with an ownership plan

Before purchase, know who installs, configures, updates and verifies the theme. Record what happens if that person becomes unavailable.

Choose a theme whose support and maintenance model fits the business, not only whose initial design is appealing.

The useful purchase remains understandable after launch. A storefront design is easier to trust when the next update has an owner and a check, rather than becoming a surprise project each time the platform changes.

title: Arrange a clothing product page around fit evidence
description: Arrange clothing product pages around measurements, garment views and option clarity so shoppers can assess fit without relying on styling alone.
body:
**A clothing page should make fit evidence easy to find.** Styling photographs can create interest, but shoppers also need to understand the garment's shape, measurements and selected option.

Build the page around the information you can verify. Do not promise that a size will fit every body or use vague labels as a substitute for measurements.

## Establish the garment identity

Show the product name, material description and the actual garment clearly. A layered outfit should not make it unclear which piece is for sale.

If accessories are styling props, distinguish them from included items.

Keep colour and variant names consistent between the image, selector and order summary.

## Choose useful views

Include views that explain silhouette, length and relevant construction details. The exact set depends on the garment.

Do not repeat several nearly identical aesthetic photographs while omitting the back or a feature that changes how the item is worn.

Use images you own or are authorised to use, and keep editing from misrepresenting the product.

## Place measurements near size selection

The size guide should be easy to reach at the moment the customer chooses a size. Explain the measurement method where necessary.

Distinguish garment measurements from body measurements. A number without that context can mislead.

Do not hide the guide in a general footer if it is essential to the buying decision.

## Use fit language carefully

Words such as relaxed or fitted can help, but they should accompany useful evidence rather than replace it.

If a model's measurements are provided, use verified information and appropriate permission. Do not invent a model height or worn size to complete the layout.

Avoid universal comfort or suitability claims that the business cannot substantiate.

## Keep options readable

Use clear size and colour labels with enough space on mobile. Show unavailable choices honestly.

Do not make a tiny colour swatch the only way to identify a variation.

When the selected option changes the image or price, keep those updates consistent and visible.

## Structure the description

Separate material, dimensions or fit, care information and delivery context using clear headings or another accessible structure.

Do not place essential fit facts inside a long brand story paragraph.

If expandable sections are used, label them clearly and check that the buyer can operate them with different input methods.

## Show relevant limitations

If the item is made to order, has a defined measurement tolerance or uses a material with specific care needs, explain the confirmed facts.

Do not add unsupported claims about stretch, shrink resistance or durability merely because they sound useful.

A clear limitation can prevent misunderstanding more effectively than a vague reassurance.

## Review the phone page

Inspect the size guide, selector and images on a narrow view. Long tables should remain usable through an appropriate responsive treatment.

Check a focused option or field with any sticky header present.

Do not judge the page only from a full-page image where the actual viewport interaction is hidden.

## Follow the selection into the bag

Confirm that the chosen size and colour remain visible after adding the item. The customer should be able to check the specification before commitment.

A beautiful product page is incomplete if the bag loses the selected identity.

Use a safe test and include an unavailable combination.

## Keep the size evidence current

When the garment pattern, supplier or specification changes, review the guide and the photographs together. A correct new description beside an old size chart can still mislead. Preserve the accepted specification for existing orders while updating future listings, rather than allowing today's product page to rewrite what an earlier customer selected.

## Review with a fit question

Ask someone to explain which measurements they would use and what remains uncertain. Do not coach them directly to the guide.

Record missing evidence rather than assuming every question is a customer's failure to read.

The strongest clothing page does not guarantee fit. It gives the shopper accurate, findable information with which to make a more informed choice.

title: Balance jewellery detail photography with readable buying information
description: Balance jewellery close-ups with scale, material and fastening information so a visually rich page still supports a clear buying decision.
body:
**Jewellery pages need both detail and context.** A close-up can reveal texture beautifully while leaving the buyer unable to judge size, fastening or what is included.

Design the page so visual interest leads into accurate specification, not away from it.

## Show the complete item

Begin with an image that makes the product identifiable. If the photograph contains a pair, set or styling combination, state the actual quantity sold.

Do not let a dramatic crop hide whether the listing is for one earring, a pair or several pieces.

Keep decorative props separate from the product promise.

## Add scale evidence

Provide measured dimensions and a useful scale view where appropriate. A close-up alone can make a small object appear much larger.

Do not rely on an unspecified hand or model as the only scale reference. The stated dimensions should remain available in text.

Use a measurement method the business can reproduce.

## Include the functional detail

Show the clasp, closure, back or attachment where it matters to the purchase. The buyer may need to understand how the item is worn.

A gallery full of front-facing beauty shots can miss this practical information.

Keep the image order purposeful: identification, detail, scale and relevant function rather than many near-duplicates.

## State materials accurately

Use verified material information and distinguish plating, base material or other relevant construction facts.

Do not add hypoallergenic, waterproof or similar claims without appropriate support. A polished design should not make an unsupported statement look authoritative.

If the supplier information is incomplete, resolve it before publishing a precise claim.

## Make variants understandable

If finishes or sizes differ, connect the option to the correct image and description. A colour label alone may not explain a material difference.

Show availability and the current selected price clearly.

Do not silently substitute another finish when the pictured one is unavailable.

## Keep text readable beside photography

A restrained type style can suit jewellery, but small pale text may make dimensions and care information difficult to read.

Use visual hierarchy to distinguish name, price, options and supporting details. Do not make every element compete with the close-up.

Check actual contrast and size rather than judging only the overall mood.

## Explain care with evidence

Provide the care instructions appropriate to the verified material and construction. Avoid copying generic advice that may not fit the item.

Keep important limitations easy to find before purchase.

Do not promise durability or permanent colour retention simply to make the care section sound reassuring.

## Inspect mobile crops

A wide desktop composition may crop the item differently on a phone. Check that the complete piece and useful detail remain available.

If enlargement is offered, test it with a real image. A zoom control does not help when the source lacks detail.

Balance file size and clarity without making an unsupported performance claim.

## Review the bag and order identity

A buyer selecting a particular finish or size should see it clearly in the bag. A small product photo should support, not replace, the text.

Use a safe test to confirm the option remains associated with the item.

The visual design should preserve the specification as the customer moves towards commitment.

## Check matching pieces and sets

If related jewellery is shown, make the relationship clear without implying it is included in the current price. A matching necklace can be a useful recommendation, but the buyer should not infer a complete set from the gallery alone. Keep the separate item's link, quantity and price understandable so the visual styling does not change the purchase promise.

## Ask a practical review question

Can a shopper tell the quantity, size, material and fastening without asking support? If not, identify the missing evidence.

Do not respond only by adding more decorative images.

A strong jewellery page lets the product feel considered while keeping the purchase concrete. Beauty draws attention; accurate scale and specification make that attention useful.

title: Design a gift catalogue around occasions without duplicating every product
description: Organise a gift catalogue around useful occasions while preserving one accurate product record and clear set contents.
body:
**Occasion-led navigation can help gift shoppers, but it should not create multiple conflicting versions of the same product.** Use collections and presentation to support discovery while keeping the underlying specification consistent.

A gift may suit several occasions without needing a separate price, stock record and description for each one.

## Choose occasions that reflect the range

Use groupings customers can understand and that the products genuinely support. Do not create dozens of thin occasion pages merely to fill navigation.

A useful collection should contain a coherent choice, not every item in the store under a different heading.

Keep seasonal groups current and remove or revise outdated promises.

## Preserve one product identity

Where the platform supports it, organise the same product into relevant collections rather than duplicating the listing unnecessarily.

Duplicated records can drift in price, images or stock. If separate products are genuinely required, document why and how availability is managed.

The customer should not encounter contradictory versions of the same gift depending on the route used.

## Make contents explicit

Gift photographs often include packaging and styling props. State what the buyer receives and the quantity of each component.

Do not rely on the image alone to define the set.

If a gift box, card or wrap is optional, show that distinction before the customer reaches checkout.

## Separate occasion from specification

A birthday collection label does not change the product's material, dimensions or contents. Keep those facts consistent.

If a seasonal edition genuinely differs, describe the difference and give it a clear identity.

Avoid changing only the title while silently using the same photograph for materially different contents.

## Support personalisation clearly

If the gift allows a name or message, explain the permitted input and any limits. Keep the selected wording visible before commitment.

Do not use an occasion page to imply customisation that the product does not offer.

For complex requests, provide an honest enquiry route rather than pretending every variation fits ordinary checkout.

## Treat dates carefully

A gift buyer may have an event deadline. Distinguish preparation time, dispatch and delivery estimates.

Do not use occasion urgency to imply guaranteed arrival without a supported commitment.

If the requested date needs review, say so before the customer assumes it has been accepted.

## Design collection cards for comparison

Show a useful image, name, price and the distinguishing feature needed to choose a product. Avoid covering the image with several competing badges.

If a set's price varies by selected contents, make the starting or selected amount clear.

The card should help the shopper choose what to inspect, not attempt to contain every detail.

## Keep recommendations honest

Labels such as best for a particular recipient should reflect a reasonable product fit, not an invented endorsement.

Avoid stereotypes that assume every person in a demographic wants the same gift.

Use practical filters or descriptions such as size, material or personalisation when they help more than broad recipient labels.

## Test the full route

Enter through an occasion collection, open a product and inspect the bag. Confirm that the product identity and chosen additions remain intact.

Check the same item through another collection and verify that its facts agree.

A navigation strategy is only useful if it leads to a consistent purchase.

## Review the empty occasion state

When the last suitable item sells out, decide whether the occasion page should show an honest unavailable state, a relevant alternative collection or be removed through the supported process. Do not automatically populate it with unrelated stock. The page's label still creates an expectation even when the original curated products are no longer available.

## Maintain seasonal content

Assign an owner to review dates, featured products and availability before each campaign. Do not leave expired delivery claims on a live collection.

Keep the catalogue structure reusable without preserving stale promises.

A good gift catalogue makes choosing easier through context while retaining one reliable account of what is actually being sold.

title: Show home-decor scale without making the page feel crowded
description: Show home-decor products with reliable scale, dimensions and setting images without overwhelming the page or implying accessories are included.
body:
**A home-decor page should help the buyer imagine the object in a space and understand its actual size.** Atmosphere and scale evidence need to work together.

A styled room photograph can inspire, but it should not replace dimensions or make the included product unclear.

## Establish the object first

Use an image that clearly identifies the item for sale. If the scene contains several objects, distinguish the listing from the surrounding styling.

State quantity and included components in text.

Do not let a decorative arrangement imply that plants, frames or accessories are included when they are not.

## Provide measured dimensions

Show the relevant height, width, depth or diameter with units. Explain any important measurement convention.

For handmade variation, describe only the tolerance the business can support.

Do not use a vague small or large label as the sole scale information.

## Use a setting image carefully

A room or surface view can help explain proportion and context. Keep perspective from exaggerating the apparent size.

Do not present a digitally placed object as an actual photograph of installation without appropriate disclosure.

The setting should support the product's meaning, not make an unsupported claim about how it fits every home.

## Add detail where it matters

Show texture, finish, attachment or underside details relevant to use. Choose angles that answer practical questions.

Avoid filling the gallery with several similar mood images while omitting the feature that determines placement or care.

A small number of purposeful images can be more informative than a long repetitive gallery.

## Keep material claims precise

Use verified descriptions for material, finish and intended use. Do not assume a decorative item is suitable outdoors, near heat or for food contact.

If the product has a relevant limitation, make it findable before purchase.

A design page should not turn an unverified supplier phrase into a safety promise.

## Arrange information in a clear sequence

Let the buyer identify the object, inspect dimensions, choose options and understand delivery or care. Use headings or another accessible structure.

Keep supporting story content from interrupting the practical route.

Do not make the page crowded by placing every fact beside the main image; distribute information while preserving easy access.

## Check variant imagery

If size or finish changes, connect the selected option with the correct information and image where available.

Do not imply that a photograph of a larger version represents the dimensions of a smaller selected item.

The current price and specification should remain consistent through the bag.

## Review mobile presentation

A wide room photograph may lose the product when cropped to a phone. Check the actual crop and provide a clearer view if necessary.

Long dimension rows should remain readable without forcing unrelated horizontal scrolling.

Do not shrink essential text to preserve a desktop composition.

## Explain delivery realistically

Bulky or fragile products may have special conditions. Use the confirmed fulfilment information rather than a generic reassurance.

If delivery needs a quote or local restriction, disclose that before commitment.

Do not let a styled page imply an ordinary shipping promise that the business cannot fulfil.

## Keep a neutral comparison view

Alongside the styled image, consider a straightforward view on a plain or restrained background. It can make the outline and finish easier to inspect without the visual competition of a room scene. This is not a requirement for every product, but it is a useful test when shoppers struggle to distinguish the object from its setting or understand where the product ends and the props begin.

## Test the buyer's understanding

Ask someone to identify the item, its dimensions and what is included. Note whether the setting image caused a mistaken assumption.

Correct the content or layout based on that observation.

A good home-decor page creates a sense of place without obscuring the physical product. The customer should leave with a clearer understanding of scale and specification, not merely an attractive room image in mind.

title: Create a coherent store palette without sacrificing text contrast
description: Build a storefront colour palette around consistent roles and readable text rather than applying brand colours indiscriminately to every surface.
body:
**A coherent palette assigns colours to roles.** It does not require every paragraph, button and background to use the most distinctive brand colour.

Choose combinations that preserve readable information and understandable states while retaining the brand's visual character.

## Start with functional roles

Define page background, primary text, secondary text, borders, main action and status colours. Keep the list small enough to apply consistently.

A single brand accent can appear in several places, but its meaning should not change unpredictably.

Do not use the same treatment for a primary action and an error if that makes the interface confusing.

## Test actual colour pairs

Contrast belongs to a foreground-and-background combination, not a colour in isolation. A gold that works as decoration may be unsuitable for small text on white.

W3C's WCAG 2.2 contrast guidance specifies at least 4.5:1 for ordinary text and 3:1 for qualifying large text, with defined exceptions. Check the actual use rather than assuming a palette is accessible because it looks dark enough. [W3C text contrast guidance](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/contrast-minimum.html).

This is one criterion, not certification of the complete store.

## Keep secondary text readable

Descriptions, delivery notes and form help are often styled more faintly than headings. They still contain information customers need.

Do not make important conditions nearly invisible to achieve a quiet visual mood.

Use size, spacing and hierarchy alongside colour to distinguish secondary information without sacrificing legibility.

## Separate decoration from meaning

A decorative accent can be subtle. A status such as unavailable or an error needs a clear non-colour explanation.

Do not rely on red versus green alone to communicate whether an option can be selected.

Labels and appropriate control states should carry the meaning even when colours are difficult to distinguish.

## Review buttons in every state

Check normal, hover where relevant, keyboard focus, disabled and loading states. A palette that works for the idle button may fail when the background changes.

The selected or focused state should remain visible against nearby surfaces.

Do not assume the template's default state colours remain suitable after changing the brand accent.

## Inspect images with overlaid text

A readable pair on a plain background does not guarantee readable text over a changing photograph.

Test the actual image crops on different screen sizes. Consider a controlled text panel when the photograph creates unpredictable contrast.

Do not force the image to accommodate text at the expense of showing the product accurately.

## Keep page families connected

Apply the role system across home, collection, product, bag and checkout. Avoid a generic cart palette that abruptly breaks the storefront identity.

At the same time, preserve the clarity of totals, errors and required actions. Brand expression should not obscure the commitment stage.

Document the roles so later pages do not invent slightly different colours for the same purpose.

## Check real content

Use long descriptions, small labels and genuine prices. A mood board with a few large words does not test the typography customers will read.

Inspect the page at ordinary viewing sizes and with relevant accessibility checks.

Do not claim a universal emotional response or conversion increase from a particular colour. The practical goal is consistent, usable presentation.

## Maintain the palette deliberately

When a colour changes, recheck its combinations and states rather than updating only the homepage screenshot.

Keep the approved values and their roles in a simple reference for the implementer.

A strong palette gives the store a recognisable character while leaving the information easy to use. Visual restraint and accessibility are not opposing goals; they require deliberate combinations rather than indiscriminate use of a fashionable shade.

## Test an ordinary maintenance change

Before freezing the palette, replace a product photograph with a much darker image and enter a longer category name. Check whether text still has a dependable background and whether labels remain readable. Then change the merchant accent to another plausible brand colour. If every change requires repairing individual buttons, the palette needs clearer functional roles. Document which colours are decorative and which are permitted for text, borders and controls so future edits do not silently undo the checks.

title: Choose storefront typography for prices, options and long descriptions
description: Choose storefront typography by testing prices, option labels and long descriptions across devices, not only the hero headline.
body:
**A storefront type system must work for a price, a size selector and a long description—not only a large brand heading.** Choose fonts through the text customers actually need to read.

A distinctive display face can be useful, but it should not make ordinary buying information harder to understand.

## Define the text roles

Separate brand display, headings, body copy, labels and prices. You may use one family for several roles if it works well.

Avoid adding a new font for every section. Too many unrelated treatments can weaken hierarchy and increase maintenance.

The roles should explain how the type is used, not merely list font names.

## Test a realistic sample

Use a long product name, a paragraph of care information, a price with paise, an unavailable label and a form instruction.

Include the characters and languages the store actually needs. Check that the selected font supports them rather than falling back unpredictably.

A short English slogan cannot reveal all of these problems.

## Inspect numerical clarity

Prices, quantities and dimensions need distinguishable digits and punctuation. Check whether the currency symbol and decimal amount remain clear at the actual size.

Do not round a meaningful amount merely because the font makes the line awkward.

Use consistent formatting across product cards, bag and checkout so the customer can compare amounts confidently.

## Keep body text comfortable

Choose a readable size, line spacing and line length for descriptions. Avoid dense blocks stretched across a very wide screen.

On mobile, check that the text does not become cramped or require unnecessary horizontal scrolling.

Do not treat a visually delicate style as a reason to make essential product information tiny.

## Use hierarchy rather than decoration

A heading should indicate the section's role and relationship. Meaningful heading structure matters beyond visual size; W3C explains how organised headings and regions support navigation. [W3C page-structure guidance](https://www.w3.org/WAI/tutorials/page-structure/).

Do not choose heading levels solely to obtain a preferred font size.

The implementation should preserve structure while the style expresses the brand.

## Check option labels

A decorative face may make short controls difficult to scan, especially with several similar choices.

Use actual size, finish and colour names. Inspect selected, unavailable and focused states.

If the brand font is unsuitable for controls, a simpler companion style can preserve usability without abandoning the identity.

## Review loading and fallback

Ask the implementer to check what appears before a web font is available and whether the layout shifts significantly when it loads.

The page should remain readable if the custom font fails.

Do not make essential text an image merely to guarantee the exact appearance of a typeface.

## Verify licensing and delivery

Use fonts with appropriate permission for the intended web use. Keep the source and licence record with the project.

Do not assume a font available on a designer's computer can automatically be embedded in the website.

Include the practical delivery and performance implications in implementation, without inventing a universal speed claim.

## Compare on real screens

Review the chosen system on a phone and a wider display, with representative content and relevant zoom settings.

A static brand presentation can look excellent while the live form labels wrap poorly.

Record the problem in terms of readability or layout rather than a vague preference.

## Keep the system small and documented

Specify which style applies to each role and how it behaves responsively. Reuse those rules across the storefront.

A good type system makes the brand recognisable while letting prices, options and descriptions remain ordinary to read. The headline should not be the only text that receives design attention.

## Include a content-editing example

Ask the person who maintains products to enter one long name, one short name and a description with a small list. They should not need to insert manual line breaks to make the page look right. Test the same entries in search results and the bag, where space is tighter. Record any length guidance as an editorial recommendation, not permission to omit essential product information. A type system is useful when ordinary catalogue edits remain readable without a designer repairing each page.

title: Keep category tiles useful when category photographs are missing
description: Use an appropriate product photograph as a category-image fallback while preserving accurate category labels, counts and destinations.
body:
**A category does not need a separate photoshoot to have a useful tile.** When no category image exists, a suitable product photograph from that category can represent it honestly.

The fallback needs a clear selection rule and a truthful result. It should not change the category's meaning or pretend that one pictured item represents every possible product.

## Prefer a deliberate category image when available

If the merchant has selected a valid category photograph, use it according to the design. It may have been chosen to represent the range more broadly than a single item.

Do not replace an intentional image unpredictably with whichever product happens to load first.

Keep the image ownership and right to publish clear.

## Choose within the same category

When falling back to a product, select from products actually belonging to that category. Do not borrow a visually attractive image from an unrelated range.

The category label and destination should remain the authoritative context.

A jewellery tile showing a home-decor item may make the grid look complete while making navigation less trustworthy.

## Make the selection repeatable

Use a stable rule rather than a random result on every visit. The exact rule can depend on the data and business preference.

For example, a curated eligible product can be preferable to an arbitrary newest item when the newest uploads include test or incomplete content.

Record the rule so the merchant understands why the tile changes when the source item changes.

## Define image eligibility

Check that the image exists, is usable and represents a legitimate product. Avoid broken links, internal screenshots or placeholder test assets.

If availability matters to the selection rule, define it explicitly. Do not imply the tile guarantees that the pictured product is currently purchasable unless the page supports that claim.

A category image is navigation, not a reservation of stock.

## Preserve the category information

Keep the title, product count and link independent of the fallback image. Replacing the photograph should not accidentally change the destination.

Use the real count if a count is shown. Do not derive it from the small set considered for image selection.

Test the tile after the data change, not only the image file in isolation.

## Handle no eligible image honestly

If no appropriate image is available, use a reserved, clearly designed state or a text-led tile. Do not fill the gap with a false product photo.

Keep the category usable where it still has a meaningful destination.

An intentional empty state is better than a broken image icon or an unrelated stock photograph.

## Check the crop

A product image suitable for a detail page may need a different crop in a category tile. Inspect tall, wide and close-up images.

Do not cut away the feature that makes the product recognisable. Consider containment or a different eligible image where necessary.

Review the phone crop as well as the desktop grid.

## Make the linked tile understandable

Use a clear category name and appropriate accessible treatment for the linked image. The text alternative should suit its function and context, not repeat an unrelated detailed product description.

Keep the label visible rather than relying on the photo alone.

Do not claim the entire grid is accessible from one image fallback check.

## Test changes over time

Remove or replace the selected image in a safe test and confirm the next state remains coherent. Check what happens when the source product leaves the category.

The fallback should fail honestly rather than showing stale or foreign content.

A stable selection rule reduces surprises, but it still needs maintenance when the catalogue changes.

## Use the fallback as a practical content rule

Document the precedence: deliberate category image, suitable same-category product image, then an honest no-image state.

This lets a small merchant build useful navigation without commissioning separate category photography, while preserving the accuracy of the catalogue and the integrity of the design.

title: Build a footer that answers practical shopping questions
description: Build a storefront footer around useful shopping, policy and contact routes rather than a dense collection of decorative or outdated links.
body:
**A footer should help a shopper resolve practical questions and continue navigating.** It is not a storage area for every page the business has ever created.

Choose links and information that remain accurate, useful and maintainable. A visually full footer is not valuable when its destinations are missing or misleading.

## Identify the likely end-of-page questions

A visitor may want delivery information, returns guidance, contact details or a route back to the catalogue.

List those tasks before selecting column headings.

Do not organise the footer solely around internal departments or decorative brand language that a customer cannot interpret.

## Group related destinations

Keep shopping, practical information and business identity in understandable groups. Use labels that describe the destination.

A small store may need fewer columns than a large template demo. Do not invent links to fill the structure.

On mobile, ensure the grouping remains clear when columns stack or collapse.

## Verify every destination

Open each link and confirm that it contains the promised information. A policy label leading to a placeholder is not a completed footer.

Do not link to routes that exist only in a design file.

If content is not ready, resolve the content gap rather than hiding it behind a professional-looking label.

## Use accurate contact information

Provide the support route the business actually monitors. State response expectations only when the business can support them.

Avoid publishing private personal details unnecessarily.

If a contact form is used, check its error and success behaviour through an authorised test, not merely its appearance.

## Keep policy wording separate from decoration

The footer should make relevant policy pages reachable, but the policy content needs its own factual and legal review.

Do not copy another store's policy to complete the design. Its products, fulfilment and obligations may differ.

This article concerns information architecture, not the legal adequacy of particular terms.

## Include genuine business identity

Use the actual merchant name and appropriate public details. Do not leave fictional template copy or a demo brand in the footer.

A short description can help, but it should say something true about the business.

Avoid unsupported trust claims or certification marks used only to fill space.

## Treat newsletter forms carefully

If a signup is present, explain its purpose and use a real supported process. Do not include a non-functional form purely for visual balance.

Keep consent and data handling appropriate to the actual use.

A footer signup should not obscure essential support or policy links, especially on a narrow screen.

## Review visual hierarchy

Make links readable and distinguish group headings from clickable items. Check contrast on dark backgrounds and focused states for keyboard users.

Do not reduce important text to a faint decorative texture.

The footer can be quieter than the main content without becoming difficult to use.

## Remove stale campaign links

Seasonal collections and old announcements can remain in the footer long after they stop being relevant. Assign an owner to review them.

Keep stable product or collection routes where useful, and handle retired destinations through the supported site process.

A broken footer link can undermine confidence even when the main product page works.

## Test a practical task

Ask someone to find delivery information or contact support from the bottom of a product page. Observe whether the label and destination make sense.

Do not coach them through the intended column.

A good footer is a dependable final navigation layer. It answers ordinary questions with accurate routes and gives the customer somewhere useful to go next, rather than ending the page with a dense block of decorative links.

## Run a footer-only support exercise

Ask someone unfamiliar with the store to find delivery information and the correct contact route using only the footer. Note the destination they choose and whether it answers the question. This is a small usability check, not a claim about conversion. If two labels lead to the same vague page, simplify them. If an important destination does not exist, create accurate content or remove the link rather than presenting an empty page as completed support.

title: Use real trust information instead of decorative assurance badges
description: Use verifiable business, delivery and payment information as trust cues instead of adding unsupported badges to a storefront.
body:
**Trust information should describe something the business can substantiate.** A decorative badge can look reassuring while implying a certification, guarantee or process that does not exist.

Choose specific, accurate facts and place them where they answer a customer's question.

## Identify the uncertainty

A shopper may want to know who sells the product, how delivery works, which payment route is used or how to ask for help.

Start with those questions rather than a generic row of shield icons.

The useful cue is one that reduces a real uncertainty with evidence.

## Use merchant identity accurately

Show the correct business name and an appropriate contact route. Keep them consistent across product, checkout and support pages.

Do not leave a demo brand or fictional address in a template.

Avoid publishing unnecessary private information simply to make the business appear more substantial.

## State delivery facts precisely

Use confirmed charges, service areas and timing language. Distinguish preparation from transit and estimates from guarantees.

Do not add a guaranteed-delivery badge unless the exact promise is supported and its conditions are clear.

A plain sentence linked to complete information can be more useful than a broad icon label.

## Describe payment without overclaiming

Use the actual provider identity and supported payment process where appropriate. Do not invent certification marks or imply that a decorative lock establishes security.

Payment confirmation should come from the real system state, not from a reassuring animation.

For technical or compliance claims, obtain the appropriate verification rather than treating this design guide as authority.

## Keep reviews genuine

Display feedback with appropriate permission and context. Do not fabricate reviews or change their meaning to fit a polished layout.

A testimonial about service is not necessarily a verified review of a specific product.

If there is no feedback yet, use an honest state or omit the section deliberately.

## Support material and quality claims

Statements about origin, materials, durability or suitability need evidence. Do not add handcrafted or premium labels automatically to every product.

Be specific about what is known. A measured dimension or verified material can be more informative than a broad quality badge.

If supplier information is incomplete, resolve it before making a precise public claim.

## Place information near the decision

A delivery condition may belong near checkout; a material fact belongs on the product page. Do not put all trust information in a footer and assume it answers every question.

Keep the amount of information proportionate to the task.

Repeated badges across every section can create noise without adding credibility.

## Link to meaningful detail

Where a short statement needs explanation, provide a working destination with the relevant information.

Do not link a badge to an empty page or generic marketing copy.

The supporting content should match the claim and remain current as the business changes.

## Review the visual treatment

Make the text readable and avoid symbols that resemble third-party certifications without authorisation.

Use consistent styling, but do not let design imply more certainty than the words support.

A restrained factual row is often clearer than an elaborate collection of seals.

## Maintain the evidence

Keep a simple record of who supplied each important fact and when it was last checked. Assign an owner to update changing delivery or support information.

Remove a claim when it is no longer true rather than leaving it because the layout needs a badge.

A trustworthy store does not need to look crowded with assurances. It needs accurate identity, clear promises and a buying process whose visible state matches what the business will actually do.

## Replace a badge with a concrete sentence

Consider a hypothetical gift shop displaying an unsupported instant-dispatch seal. If the real process requires two working days for packing, replace the seal with that preparation information and explain how the delivery estimate is calculated. Check the same statement on product and checkout pages. This change may look less dramatic, but it gives the customer a usable expectation. Keep a dated note of the operational source so a future designer does not restore the old claim from a saved screenshot.

title: Create an inspiration board without copying another store
description: Build a useful storefront inspiration board by recording design principles, content needs and constraints without copying another brand's work.
body:
**An inspiration board should help you explain a direction, not supply a store to reproduce.** Save references because they demonstrate a useful decision: readable product information, a clear category structure or a calm way to present a large photograph.

Then translate that decision into your own content and customer journey. Changing a logo on someone else's composition is not a substitute for that work.

## Begin with the problem

Write down three things your current store makes difficult. Perhaps shoppers cannot compare sizes, categories feel indistinguishable or the homepage hides available products.

Look for references that address those problems. A spectacular animation is less relevant if the urgent task is helping a customer choose the correct option.

Keep the board focused enough that another person can understand why each reference belongs.

## Annotate every reference

For each saved page, record its source, the date viewed and the specific feature you noticed. Separate observation from inference.

You can observe that a product title appears above the price. You cannot infer that the arrangement increased sales without evidence.

An annotation such as “the category label stays readable over different photographs” gives the designer something useful to investigate. “Make ours like this” leaves too much unexplained.

## Separate principles from assets

A reference may illustrate generous spacing, but that does not make its photographs, illustrations or wording available for your use.

Use your own materials or assets with suitable permission. Keep licence and attribution requirements with the files rather than relying on the fact that an image was publicly accessible.

If rights are uncertain, use a clearly labelled internal placeholder during exploration and resolve the asset before publication.

## Compare several approaches

Collect different solutions to the same problem. One store may use a compact category list; another may use photographed tiles.

Compare what each requires. Tiles need useful images and space. A list can accommodate longer names but may provide less visual context.

Do not assemble every attractive feature into one page. A board is valuable when it helps you choose between alternatives, not when it encourages an overloaded layout.

## Test against your own catalogue

Put three real products beside the references: a short name, a long name and an item with several choices. Include genuine prices and ordinary photographs.

Ask whether the admired layout can handle them without hiding important information.

A design that depends on uniformly short names and studio photography may need substantial adaptation for a handmade catalogue. Identify that early instead of discovering it after the homepage is approved.

## Define what should feel different

Describe your own direction in concrete terms. For example, a crochet shop might want close-up material detail, visible preparation times and space for colour choices.

Those requirements are more actionable than borrowing another brand's personality.

Keep the business's real identity in the brief. Do not invent a heritage story or luxury claim simply because the references use them.

## Sketch before polishing

Make a simple arrangement of sections using your own labels and content. It can be a rough drawing or plain boxes.

Explain what each section helps a shopper do and where its main link goes. Remove a section that exists only because it appeared in a reference.

This step exposes dependence on someone else's page order before time is spent on polished graphics.

## Add constraints to the board

Record mobile needs, available assets, editing responsibilities and important commerce states. Include sold-out products, missing photographs and longer delivery explanations.

If the team cannot maintain a weekly editorial feature, do not make it the centre of the design.

Constraints are not a reduction in ambition. They help produce a design that remains useful after launch.

## End with decisions, not a collage

Create a short summary of what to adopt, what to adapt and what to avoid. Link each decision to a customer task or content requirement.

Keep the source references for internal traceability, but write the final brief in original language.

The finished board should enable an independent design. Someone should be able to explain the resulting store through its own products, information and buying journey without pointing to a competitor as the reason for every choice.

## Use a final independence check

Hide the reference screenshots and review your sketch with the merchant's actual content. Can the team explain every major section without reconstructing the reference from memory? If not, return to the customer task and explore another arrangement. The aim is not to make borrowed work harder to recognise. It is to create a genuinely appropriate solution whose assets, copy and decisions belong to this business.

title: Turn a visual reference into a testable design brief
description: Turn storefront visual references into a practical brief with real content, required states, mobile checks and clear acceptance criteria.
body:
**A visual reference becomes useful when you explain what it must accomplish.** A screenshot cannot tell a designer how your stock behaves, which delivery information matters or what happens when a photograph is missing.

Translate the reference into requirements that can be demonstrated with your real catalogue. This prevents a polished mock-up from being mistaken for a finished buying experience.

## State the customer task first

Describe the person’s immediate purpose without inventing a demographic profile. They may be choosing a gift within a budget or checking whether a garment is available in their size.

Write the action they should complete and the information they need before doing it.

This gives the designer a basis for decisions beyond visual resemblance.

## Name the reference's useful quality

Be precise about what attracted you. Was it readable navigation, a clear product comparison or the relationship between a photograph and its description?

Do not request an entire page simply because one detail works well.

Record the reference as inspiration, then express the requirement independently. “Keep the category name readable on every tile” is testable; “give it the same premium feel” is not.

## Supply representative content

Provide a small but demanding set of real products. Include a long title, an ordinary photograph, several variants and an unavailable item.

Add the actual delivery explanation and merchant contact information. Mark unknown facts instead of filling gaps with invented copy.

The layout should be evaluated with material that resembles the live store, not only with ideal samples selected to fit the design.

## Describe the required states

For each important component, list what happens when content is present, absent, loading or unavailable.

A product card may need a price range, a sold-out state and an image fallback. A button may need a pending state and a clear failure message.

Ask which information remains visible in each state. A brief that covers only the perfect screen leaves the difficult decisions until implementation.

## Specify the full route

Outline the journey from landing page to collection, product, bag and checkout. Include direct entry from a shared product link.

Name the intended destination of each major action. A homepage button should not lead to a generic page simply because the visual reference did.

Keep the same product identity and selected options understandable as the customer moves between pages.

## Make mobile requirements concrete

Use real narrow-screen content rather than requesting a small version of the desktop screenshot.

Check long titles, option controls, keyboard use and the position of important messages. Specify that information must remain available without horizontal page overflow.

Do not rely on one ideal device screenshot as evidence for every viewport. Include the widths and interactions the team will actually inspect.

## Separate behaviour from appearance

Write visual requirements and functional requirements in different lines. A dark button is a visual choice; preventing a second submission while the first is pending is behaviour.

Both matter, but a screenshot proves only a limited part of either.

This separation also makes it easier to identify who must supply an answer when a design decision depends on the underlying platform.

## Define observable acceptance checks

Use statements that someone can demonstrate: the long product title remains readable; the missing image does not remove the product link; a selected size remains visible in the bag.

Avoid promises such as “the design will increase conversion” unless a separate measurement plan supports that claim.

A small usability session can reveal confusion, but its observations should not be presented as statistically established sales results.

## Identify exclusions and ownership

List assets still required, content awaiting confirmation and platform limitations. Name the person responsible for each unresolved item.

Distinguish a design limitation from an approved omission. If the store needs a returns page but no content exists, the brief should retain that dependency rather than silently dropping the link.

Keep a dated version so later changes can be understood.

## Close with a demonstration script

Write a short sequence using one real product: arrive from the homepage, choose an option, add it to the bag, edit quantity and read delivery information.

Add an unavailable-product check and a return to the previous page. The designer and implementer can use the same sequence when presenting their work.

The strongest brief is not the longest. It connects the visual direction to actual content, ordinary failures and a buying task that can be demonstrated without guessing what “finished” means.

## Keep revisions traceable

When a requirement changes, record the reason and the affected checks. Replacing a large hero with a compact introduction may be sensible, but the change should not accidentally remove the route to a key collection. Review the consequence for the customer task rather than debating the screenshot alone.

title: Prepare the content a store designer needs before layout work
description: Prepare merchant facts, product examples, photographs and page content before store design so layouts do not depend on invented copy.
body:
**A designer needs more than a logo and a colour preference.** Real product names, photographs, delivery information and support content determine whether a storefront layout can work outside a demonstration.

Prepare a compact content pack before detailed layout work. It does not need to contain perfect prose, but it should distinguish confirmed facts from missing information.

## Start with the business identity

Provide the name customers should see, the preferred contact route and the language the merchant normally uses.
