Include approved logo files where available. State whether a text wordmark is acceptable if a suitable logo file does not exist.

Do not add fictional credentials or a made-up founding story to make the design feel complete. Mark those sections as unavailable until the merchant supplies accurate material.

## Select demanding product examples

Choose products that expose real layout needs. Include a long name, several sizes or colours, a product with no image and an item with a preparation period.

Supply actual descriptions, prices and option labels. Keep internal notes separate from public copy.

A collection of only short names and beautiful photographs creates a misleading test. Ordinary catalogue content is what the design must support every day.

## Organise the image files

Name each image so its product or purpose is clear. Identify the primary photograph, detail views and any restrictions on use.

Record who supplied the asset and whether permission has been confirmed. A downloaded reference image is not automatically a usable store photograph.

Keep original files as well as working copies. Explain important crop details, such as a clasp or embroidery that must remain visible.

## Explain categories in plain language

List the current category names and the products that belong to them. Note categories with overlapping meaning or unusually long labels.

If category photographs do not exist, state the intended fallback: a suitable product image from that category or an honest reserved image area.

The designer should not have to invent category relationships merely to fill a grid.

## Supply delivery and availability facts

Separate preparation time, dispatch and transit estimates. Include known service-area limits and how charges are determined.

Describe made-to-order and ready-stock products separately where the distinction matters.

Do not ask the designer to turn an uncertain operational process into a confident guarantee. Accurate wording can be refined, but the underlying fact must come from the business.

## Prepare customer-help content

Collect the questions customers repeatedly ask before buying. These might concern measurements, personalisation, care or what happens after an order request.

Provide the current answer and an owner who can confirm it. Keep policy wording subject to the appropriate business or professional review when needed.

A design team can make information easier to find; it should not invent the merchant's obligations.

## Decide what the homepage can honestly contain

Identify available hero copy, featured products, category links and genuine feedback. Explain why a featured selection is being used.

If there is no brand story or customer review, record that clearly. Do not populate the layout with fabricated testimonials.

The decision to retain an honest empty state or omit a section should be deliberate and consistent with the design brief.

## Include content length variation

Supply both concise and detailed examples. A short product explanation may fit one screen; a care guide needs paragraphs and lists.

Check the longest plausible navigation label and contact text. Include actual currency formatting and option names.

This lets the designer create flexible components rather than pages that only work with a particular sentence length.

## Assign maintenance ownership

For every content group, name who can update it and how often it changes. Prices and stock may update frequently; a business introduction may change rarely.

Explain whether the merchant will edit through a content system or request changes from someone else.

Do not centre the design on a demanding editorial schedule the business cannot maintain.

## Deliver a usable pack

Create a simple index linking to product examples, images, business facts and page copy. Mark each item confirmed, draft or missing.

Avoid sending several contradictory versions without identifying the current one.

Before handover, ask someone outside the preparation process to find one product photograph and its approved description. If that takes a long search, simplify the pack.

Good content preparation makes design decisions faster because the team is solving the real storefront, not repeatedly replacing invented demonstration material.

## Keep private material separate

The design pack should not contain customer records, passwords or payment credentials. Use synthetic examples where a layout needs an order number or address. Public merchant content and operational access are different things; keeping them separate makes collaboration safer without depriving the designer of useful examples.

title: Review design handover files before the project ends
description: Check storefront handover files, access, asset permissions and editing instructions before a design project ends.
body:
**A store-design handover should leave the merchant able to operate the result.** A folder of polished screenshots is not enough if nobody knows where the editable files are, which assets are licensed or how to correct a product description.

Review the handover against the agreed scope before the project ends. Separate delivered design work from hosting, content and ongoing maintenance responsibilities.

## Match files to the agreed deliverables

Start with the project brief. List the pages, components, responsive layouts and states that were promised.

Check that the handover contains the final versions rather than a mixture of experiments with similar names. Ask for a short index explaining which file is current.

If a deliverable changed during the project, record the agreed replacement. Do not assume an omitted page was intentionally removed.

## Confirm ownership and access

Identify which accounts belong to the business and who can administer them. Use the platform's appropriate access roles instead of exchanging passwords in a document.

Check that the merchant can reach the files and editing tools independently. A link that only works for the designer is not a completed transfer.

Access changes should be planned carefully so ongoing services are not accidentally interrupted.

## Check editable sources

Confirm whether the agreement includes editable design files, component definitions and original asset files.

Open a representative file and make a harmless copy for an editing exercise. Check whether text, colours and images can be changed as expected.

A flattened image may be appropriate for a reference export, but it does not replace an editable source when that was part of the scope.

## Keep asset permissions with the assets

Request a clear record of fonts, photographs, icons and other third-party materials used in the final design. Identify applicable licences and any continuing subscription requirements.

Do not assume that a designer's personal account transfers rights to the merchant. Resolve uncertainty with the relevant provider or agreement.

Keep this information alongside the handover so a future redesign does not accidentally reuse an asset outside its permitted use.

## Review normal and difficult states

Look beyond the homepage. Include product options, unavailable stock, an empty bag, missing photographs and long content.

Confirm which states were designed and which depend on implementation. A static design file does not prove that checkout behaviour works.

Record remaining functional checks separately rather than signing them off because the screen looks correct.

## Practise a routine content change

Use a safe draft or staging environment to update one product title, replace a photograph and edit a delivery sentence.

The person responsible for maintenance should be able to complete the task using the supplied instructions. Note where they become stuck.

This exercise is more informative than receiving a long manual that has never been followed by its intended reader.

## Document the design rules

Ask for concise guidance on type roles, colours, spacing, image ratios and common components. Include examples of what not to change casually.

Explain how a new product or category should fit the existing system.

The aim is consistency during ordinary maintenance, not a document so elaborate that nobody consults it.

## Separate design from service operation

Identify responsibility for hosting, renewals, backups, security updates and payment settings. Some may sit outside the design contract entirely.

Record the responsible person and where the process is documented. Do not leave the merchant assuming a one-time design fee includes indefinite technical support.

Avoid placing credentials in the handover pack; provide secure access through the appropriate mechanism.

## Agree how remaining defects are handled

Create a finite list of unresolved issues with examples and owners. Distinguish an agreed correction from a new feature request.

State the support period and contact method according to the actual agreement, not an assumed industry standard.

Keep evidence of the final delivered state so future changes can be distinguished from original defects.

## Close with an independent opening test

From the merchant's account, open the final files, locate an asset, find the maintenance instructions and identify the person responsible for a technical problem.

Then verify that a future editor can understand the same structure without the original designer explaining it live.

A useful handover is not merely a transfer of files. It is a transfer of enough knowledge and access for the business to maintain the design responsibly.

## Archive without losing the current version

Keep older experiments separate from the final package. Preserve a dated copy of the accepted files before routine editing begins. This makes recovery and comparison easier without encouraging the team to publish an outdated mock-up by mistake.

title: Design a campaign landing page that keeps the advertised promise
description: Design a campaign landing page that matches the offer, shows relevant products and explains conditions without misleading shoppers.
body:
**A campaign landing page should deliver the promise that brought the visitor there.** If an advertisement features a particular gift range, the destination should make that range easy to find rather than opening a general homepage with unrelated products.

Start with the offer and the customer's next decision. Use the design to clarify them, not to hide conditions behind a dramatic presentation.

## Write down the exact promise

Collect the advertisement, message or social post that links to the page. Identify the product, price claim, timing and intended action.

Make sure the landing page uses compatible wording. A broad “shop now” advertisement and a personalised-order enquiry may need different destinations.

Do not improve the offer in the page copy unless the business can actually honour the stronger promise.

## Choose a single primary task

Decide whether the visitor should browse a collection, choose one product or submit an enquiry.

Keep other navigation available where useful, but do not give every possible action equal emphasis. The page should help the visitor understand what to do next.

A single primary task does not mean removing essential product, delivery or merchant information.

## Show relevant products early

Use the products named or clearly implied by the campaign. Check that the photographs and descriptions represent the available items.

If the campaign covers a category, provide a meaningful route to that category rather than a decorative grid with unrelated links.

Do not substitute a more expensive product without explaining the difference. Relevance matters more than filling a fixed number of tiles.

## Keep price conditions visible

Explain the basis of a starting price, bundle or discount near the claim. Clarify whether options change the total.

Use the actual store pricing process and check that the destination product agrees with the landing page.

Examples and promotional copy should not imply a saving that cannot be demonstrated. If an offer has ended, update the page and the traffic source rather than leaving an attractive but unavailable promise.

## Explain timing honestly

Separate order deadlines, preparation time and delivery estimates. If the campaign is seasonal, make clear what the stated date refers to.

Avoid a countdown that resets simply to create urgency. Use a deadline only when it corresponds to a real business condition.

For made-to-order products, explain the information the customer must provide before preparation can begin.

## Build for the arrival device

Open the destination from the actual campaign link on a narrow screen. Check the first visible content, image loading and the primary action.

A visitor should not have to dismiss several overlays before discovering the advertised product.

Inspect long titles and option controls as well as the hero. The experience after the first tap is part of the campaign, not a separate concern.

## Support the decision with specific facts

Include the measurements, materials, personalisation limits or care information relevant to the products.

Use genuine feedback only with suitable permission and context. Do not manufacture a testimonial to complete the template.

Keep supporting content proportionate. A small campaign page can still answer the important questions without reproducing the entire store.

## Plan the unavailable state

Decide what happens when a featured item sells out. Show the real availability and offer a clearly described alternative where appropriate.

Do not continue presenting an unavailable item as immediately purchasable because the advertisement is still running.

Assign someone to review the campaign while it is active. A correct page at launch can become misleading when stock or timing changes.

## Measure the route, not just page visits

Choose a small set of observable events, such as opening a product or beginning the intended enquiry. Define them consistently before evaluating results.

Use the analytics and consent arrangements appropriate to the site. Do not collect unnecessary personal information merely to make the report look detailed.

A high visit count alone does not show that the offer is understood or that orders are profitable.

## Prepare the end of the campaign

Record when the offer should be reviewed, who updates the copy and where the link should lead afterwards.

Keep useful information accessible where possible, but remove expired claims. Check old social links and email links before replacing the destination.

The page succeeds when the shopper can follow a clear line from the original promise to the real product and its conditions. Visual impact should strengthen that line, not replace it.

## Run one final promise check

Ask a colleague to read only the advertisement and state what they expect to receive. Then let them use the page without explanation. Compare their expectation with the actual product, price and delivery information. Treat any mismatch as a concrete correction to the message or destination, not as evidence that the visitor needs more persuasion.
